question.source_text: 13. The length of a rectangle is (x + 9) cm and its width is (x − 4) cm. If the area of the rectangle is 77 cm², calculate the value(s) of x.
question.display_policy: Render verified structured mathematics when available; always retain the linked source visual for fidelity.
question.question_restated: The length of a rectangle is (x + 9) cm and its width is (x − 4) cm. The area is 77 cm². Calculate the value(s) of x.

app_sections.think_first: Area of a rectangle is length × width, so multiply the two expressions and set the product equal to 77.
app_sections.strategy: Form the equation (x + 9)(x − 4) = 77, expand and rearrange, solve with the formula, then discard any root that makes a side length negative.

guided_solution.instruction: Write the area as a product and set it equal to 77.
Expand the brackets.
Rearrange into standard form.
Apply the quadratic formula.
Evaluate both roots and reject the one that gives negative side lengths.
guided_solution.note: x ≈ 8.42 or x ≈ −13.42; if x ≈ −13.42 then x − 4 is negative, which is impossible for a width

app_sections.final_answer: x = (−5 + √477)/2 ≈ 8.42 (2 d.p.). The negative root x ≈ −13.42 is rejected because it would give a negative width.
app_sections.why_it_works: Multiplying two linear expressions produces a quadratic, so any 'area equals a number' problem with linear sides leads to a quadratic equation. Algebra returns both roots of that equation, but geometry imposes an extra condition the algebra knows nothing about: lengths must be positive. Checking each root against that condition is part of the answer, not an optional extra.
common_mistakes: Adding the two expressions instead of multiplying them.
Setting each bracket equal to 77.
Keeping the negative root because it satisfies the equation, without checking the side lengths.
app_sections.exam_tip: In any geometry problem that produces a quadratic, state explicitly why you are rejecting a root — the reasoning earns marks.

question.question_restated: The length of a rectangle is (2x + 1) cm and its width is (x − 2) cm. The area is 45 cm². Calculate the value(s) of x.

app_sections.think_first: Form the area equation first; only afterwards worry about whether the roots make geometric sense.
app_sections.strategy: Set (2x + 1)(x − 2) = 45, expand and rearrange to standard form, solve with the formula, then reject the root that gives a negative width.

guided_solution.instruction: Write the area as a product.
Expand the brackets.
Rearrange into standard form.
Apply the quadratic formula with a = 2, b = −3, c = −47.
Evaluate and reject the invalid root.
guided_solution.note: x ≈ 5.66 or x ≈ −4.16; the negative root makes x − 2 negative

app_sections.final_answer: x = (3 + √385)/4 ≈ 5.66 (2 d.p.). The root x ≈ −4.16 is rejected because it gives a negative width.
app_sections.why_it_works: The equation encodes the whole situation: the product of the two side expressions must equal the given area. Because the discriminant 385 is not a perfect square, the sides are not whole numbers — that is perfectly acceptable, real rectangles need not have integer sides. The rejection step is what turns two algebraic roots into one physical answer.
common_mistakes: Expanding (2x + 1)(x − 2) as 2x² − 2 and losing the middle term.
Subtracting 45 from only the constant on the left and forgetting it changes the equation's constant.
Reporting both roots without checking the width.
app_sections.exam_tip: Once you have x, substitute it back to state the actual side lengths — it confirms both roots and the rejection at once.

question.source_text: 15. The area of a rectangle is x² + 11x + 24 cm². Determine possible expressions for the length and width of the rectangle. Hence, calculate its perimeter.

question.question_restated: The area of a rectangle is x² + 11x + 24 cm². Determine possible expressions for the length and the width, and hence calculate its perimeter.

app_sections.think_first: Area is length × width, so factorising the area expression hands you the two sides.
app_sections.strategy: Factorise x² + 11x + 24 into two brackets, take those as the length and width, then apply P = 2(l + w).

guided_solution.instruction: Find two numbers whose product is 24 and whose sum is 11.
Write the area in factorised form.
Take the two factors as the side lengths.
guided_solution.note: the longer side is the one with the larger constant

guided_solution.instruction: Apply the perimeter formula and simplify.

app_sections.final_answer: Length (x + 8) cm and width (x + 3) cm; perimeter = 2[(x + 8) + (x + 3)] = (4x + 22) cm.
app_sections.why_it_works: Factorising reverses the multiplication that produced the area, so the two brackets are a valid pair of side lengths. The word 'possible' matters: any pair of expressions multiplying to the same quadratic would do, but the integer factorisation is the intended one. The perimeter then follows from adding the four sides, which is why the x-terms double to 4x.
common_mistakes: Adding the brackets instead of doubling their sum, giving 2x + 11 instead of 4x + 22.
Choosing 12 and 2 or 6 and 4, which multiply to 24 but do not add to 11.
Leaving the perimeter as 2(2x + 11) when a simplified expression is asked for.
app_sections.exam_tip: Perimeter answers should be fully simplified single expressions — expand the outer bracket before you write your final line.

question.question_restated: A square has side (2x − 5) cm and an area of 49 cm². Calculate the value(s) of x and hence determine the length of each side.

app_sections.think_first: A square's area is the side squared, so the equation is already in completed-square form.
app_sections.strategy: Set (2x − 5)² = 49, square-root both sides with a ±, solve the two linear equations, then check which value gives a positive side.

guided_solution.instruction: Write the area equation from the diagram.
Take the square root of both sides, keeping both signs.
Solve each linear equation.
Test each value in the side expression and keep the one that is positive.
guided_solution.note: x = 6 gives 2(6) − 5 = 7; x = −1 gives 2(−1) − 5 = −7, which is impossible

app_sections.final_answer: x = 6 (rejecting x = −1, which gives a negative side); each side is 7 cm.
app_sections.why_it_works: Squaring destroys sign information, so undoing it with a square root reintroduces two possibilities — that is where the second root comes from. Both values satisfy the algebraic equation, but only x = 6 produces a side of positive length. The check is quick because you only need to substitute into the single side expression.
common_mistakes: Writing 2x − 5 = 7 only and never considering −7.
Expanding to 4x² − 20x + 25 = 49 and doing far more work than needed.
Giving x = 6 as the side length instead of 7 cm.
app_sections.exam_tip: When a question asks for x and then 'hence' the length, make sure your final line answers both — the length is not the same number as x.

question.question_restated: A right-angled triangle has base (x − 1) cm and perpendicular height (x + 2) cm, with an area of 30 cm². Calculate the value(s) of x and hence the lengths of the base and the perpendicular height.

app_sections.think_first: Use area = ½ × base × height, and clear the half straight away by doubling both sides.
app_sections.strategy: Write ½(x − 1)(x + 2) = 30, double both sides, expand and rearrange, solve with the formula, then reject the root giving negative lengths.

guided_solution.instruction: Write the area formula using the two perpendicular sides from the diagram.
Multiply both sides by 2 to remove the fraction.
Expand and rearrange into standard form.
Apply the quadratic formula with a = 1, b = 1, c = −62.
Evaluate, reject the negative root, and find the two lengths.
guided_solution.note: x ≈ 7.39 or x ≈ −8.39; the latter makes both sides negative. Base = x − 1 ≈ 6.39, height = x + 2 ≈ 9.39

app_sections.final_answer: x = (−1 + √249)/2 ≈ 7.39; base ≈ 6.39 cm and perpendicular height ≈ 9.39 cm (2 d.p.). The root x ≈ −8.39 is rejected as it gives negative lengths.
app_sections.why_it_works: In a right-angled triangle the two legs are perpendicular, so they serve directly as base and height in the area formula — no extra construction is needed. Doubling first avoids carrying a fraction through the expansion. As a check, ½ × 6.39 × 9.39 ≈ 30, which recovers the given area.
common_mistakes: Forgetting the ½ and solving (x − 1)(x + 2) = 30.
Using the hypotenuse as the height.
Rounding x before computing the side lengths, which compounds the error.
app_sections.exam_tip: Clear fractions at the very first step — a quadratic with a ½ in front invites arithmetic slips later on.

question.question_restated: Seven chairs and nine desks cost $1200. Thirteen chairs and six desks also cost $1200. Taking c as the cost of one chair and d as the cost of one desk, form two simultaneous equations and find the cost of each item.

app_sections.think_first: Translate each sentence into an equation, then eliminate one unknown by matching its coefficients.
concepts_required: Substitution to find the second unknown
app_sections.strategy: Write the two equations, scale them so the d-terms match, subtract to find c, then substitute back for d.

guided_solution.instruction: Translate each statement into an equation.
guided_solution.note: 7 chairs and 9 desks cost $1200; 13 chairs and 6 desks cost $1200

guided_solution.instruction: Scale both equations so the d-coefficients match.
Subtract to eliminate d.
Substitute c = 48 into equation (1) to find d.
Check the pair in equation (2).

app_sections.final_answer: 7c + 9d = 1200 and 13c + 6d = 1200; one chair costs $48 and one desk costs $96.
app_sections.why_it_works: Each purchase gives one linear relationship between the two unknown prices, and two independent relationships are exactly what is needed to pin both down. Multiplying an equation through by a constant does not change its solutions, so scaling to match coefficients is safe; subtracting then removes one unknown entirely. The equal totals of $1200 are a feature of this problem, not a shortcut, because the coefficients still differ and the equations remain independent.
common_mistakes: Concluding that 7c + 9d = 13c + 6d means the two items cost the same.
Scaling only one equation and subtracting anyway.
Substituting c back into the equation it was derived from and getting a circular result.
app_sections.exam_tip: Always verify your pair in the equation you did not use for the substitution — it catches almost every arithmetic error.

question.question_restated: Mary paid $2100 for four parrots and three dogs. Had she bought one more dog and two fewer parrots, she would have paid $2300. Taking d as the cost of a dog and p as the cost of a parrot, find the cost of a dog and of a parrot.

app_sections.think_first: The second sentence describes a changed basket — work out how many of each animal it contains before writing the equation.
app_sections.strategy: Write the first equation directly, adjust the quantities for the second, then eliminate p and solve.

guided_solution.instruction: Translate the first purchase into an equation.
guided_solution.note: four parrots and three dogs cost $2100

guided_solution.instruction: Work out the second basket: one more dog means 3 + 1 = 4 dogs, and two fewer parrots means 4 − 2 = 2 parrots.
Scale equation (2) so the p-coefficients match.
Subtract equation (1) to eliminate p.
Substitute d = 500 into equation (1), then check in (2).

app_sections.final_answer: 4p + 3d = 2100 and 2p + 4d = 2300; a dog costs $500 and a parrot costs $150.
app_sections.why_it_works: The hypothetical purchase is just as valid an equation as the real one, because the price per animal is the same in both cases. The phrases 'one more' and 'two fewer' change the quantities, not the prices, so they only alter the coefficients. Two independent equations in two unknowns then determine both prices uniquely.
common_mistakes: Reading 'one more dog and two fewer parrots' as 1 dog and 2 parrots rather than 4 dogs and 2 parrots.
Changing the prices instead of the quantities.
Adding the equations when subtracting is what eliminates the unknown.
app_sections.exam_tip: Write the second basket out in words ('2 parrots, 4 dogs') before converting it to symbols — comparison wording is where marks are usually lost.

concepts_required: Expressing one quantity in terms of another
app_sections.strategy: Write the two cost equations using 2t for the large table, substitute for t from the first equation into the second, solve for c, then find t and double it.

guided_solution.instruction: Translate the first purchase.
guided_solution.note: four chairs and one small table cost $684

guided_solution.instruction: Translate the second purchase, writing the large table as 2t.
guided_solution.note: six chairs and one large table cost $1196

Solve for c.
Find t, then double it for the large table, and check.

app_sections.final_answer: 4c + t = 684 and 6c + 2t = 1196; a chair costs $86, the small table costs $340, and the large table costs $680.
app_sections.why_it_works: Three unknown prices would normally need three equations, but the relationship 'large = 2 × small' removes one unknown before you start, leaving a standard two-by-two system. Substitution suits this problem because t already appears with coefficient 1 in equation (1). The final doubling converts the small-table price into the quantity the question actually asks for.
common_mistakes: Introducing a third variable for the large table and then having too few equations.
Writing the large table as t/2 instead of 2t.
Stopping at t = 340 and offering that as the large table's cost.

Scaling to make both eraser coefficients 15 lets a single subtraction remove e completely. Once both unit prices are known, any other combination of the two items can be costed directly.

Losing a decimal place when scaling, for example writing 34.8 as 348.
Answering only the unit prices and skipping the cost of eight erasers.

question.display_policy: Render verified structured mathematics when available; always retain the linked source visual for fidelity.
question.question_restated: The distance d needed to stop a car varies directly as the square of its speed s. A car travelling at 70 km/h requires a stopping distance of 40 m. Find the stopping distance when the speed is 80 km/h.

app_sections.think_first: The distance depends on the square of the speed, so the speeds must be squared before you compare them.
app_sections.strategy: Write d = ks², use d = 40 when s = 70 to find k, then substitute s = 80.

guided_solution.instruction: Write the variation statement as an equation.
Substitute d = 40 and s = 70 to find k.
Substitute s = 80 into d = ks².
Round sensibly for a practical distance.

app_sections.final_answer: The stopping distance is 12800/245 m ≈ 52.2 m
app_sections.why_it_works: Because d is proportional to s², multiplying the speed by a factor multiplies the stopping distance by the square of that factor. Here the speed rises by a factor of 80/70, so the distance rises by (80/70)² ≈ 1.31 — a 14% increase in speed causes roughly a 31% increase in stopping distance. That squared relationship is the reason small increases in speed matter so much on the road.
common_mistakes: Using d = ks and scaling the distance by 80/70 instead of (80/70)².
Squaring only after dividing, e.g. computing 40 × 80²/70 rather than 40 × (80/70)².
Rounding k too early and losing accuracy in the final answer.
app_sections.exam_tip: For a square-law variation you can skip finding k: use d₂ = d₁ × (s₂/s₁)², which is faster and avoids rounding errors.

question.source_text: 1. The height ℎ varies directly as the square root of the perimeter 𝑝. (a) Write an equation connecting ℎ and 𝑝. (b) Given that ℎ= 5.4 when 𝑝= 1.44, find ℎ when 𝑝= 2.89.
question.display_policy: Render verified structured mathematics when available; always retain the linked source visual for fidelity.
question.question_restated: The height h varies directly as the square root of the perimeter p. (a) Write an equation connecting h and p. (b) Given that h = 5.4 when p = 1.44, find h when p = 2.89.

app_sections.think_first: Direct variation with a square root still follows the same pattern: one quantity equals a constant times the other.
app_sections.strategy: Write h = k√p, use the given pair to find k, then substitute p = 2.89 into the completed equation.

guided_solution.instruction: Write the variation statement as an equation with a constant k.
Substitute h = 5.4 and p = 1.44 to find k.
Write the completed equation.
Substitute p = 2.89.

app_sections.final_answer: (a) h = k√p  (b) k = 4.5, so h = 4.5√p and h = 7.65 when p = 2.89
app_sections.why_it_works: Direct variation means the ratio of h to √p never changes, so a single known pair fixes the constant k for every other pair. Once k is known the relationship is a complete formula, and any value of p can be converted to its h. Taking the square root first is essential — h is proportional to √p, not to p itself.
common_mistakes: Writing h = kp and ignoring the square root.
Substituting p = 2.89 without taking its square root.
Treating k as if it changes from one pair of values to the next.
app_sections.exam_tip: Write the equation with k in it before you touch any numbers — it keeps the square root in the right place.

question.source_text: 3. The mass 𝑚 of a body varies directly as its volume 𝑉. Given that 𝑚= 12 when 𝑉= 3, find the mass when 𝑉= 5.

app_sections.think_first: Direct variation means mass divided by volume is the same number every time.
app_sections.strategy: Write m = kV, find k from the given pair, then substitute V = 5.

guided_solution.instruction: Write the variation statement as an equation.
Substitute m = 12 and V = 3 to find k.
Substitute V = 5 into m = 4V.

app_sections.why_it_works: The constant k here is the density of the body — the mass carried by each unit of volume. Because the material does not change, that ratio stays fixed, so once you know it for one pair of values you can find the mass for any volume.
common_mistakes: Adding 2 to the volume and adding the same to the mass, treating the relationship as linear-with-an-intercept.
Dividing 3 by 12 instead of 12 by 3 when finding k.
Forgetting to substitute the new volume back into the equation.
app_sections.exam_tip: In direct variation always state k explicitly on its own line — most marks in these questions are awarded for finding it.

question.question_restated: The cost C of printing leaflets varies directly as the number of leaflets n. If 500 leaflets cost $120, find the cost of printing 750 leaflets.

app_sections.think_first: Cost per leaflet stays the same, so find it once and then multiply.
app_sections.strategy: Write C = kn, find the cost per leaflet from the given pair, then multiply by 750.

guided_solution.instruction: Write the variation statement as an equation.
Substitute C = 120 and n = 500 to find k.
Substitute n = 750 into C = 0.24n.

app_sections.final_answer: The cost of printing 750 leaflets is $180
app_sections.why_it_works: The constant of variation is simply the price of one leaflet, so direct variation here is the unitary method written algebraically. Because 750 is 1.5 times 500, the cost is 1.5 times $120 — the same answer reached by scaling instead of by finding k.
common_mistakes: Adding $120 × 250/500 to the wrong base figure.
Finding k as 500 ÷ 120 rather than 120 ÷ 500.
Leaving the answer without a dollar sign or units.
app_sections.exam_tip: Sanity-check money answers by scale: 750 is one and a half times 500, so the cost should be one and a half times $120.

Apply the definition of a function.

app_sections.why_it_works: The form y = mx + c is useful precisely because m and c can be read directly, so any linear equation is worth rearranging before answering questions about slope or intercepts. Reading the gradient as 4 straight from 4x − 2y = 10.

app_sections.strategy: Read A and B from the diagram, apply the distance formula √((x₂−x₁)² + (y₂−y₁)²) for the length, then average the coordinates for the midpoint.

Apply the distance formula.
Average the x-coordinates for the midpoint.
Average the y-coordinates.
State the midpoint.

app_sections.why_it_works: The distance formula is Pythagoras' theorem applied to the right-angled triangle whose legs are the horizontal and vertical changes between the two points. Squaring removes any negative signs, so the length never depends on which point you call first — unlike the gradient, where order controls the sign. The midpoint averages each coordinate because halfway across and halfway up locates the centre of the segment.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to square root at the end and giving 100 as the length.
Misreading the negative coordinates of A from the grid.
Using the midpoint formula with subtraction instead of addition.

Subtracting the y-coordinates as 4 − 2 and getting a vertical change of 2.

app_sections.think_first: Every length here is a distance between two known points, so one formula does all three parts.
app_sections.strategy: Apply the distance formula d = √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²) to each pair of vertices, then compare the three lengths.

app_sections.why_it_works: The distance formula is Pythagoras' theorem written in coordinates: the horizontal gap and the vertical gap between two points are the two shorter sides of a right-angled triangle, and the join of the points is the hypotenuse. Because squaring removes signs, the order of the points never matters. Classifying the triangle then needs nothing more than a comparison of the three numbers you produced.
common_mistakes: Subtracting the coordinates the wrong way and then losing the square, e.g. writing 4 − (-2) = 2.
Adding the differences instead of squaring them: (3 + 4) = 7 instead of √(9 + 16) = 5.
Calling the triangle equilateral because two sides matched, without checking the third.

app_sections.think_first: The centre of a circle is the midpoint of any diameter, so read A and B off the grid first and everything else follows.
concepts_required: Radius and diameter of a circle
app_sections.strategy: Read A and B from the graph, use the midpoint formula for the centre and the distance formula for AB, halve AB for the radius, then test D by comparing CD with the radius.

guided_solution.instruction: Read the endpoints of the diameter from the grid.

Find AB with the distance formula.
Halve the diameter to get the radius.
Find CD from C(-1, -1) to D(4, -1).
Compare CD with the radius.
guided_solution.note: CD = 5 = r, so D is exactly one radius from the centre

app_sections.why_it_works: A circle is the set of all points a fixed distance — the radius — from one fixed point. That single fact does all the work here: the diameter passes through the centre, so its midpoint is the centre; the radius is half the diameter; and any point is on the circle exactly when its distance from the centre equals that radius. Checking membership of a circle is therefore always a distance calculation, never a guess from the picture.
common_mistakes: Using the distance formula when the midpoint formula is wanted (subtracting instead of averaging).
Taking the radius as 10 because AB was 10 — AB is the diameter.
Deciding D is on the circle just because it looks close on the diagram.
app_sections.exam_tip: When a diagram gives you the points, write the coordinates down as an ordered pair before you calculate — misreading one sign off a grid ruins every part that follows.

app_sections.why_it_works: The segment joining the midpoints of two sides of a triangle is always parallel to the third side and exactly half its length — the midpoint theorem. In coordinates, halving both the horizontal and the vertical step scales the whole segment by ½ without changing its direction, which is why the gradients come out identical and the lengths come out in the ratio 1 : 2. Equal gradients are the proof of parallelism; the diagram alone is not.
common_mistakes: Proving parallelism by saying the lines “look parallel” instead of showing equal gradients.
Leaving BC as √104 and failing to see it is 2√26, so missing the exact half relationship.
Mixing up which pair of vertices M and N come from.

guided_solution.result: Two straight lines drawn and labelled

app_sections.why_it_works: A straight-line graph is a picture of every (x, y) pair that satisfies its equation. A point lying on both lines therefore satisfies both equations at once, which is exactly what solving a simultaneous pair means. Rearranging x + y = 5 into y = 5 − x changes the way the equation looks but not the set of points it describes, so the same graph answers both parts.

question.question_restated: The graph compares the cost, C dollars, of two taxi plans for a journey of d kilometres. (a) State the cost at which the plans are equal. (b) State the distance for which the costs are equal. (c) Write the two equations represented by the graph. (d) State which plan is cheaper for an 8 km journey.

app_sections.think_first: The point where the two lines cross is the only journey for which the plans cost the same — everything else is read from the intercepts and slopes.
concepts_required: Gradient as a rate of change
app_sections.strategy: Read the crossing point for parts (a) and (b), read each line's starting cost and cost per kilometre for part (c), then compare the two lines at d = 8.

guided_solution.instruction: Locate the point where the two lines cross.
guided_solution.note: The lines meet directly above d = 6, level with C = 170

guided_solution.instruction: State the equal cost and the distance at which it happens.
guided_solution.note: The C-value of the crossing point is the cost; the d-value is the distance

guided_solution.instruction: Form the equation for Plan A.
guided_solution.note: Plan A starts at C = 50 when d = 0 and reaches C = 290 at d = 12, so the rate is (290 − 50)/12 = 20

guided_solution.instruction: Form the equation for Plan B.
guided_solution.note: Plan B starts at C = 110 and reaches C = 230 at d = 12, so the rate is (230 − 110)/12 = 10

guided_solution.instruction: Compare the two plans at d = 8.
guided_solution.result: Plan B is cheaper at 8 km

app_sections.final_answer: (a) $170  (b) 6 km  (c) Plan A: C = 50 + 20d and Plan B: C = 110 + 10d  (d) Plan B is cheaper for an 8 km journey ($190 against $210).
app_sections.why_it_works: In a cost model the intercept is the fixed charge you pay before travelling at all and the gradient is the charge per kilometre. Plan A has the smaller fixed charge but the larger rate, so it wins on short trips and loses on long ones; the crossing point is the exact distance where the two effects balance. Reading which line is lower on the side of the crossing point you care about answers any “which is cheaper” question instantly.
common_mistakes: Swapping the two answers in (a) and (b) — cost is read on the vertical axis, distance on the horizontal.
Taking the gradient from a single point instead of the change between two points.
Assuming the plan that is cheaper at the start is cheaper everywhere.
app_sections.exam_tip: For gradients on a real-world graph, use two points that sit exactly on gridlines and far apart — a wide run makes small reading errors matter far less.

question.question_restated: Given that f(x) = (x + 1)/(2x − 5), g(x) = (2x − 5)/(x + 1) and h(x) = (5x + 1)/(2x − 1): (i) Evaluate f(3) and g(4). (ii) Show that h(3) = 3. (iii) Write down the expression for f⁻¹(x).

app_sections.think_first: Evaluating means substituting the number into the top and the bottom separately; finding an inverse means making x the subject.
app_sections.strategy: Substitute the given values into each rational expression, then invert f by writing y = f(x), clearing the fraction and solving for x.

guided_solution.instruction: Evaluate f(3).
Evaluate g(4).
Substitute x = 3 into h.
Note where the value 3 does occur.
guided_solution.note: h(4) = (5(4) + 1)/(2(4) − 1) = 21/7 = 3, which matches f(3) = 4 because h is the inverse of f

guided_solution.instruction: Set y = f(x) and clear the fraction to find the inverse.
Write the inverse as a function of x.

app_sections.final_answer: (i) f(3) = 4 and g(4) = 3/5  (ii) Substituting gives h(3) = 16/5 = 3.2, so the printed statement h(3) = 3 does not hold as written; the value 3 is produced by h(4) = 21/7 = 3  (iii) f⁻¹(x) = (5x + 1)/(2x − 1), x ≠ 1/2.
app_sections.why_it_works: An inverse function undoes the original, so finding it means asking which input produced a given output — exactly what making x the subject does. The algebra reveals something worth noticing: f⁻¹ turns out to be h itself. That is why f(3) = 4 forces h(4) = 3, and it is a useful self-check whenever you invert a rational function.
common_mistakes: Multiplying top and bottom by x when substituting instead of just replacing x by the number.
Failing to collect the x terms on one side, so x cannot be factored out.
Giving the inverse as 1/f(x) — the reciprocal is not the inverse function.
app_sections.exam_tip: After finding an inverse, test it: run one value through f, then through f⁻¹, and check you return to where you started.

question.question_restated: The function g is defined by g(x) = (x + 1)/(x − 1). (i) Calculate g(1/2). (ii) Given that g²(x) = g[g(x)], g³(x) = g[g²(x)] and so on, show that g²(x) = x and hence deduce the value of g²¹(1/2).

app_sections.think_first: Once you show that applying g twice returns x, applying g twenty-one times is the same as applying it once.
app_sections.strategy: Substitute x = 1/2 to get g(1/2), then form g[g(x)] and simplify it to x; use that to reduce g²¹ to a single application of g.

guided_solution.instruction: Substitute x = 1/2 into g.
Write g[g(x)] with (x + 1)/(x − 1) in place of x.
Combine top and bottom over the denominator x − 1.
Divide the two fractions.
Reduce g²¹ using this result.
guided_solution.note: Every pair of applications returns to x, and 21 = 2 × 10 + 1

guided_solution.instruction: Deduce the required value.

app_sections.final_answer: (i) g(1/2) = -3  (ii) g²(x) = x, so g is self-inverse; since 21 is odd, g²¹(x) = g(x) and therefore g²¹(1/2) = -3.
app_sections.why_it_works: A function satisfying g[g(x)] = x is its own inverse: it maps every value to a partner and that partner straight back again. Repeated application therefore alternates between just two states, so only whether the exponent is odd or even matters — even numbers of applications give x, odd numbers give g(x). Recognising this replaces twenty-one calculations with one.
common_mistakes: Trying to evaluate g twenty-one times instead of finding the pattern.
Treating g²(x) as [g(x)]², which is squaring the output, not composing.
Slipping a sign when simplifying (1/2 − 1) to -1/2.
app_sections.exam_tip: When a large exponent appears on a function, look for a repeating cycle first — the examiner is testing the pattern, not your stamina.

app_sections.strategy: Substitute x = -2 into f, feed that output into g, then invert f by writing y = f(x), clearing the fraction and solving for x.

guided_solution.instruction: Evaluate f(-2).
Apply g to that result.
Set y = f(x) and clear the fraction.
Factor out x and solve.
Write the inverse in terms of x.

app_sections.why_it_works: Composition is a chain: the inner function converts the input into an intermediate value and the outer function converts that into the final answer, which is why gf is not the same as fg. Inverting a rational function always follows the same route — clear the denominator, gather every x term on one side, factor and divide — and the value making the new denominator zero is excluded from the domain.
common_mistakes: Working gf(-2) as g first, giving f(0) instead of g(7).
Losing a sign in (-4 − 3)/(-1) and writing -7.
Forgetting to factor x out after collecting terms, so the rearrangement stalls.
app_sections.exam_tip: Read composite notation from right to left, and write the intermediate value down before applying the outer function.

question.question_restated: Given that f: x ↦ 3x − 2, g: x ↦ 2x + 5 and h: x ↦ (2x + 3)/(x − 1): (a) Evaluate (i) g(-6) and (ii) fg(3). (b) If f(x) = 8, calculate the value of x. (c) Obtain an expression, in terms of x, for h⁻¹(x).

app_sections.think_first: Three skills are being tested: substituting into a function, composing two of them, and reversing one.
app_sections.strategy: Substitute directly for (a)(i), work inner-then-outer for (a)(ii), solve 3x − 2 = 8 for (b), and rearrange y = h(x) to make x the subject for (c).

guided_solution.instruction: Evaluate g(-6).
Evaluate fg(3): apply g first, then f.
Solve f(x) = 8.
Set y = h(x) and clear the fraction.
Factor out x and divide.
Write the inverse in terms of x.

app_sections.why_it_works: Every part rests on the same idea: a function is a rule turning an input into an output. Evaluating runs the rule forwards, solving f(x) = 8 runs it backwards for one particular output, and finding the inverse runs it backwards for every output at once. That is why parts (b) and (c) feel like the same algebra — they are.
common_mistakes: Computing fg(3) as f first, giving g(7) instead of f(11).
Answering part (b) with x = 2 by dividing 8 by 3 before adding the 2.
Leaving x on both sides in part (c) instead of collecting and factoring.
app_sections.exam_tip: State any excluded value with an inverse — writing 'x ≠ 2' shows you understand the function and is often worth a mark.

question.question_restated: Given that f(x) = 5x and g(x) = x − 2: (i) Calculate f(2) and gf(2). (ii) Determine x when fg(x) = 0. (iii) Prove that (gf)⁻¹(23) = 5.

app_sections.think_first: Watch the order carefully — gf and fg are different functions, and this question uses both.
app_sections.strategy: Substitute for f(2) and apply g to it, form fg(x) and set it to zero, then form gf(x) and show that gf(5) = 23.

guided_solution.instruction: Evaluate f(2) and then gf(2).
Form fg(x): apply g first, then f.
Set fg(x) = 0 and solve.
Form gf(x): apply f first, then g.
Find the input that gives an output of 23.
State the conclusion about the inverse.
guided_solution.note: gf(5) = 23, so the inverse sends 23 back to 5

app_sections.final_answer: (i) f(2) = 10 and gf(2) = 8  (ii) x = 2  (iii) gf(x) = 5x − 2, and 5x − 2 = 23 gives x = 5, so (gf)⁻¹(23) = 5.
app_sections.why_it_works: Composing functions builds a single new rule: gf multiplies by 5 then subtracts 2, while fg subtracts 2 then multiplies by 5 — different rules, different graphs. An inverse asks the reverse question, 'which input gave this output?', so proving (gf)⁻¹(23) = 5 needs nothing more than showing gf(5) = 23.
common_mistakes: Treating gf and fg as the same function.
Expanding 5(x − 2) as 5x − 2.
Deriving the full inverse formula when a single substitution proves the statement.
app_sections.exam_tip: To prove an inverse value, run the forward function on the claimed answer — one line of substitution beats a full rearrangement.

app_sections.think_first: Substituting a negative number needs care with the square; substituting an expression follows exactly the same rule.
app_sections.strategy: Replace x by -4 in the numerator and denominator separately, then replace x by (x − 1) throughout and expand.

guided_solution.instruction: Substitute x = -4 into the numerator.
Substitute x = -4 into the denominator.

Expand and simplify the numerator.

guided_solution.note: The denominator 5(x − 1) must not be zero

app_sections.why_it_works: A function rule tells you what to do to whatever sits in the input slot, whether that is a number or a whole expression. Composing means putting the inner function into that slot and tidying up, so the algebra is identical to substituting a number — just longer. The restriction moves with the substitution: f excluded x = 0, so fg must exclude the x making x − 1 zero.
common_mistakes: Writing (-4)² as -16 and getting a numerator of -30.
Expanding (x − 1)² as x² − 1.
Losing the bracket in the denominator and writing 5x − 1 instead of 5(x − 1).
app_sections.exam_tip: When substituting an expression, put it in brackets everywhere before simplifying — most composite errors are dropped brackets, not bad algebra.

(i) Determine the range of values of ℎ(𝑥)such that ℎ(𝑥) > 1. (ii) Show that if ℎ(𝑥) < 25, then −2 < 𝑥< 8. c. Hence or otherwise, for 𝑥∈ℝ, determine the range of values of 𝑥for which 1 < ℎ(𝑥) < 25 and represent your answer on a number line.

question.question_restated: The functions f, g and h are defined by f: x ↦ x − 3, g: x ↦ x² and h: x ↦ x² − 6x + 9. (a) Given that f²(x) = f[f(x)], f³(x) = f[f²(x)] and so on, (i) deduce an algebraic expression in terms of x for f⁴(x) and hence calculate f⁴(3); (ii) show that gf(x) = h(x). (b)(i) Determine the values of x for which h(x) > 1. (b)(ii) Show that if h(x) < 25, then -2 < x < 8. (c) Hence or otherwise, for x ∈ ℝ, determine the range of values of x for which 1 < h(x) < 25 and represent your answer on a number line.

app_sections.think_first: Notice first that h(x) = (x − 3)² — writing it that way turns every inequality into a simple square-root step.
app_sections.strategy: Track the repeated subtraction to get f⁴, compose g with f to recognise h as a perfect square, then solve each inequality using (x − 3)² and combine the two solution sets.

guided_solution.instruction: Apply f repeatedly.
guided_solution.note: f(x) = x − 3, f²(x) = x − 6, f³(x) = x − 9, so each application subtracts a further 3

guided_solution.instruction: Evaluate f⁴(3).
Form gf(x) and compare with h.
Solve h(x) > 1 using the square form.
Solve h(x) < 25.
Combine both conditions for 1 < h(x) < 25.
guided_solution.note: Take the overlap of (x < 2 or x > 4) with -2 < x < 8

app_sections.final_answer: (a)(i) f⁴(x) = x − 12 and f⁴(3) = -9  (a)(ii) gf(x) = (x − 3)² = x² − 6x + 9 = h(x)  (b)(i) x < 2 or x > 4  (b)(ii) (x − 3)² < 25 gives -5 < x − 3 < 5, hence -2 < x < 8  (c) -2 < x < 2 or 4 < x < 8, drawn on a number line as two open intervals with open circles at -2, 2, 4 and 8.
app_sections.why_it_works: Because h(x) is the perfect square (x − 3)², its value depends only on how far x is from 3. So h(x) < 25 means x is within 5 of 3, and h(x) > 1 means x is more than 1 away from 3 — the first gives a single interval, the second gives two. Combining them leaves the points more than 1 but less than 5 away from 3, which is exactly the pair of intervals in the answer.
common_mistakes: Taking only the positive root of (x − 3)² > 1 and losing the branch x < 2.
Treating a two-sided condition as one-sided.
Using filled circles on the number line when the inequalities are strict.
app_sections.exam_tip: Rewrite a quadratic inequality in completed-square form before solving — the distance-from-a-point reading makes both branches obvious.

Check the inverse value.

app_sections.why_it_works: The inverse answers the question 'which input does f send to 3?', so it is found by undoing each operation in reverse order: f multiplies by 2, adds 1 and divides by 3, so f⁻¹ multiplies by 3, subtracts 1 and divides by 2. Because the inverse undoes f exactly, substituting the answer back into f is a complete check.
common_mistakes: Reading fg(2) as f(2) × g(2).
Multiplying only the 2x by 3 when clearing the denominator.
Confusing f⁻¹(3) with 1/f(3).

question.question_restated: Complete the table and draw the graph of y = x² + 2x − 3 for -4 ≤ x ≤ 2, with x taking the values -4, -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2. (a) Complete the table. (b) Draw a smooth curve through the plotted points. (c) State the roots and the coordinates of the minimum point. (d) State the minimum value. (e) Write the equation of the axis of symmetry. (f) State the range for the given domain.

app_sections.think_first: Fill the table one x-value at a time, squaring before you multiply, and the shape of the parabola will appear from the numbers alone.
concepts_required: Minimum point and axis of symmetry
app_sections.strategy: Substitute each x-value into y = x² + 2x − 3, plot the seven points and join them with a smooth curve, then read the roots, vertex, axis of symmetry and range from the completed table and curve.

guided_solution.instruction: Substitute the negative x-values.
Substitute the remaining x-values.
Plot the seven points and join them with a smooth curve.
Read the roots and the lowest point.
guided_solution.note: The curve crosses the x-axis where y = 0, at x = -3 and x = 1; the lowest table value is -4 at x = -1
guided_solution.result: Roots x = -3 and x = 1; minimum point (-1, -4)

guided_solution.instruction: State the minimum value and the axis of symmetry.
guided_solution.note: The minimum value is the y-value at the vertex; the axis is the vertical line through it
guided_solution.result: Minimum value -4; axis of symmetry x = -1

guided_solution.instruction: State the range over the given domain.
guided_solution.note: The y-values run from the minimum -4 up to the largest table value 5

app_sections.final_answer: (a) y = 5, 0, -3, -4, -3, 0, 5 for x = -4, -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2  (b) A smooth U-shaped curve through those points  (c) Roots x = -3 and x = 1; minimum point (-1, -4)  (d) Minimum value -4  (e) Axis of symmetry x = -1  (f) Range: -4 ≤ y ≤ 5.
app_sections.why_it_works: A quadratic graph is symmetric about the vertical line through its vertex, which is why the table values 5, 0, -3, -4, -3, 0, 5 read the same forwards and backwards. That symmetry places the vertex halfway between the two roots, at x = (-3 + 1)/2 = -1, and the minimum value is simply the y-value there. The range is the set of outputs the curve actually reaches over the stated domain, so it runs from the vertex up to the highest endpoint value.
common_mistakes: Calculating (-4)² as -16, which wrecks the left half of the table.
Joining the points with straight line segments instead of a smooth curve.
Giving the minimum point as -4 instead of the coordinate pair (-1, -4).
app_sections.exam_tip: Use the symmetry of your completed table as a free check — if the y-values do not mirror each other about one column, a substitution has gone wrong.

app_sections.think_first: The curve opens downwards because of the negative x² term, so its turning point is a maximum.
app_sections.strategy: Read where the curve meets each axis, locate the highest point of the curve, and use the symmetry of the parabola to write the axis of symmetry.

guided_solution.instruction: Read where the curve crosses the x-axis.
guided_solution.note: The curve meets the axis at x = -1 and x = 5, confirmed by -x² + 4x + 5 = 0 → x² − 4x − 5 = 0 → (x − 5)(x + 1) = 0

guided_solution.instruction: Read where the curve crosses the y-axis.
Locate the highest point of the curve.

app_sections.why_it_works: The sign of the x² coefficient decides the shape: negative means the arms point downwards, so the turning point is the highest value the function reaches. A parabola is symmetric, so the vertex always sits exactly halfway between the two x-intercepts — that gives the x-value of the maximum without any further algebra, and substituting it gives the maximum value itself.

(d) Write the equation of the axis of symmetry. (e) State the range for the given domain. (f) State the interval of x for which y < 0. (g) State the intervals of x for which y > 6.

app_sections.think_first: 'Elements of the domain whose image is 0' is function language for the roots — where the curve meets the x-axis.
concepts_required: Minimum point and axis of symmetry
app_sections.strategy: Factorise to confirm the roots, substitute x = 0 for the y-intercept, use symmetry for the vertex, then read each inequality from where the curve lies above or below the relevant horizontal line.

guided_solution.instruction: Find the roots by factorising.
Find f(0).
Locate the vertex using symmetry.
guided_solution.note: Midway between the roots, x = (1 + 3)/2 = 2, and y = 2(4) − 16 + 6 = -2

guided_solution.instruction: State the axis of symmetry.
guided_solution.note: The vertical line through the vertex

guided_solution.instruction: State the range covered by the curve as drawn.
guided_solution.note: The curve falls to -2 at the vertex and rises to the top of the grid at y = 10
guided_solution.result: -2 ≤ y ≤ 10 on the section shown (never below -2)

guided_solution.instruction: Read the intervals for y < 0 and y > 6.
guided_solution.note: Below the x-axis between the roots; above y = 6 where 2x(x − 4) > 0
guided_solution.result: y < 0 for 1 < x < 3;  y > 6 for x < 0 or x > 4

app_sections.final_answer: (a) x = 1 and x = 3  (b) f(0) = 6  (c) Minimum value -2  (d) Axis of symmetry x = 2  (e) The curve never goes below -2; over the section drawn the range is -2 ≤ y ≤ 10  (f) y < 0 for 1 < x < 3  (g) y > 6 for x < 0 or x > 4.
app_sections.why_it_works: A quadratic is negative only between its roots, because that is the only stretch where the upward-opening curve dips below the x-axis. The same reasoning answers part (g): solving 2x² − 8x + 6 > 6 reduces to 2x(x − 4) > 0, whose roots 0 and 4 mark where the curve crosses the line y = 6, and the curve is above that line outside those two values. Symmetry places the vertex exactly halfway between any pair of such crossing points.
common_mistakes: Giving the interval for y < 0 as x < 1 or x > 3 — that is where the curve is positive.
Reading the roots as the y-intercept values.
Forgetting that y > 6 has two separate intervals, not one.
app_sections.exam_tip: For a 'greater than' inequality on an upward parabola the answer is always two outer intervals; for 'less than' it is the single interval between the crossings.

app_sections.think_first: Choose two points where the tangent line passes exactly through grid corners — accuracy depends entirely on that choice.
app_sections.strategy: Pick two clean points on the tangent, compute the rise over the run, then use y − y₁ = m(x − x₁) through P, and read the vertex of y = x² directly.

guided_solution.instruction: Choose two convenient points on the tangent.
guided_solution.note: The tangent passes through the grid corners (1, 0) and P(2, 4)

guided_solution.instruction: Calculate the gradient.
Form the equation through P(2, 4) with gradient 4.
Check the equation against the graph.
guided_solution.note: At x = 0 the equation gives y = -4, which matches where the drawn tangent cuts the y-axis

guided_solution.instruction: State the turning point of y = x².
guided_solution.note: The lowest point of y = x² is at the origin, since x² ≥ 0 for all x

app_sections.final_answer: (a) Gradient ≈ 4, using (1, 0) and (2, 4)  (b) y = 4x − 4  (c) The turning point of the curve is (0, 0).
app_sections.why_it_works: A tangent touches the curve at a single point and its gradient is the steepness of the curve right there, so estimating it from a drawn line is how gradients are found before calculus. Choosing two widely separated grid intersections makes the estimate reliable, because a small reading error spread over a longer run has much less effect. The turning point of y = x² is the origin because a square is never negative, so 0 is the least value the function can take.
common_mistakes: Using two points on the curve rather than on the tangent line.
Choosing points that fall between gridlines, so the gradient is guessed.
Substituting the gradient into y = mx + c but forgetting to solve for c.
app_sections.exam_tip: When estimating a gradient from a drawn line, pick the two grid corners furthest apart that the line clearly passes through — a longer run means a more trustworthy answer.

This is the standard trick for solving an equation graphically: split it into two familiar graphs whose intersection you can read. The exact roots are (1 ± √17)/2, which agree with the graphical estimates.

question.source_text: 1. The quadratic function f is defined by 𝑓(𝑥) = 𝑥² − 8𝑥 + 11. (a) Express f(x) in the form (𝑥 + ℎ)² + 𝑘, where h and k are constants. (b) Hence, state the coordinates of the minimum point of f. (c) Determine the equation of the axis of symmetry of the graph of f.
question.display_policy: Render verified structured mathematics when available; always retain the linked source visual for fidelity.
question.question_restated: The quadratic function f is defined by f(x) = x² − 8x + 11. (a) Express f(x) in the form (x + h)² + k, where h and k are constants. (b) Hence state the coordinates of the minimum point of f. (c) Determine the equation of the axis of symmetry of the graph of f.

app_sections.think_first: Halve the coefficient of x to find the number inside the bracket, then correct for what squaring the bracket adds.
app_sections.strategy: Take half of -8 to build the bracket (x − 4)², subtract the extra 16 it introduces, then read the vertex and axis directly from the completed-square form.

guided_solution.instruction: Halve the coefficient of x to form the bracket.
guided_solution.note: Half of -8 is -4, so start with (x − 4)²

guided_solution.instruction: Correct for the extra constant.
guided_solution.note: (x − 4)² gives 16, but the function has 11, so subtract 5

guided_solution.instruction: Read the minimum point.
guided_solution.note: (x − 4)² is never negative and equals 0 when x = 4, so the least value of f is -5

guided_solution.instruction: State the axis of symmetry.
guided_solution.note: The vertical line through the vertex

app_sections.final_answer: (a) f(x) = (x − 4)² − 5, so h = -4 and k = -5  (b) Minimum point (4, -5)  (c) Axis of symmetry x = 4.
app_sections.why_it_works: Completing the square rewrites a quadratic so the variable appears only once, inside a squared bracket. Since a square is never negative, the smallest possible value of (x − 4)² is 0, reached when x = 4, and the function's least value is then just the constant outside — here -5. The vertex and the axis of symmetry therefore fall straight out of the form with no further work.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to subtract the square of the halved coefficient, giving (x − 4)² + 11.
Reading the minimum point as (-4, -5) — the bracket (x − 4)² is zero at x = +4.
Writing the axis of symmetry as y = 4 instead of x = 4.
app_sections.exam_tip: Expand your completed-square answer mentally as a check — it must return the original quadratic exactly.

quick_check.prompt: Write x² + 6x + 2 in completed-square form.

question.source_text: 2. The quadratic function g is defined by 𝑔(𝑥) = −𝑥² + 6𝑥 + 7. (a) Express g(x) in the form 𝑎(𝑥 + ℎ)² + 𝑘, where a, h and k are constants. (b) Hence, state the coordinates of the maximum point of g. (c) Write down the equation of the line of symmetry of the graph of g.

question.question_restated: The quadratic function g is defined by g(x) = -x² + 6x + 7. (a) Express g(x) in the form a(x + h)² + k, where a, h and k are constants. (b) Hence state the coordinates of the maximum point of g. (c) Write down the equation of the line of symmetry of the graph of g.

app_sections.think_first: Factor the -1 out of the x terms first — completing the square inside a negative bracket is where most marks are lost.
concepts_required: Completing the square with a negative coefficient
app_sections.strategy: Take -1 out of the x² and x terms, complete the square inside the bracket, expand the -1 back through and read off the vertex.

guided_solution.instruction: Factor -1 from the x terms.
Complete the square inside the bracket.
guided_solution.note: Half of -6 is -3, and (x − 3)² = x² − 6x + 9, so x² − 6x = (x − 3)² − 9

guided_solution.instruction: Expand the -1 back through.
Read the maximum point.
guided_solution.note: -(x − 3)² is never positive and equals 0 when x = 3, so the greatest value of g is 16

guided_solution.instruction: State the line of symmetry.
guided_solution.note: The vertical line through the vertex

app_sections.final_answer: (a) g(x) = -(x − 3)² + 16, so a = -1, h = -3 and k = 16  (b) Maximum point (3, 16)  (c) Line of symmetry x = 3.
app_sections.why_it_works: With a negative leading coefficient the squared bracket is subtracted, so the expression is largest when the bracket is zero — the turning point becomes a maximum instead of a minimum. Factoring the -1 out before completing the square keeps the inside a standard x² − 6x, and multiplying back through at the end is what converts the -9 into +9. The vertex form then displays the maximum value and its position at a glance.
common_mistakes: Failing to multiply the -9 by the factored -1, giving -(x − 3)² − 2.
Halving 6 to get +3 but forgetting the sign change caused by the factored -1.
Calling (3, 16) a minimum because the constant k is positive.
app_sections.exam_tip: After completing the square with a negative leading coefficient, expand your answer back out — this is the single most common place to lose a sign.

app_sections.think_first: Factor the 2 out of the x terms before completing the square, then multiply it back through at the end.
concepts_required: Completing the square with a leading coefficient
Minimum point and axis of symmetry
app_sections.strategy: Take 2 out of the x² and x terms, complete the square inside the bracket, multiply the 2 back through, then read the minimum value, minimum point and axis from the result.

guided_solution.instruction: Factor 2 from the x terms.
Complete the square inside the bracket.
guided_solution.note: Half of 6 is 3, and (x + 3)² = x² + 6x + 9, so x² + 6x = (x + 3)² − 9

guided_solution.instruction: Multiply the 2 back through and simplify.
Determine the minimum value.
guided_solution.note: 2(x + 3)² is never negative and equals 0 when x = -3

guided_solution.instruction: State the minimum point and the axis of symmetry.
guided_solution.note: The least value occurs at x = -3
guided_solution.result: Minimum point (-3, -5); axis of symmetry x = -3

app_sections.final_answer: (a) p(x) = 2(x + 3)² − 5, so a = 2, h = 3 and k = -5  (b) Minimum value -5  (c) Minimum point (-3, -5)  (d) Axis of symmetry x = -3.
app_sections.why_it_works: Completing the square isolates the variable inside a single squared bracket, and because a square cannot be negative the whole expression is smallest when that bracket is zero. The factor 2 stretches the parabola vertically but does not move the turning point sideways, which is why the minimum still occurs at x = -3; it does, however, multiply the -9 into -18, so it must be carried through carefully.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to multiply the -9 by 2, giving p(x) = 2(x + 3)² + 4.
Reading the minimum point as (3, -5) instead of (-3, -5).
Halving 12 rather than the 6 that remains after factoring out the 2.
app_sections.exam_tip: When the coefficient of x² is not 1, factor it out of the first two terms only — never out of the constant — and check by expanding at the end.

(b) Hence determine the maximum value of q(x). (c) State the coordinates of the maximum point of q. (d) Determine the equation of the line of symmetry of the graph of q.

app_sections.think_first: The coefficient of x² is negative, so this parabola opens downwards and the completed square form will hand you a maximum, not a minimum.
concepts_required: Maximum and minimum of a quadratic
Vertex and line of symmetry of a parabola
app_sections.strategy: Factor the −3 out of the two x-terms, complete the square inside the bracket, then read the vertex straight off the a(x + h)² + k form.

guided_solution.instruction: Factor −3 out of the terms containing x.
Complete the square inside the bracket.
Expand the −3 across the bracket and simplify the constants.
Read off the maximum.
guided_solution.note: −3(x + 2)² is never positive, so q(x) is largest when (x + 2)² = 0, i.e. x = −2

guided_solution.instruction: State the vertex and its line of symmetry.
guided_solution.note: The vertex is (−h, k) = (−2, 13); the parabola is symmetric about the vertical line through it

app_sections.final_answer: (a) q(x) = −3(x + 2)² + 13  (b) maximum value = 13  (c) maximum point (−2, 13)  (d) line of symmetry x = −2
app_sections.why_it_works: Completing the square rewrites the quadratic as a single squared term plus a constant. A square is never negative, so when it is multiplied by a negative number the whole term is never positive — the expression reaches its largest value exactly when the square is zero. That single condition, x + 2 = 0, gives the x of the turning point, and the leftover constant is the turning value itself.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to multiply the −4 by the factored −3, giving k = −3 instead of 13.
Reading the vertex as (2, 13) instead of (−2, 13) — the sign of h flips.
Calling 13 a minimum because the number is positive, without checking the sign of a.
app_sections.exam_tip: Always check a completed square by substituting the vertex x-value back into the original expression — here q(−2) = −12 + 24 + 1 = 13 confirms it in seconds.

app_sections.think_first: A square is just a 90° construction repeated, so the whole figure follows from one perpendicular raised at E.
concepts_required: Constructing a perpendicular at a point on a line
app_sections.strategy: Draw EF = 6 cm, construct a perpendicular at E, mark H 6 cm up it, then use arcs of radius 6 cm from F and H to fix G; finally join FH and measure it.

guided_solution.instruction: Draw a base line and mark EF = 6 cm on it with the ruler.
Construct a perpendicular to EF at E.
guided_solution.note: With centre E draw arcs cutting the line each side, then from those two points draw equal arcs that cross above E; join the crossing point to E

guided_solution.instruction: Mark H on that perpendicular with EH = 6 cm.
guided_solution.note: Compasses set to 6 cm, centre E

guided_solution.instruction: Locate G with two arcs of radius 6 cm.
guided_solution.note: Centre F and centre H, radius 6 cm each; they cross at G

guided_solution.instruction: Join FG and HG to complete EFGH, then draw the diagonal FH and measure it.

app_sections.final_answer: (i) FH ≈ 8.5 cm (the exact value is 6√2 = 8.49 cm)
app_sections.why_it_works: Every angle of a square is a right angle and every side is equal, so a single constructed perpendicular plus two equal arcs pins the whole shape. The diagonal then closes a right-angled isosceles triangle with two sides of 6 cm, so Pythagoras gives FH = √(6² + 6²) = 6√2 — which is exactly what a correct drawing must measure.
common_mistakes: Using a protractor for the right angle when the question demands compasses.
Rubbing out the construction arcs — marks are given for them.
Measuring the side instead of the diagonal FH.
app_sections.exam_tip: Compute the expected answer with Pythagoras before you measure; if your ruler reading is more than about 0.2 cm away from it, your construction has drifted.

app_sections.why_it_works: Angle–side–angle fixes a triangle uniquely, so once the 5 cm side and the two angles at its ends are drawn, the third vertex has only one possible position. The angle sum of 180° then forces ∠PRQ = 30°, and because the triangle is right-angled at P, the tangent ratio predicts PR = PQ tan 60° — an independent check on the drawing.
common_mistakes: Placing the 60° at P and the 90° at Q, which swaps the triangle.
Measuring ∠PRQ with a protractor and accepting a badly drawn 29° or 32° instead of checking with the angle sum.
Setting different compass radii partway through the 60° construction.
app_sections.exam_tip: In construction questions, always compute one length or angle by trigonometry first — it tells you immediately whether your drawing is accurate enough for the mark.

quick_check.prompt: In a right-angled triangle, the side adjacent to a 60° angle is 4 cm and the right angle is at the far end of that side. How long is the opposite side?

question.source_text: 14. Using a ruler, a pencil and a pair of compasses, construct the trapezium ABCD with: • AB = 8 cm • BAD = 60° • AD = 6 cm • ABC = 90° • AB parallel to CD (Credit will be given for clearly drawn construction lines.)
question.display_policy: Render verified structured mathematics when available; always retain the linked source visual for fidelity.
question.question_restated: Using a ruler, a pencil and a pair of compasses, construct the trapezium ABCD with AB = 8 cm, ∠BAD = 60°, AD = 6 cm, ∠ABC = 90° and AB parallel to CD. Credit is given for clearly drawn construction lines.

app_sections.think_first: Build the two given angles on the fixed side AB first; the parallel condition then decides where C must sit.
concepts_required: Constructing a perpendicular at a point on a line
Constructing a line parallel to a given line
app_sections.strategy: Draw AB = 8 cm, construct 60° at A and mark AD = 6 cm, construct the perpendicular at B, then draw the line through D parallel to AB and let it cut that perpendicular at C.

guided_solution.instruction: Draw AB = 8 cm.
Construct a 60° angle at A and mark D on its arm with AD = 6 cm.
guided_solution.note: Standard 60° arc construction, then compasses set to 6 cm from A

guided_solution.instruction: Construct a perpendicular to AB at B, on the same side as D.
guided_solution.note: Equal arcs each side of B, then equal larger arcs crossing above B

guided_solution.instruction: Construct the line through D parallel to AB.
guided_solution.note: Copy the 60° angle at D on the other side of AD, or mark the equal perpendicular distance above AB
guided_solution.result: line through D parallel to AB

guided_solution.instruction: Mark C where that parallel meets the perpendicular from B, then join DC and BC.
guided_solution.note: Check by measurement: DC ≈ 5 cm and BC ≈ 5.2 cm

app_sections.final_answer: A correctly drawn trapezium ABCD with AB = 8 cm, AD = 6 cm, ∠BAD = 60°, ∠ABC = 90° and DC parallel to AB. Accuracy checks: DC ≈ 5 cm and BC ≈ 5.2 cm (= 6 sin 60°).
app_sections.why_it_works: The two given angles at the ends of AB fix the directions of AD and BC, and the given length AD fixes D. Requiring DC parallel to AB forces D and C to lie the same perpendicular distance above AB, so C is the single point where that line crosses the perpendicular from B. The height 6 sin 60° ≈ 5.20 cm and the horizontal shift 6 cos 60° = 3 cm are what make DC = 8 − 3 = 5 cm.
common_mistakes: Making CD parallel to AD instead of to AB.
Erasing the arcs used for the 60° and 90° constructions, losing the method marks.
Labelling the vertices out of order so the shape crosses over itself.
app_sections.exam_tip: Label vertices strictly in the order given (A, B, C, D around the shape) before you draw — most lost marks in construction come from a correctly built figure with the wrong letters on it.

question.source_text: 15. Using a ruler, a pencil and a pair of compasses: (i) Construct accurately the square ABCD, with sides 6 cm.
question.display_policy: Render verified structured mathematics when available; always retain the linked source visual for fidelity.
question.question_restated: Using a ruler, a pencil and a pair of compasses: (i) Construct accurately the square ABCD with sides 6 cm.

app_sections.think_first: One accurately constructed right angle is all a square needs — the rest is equal arcs of 6 cm.
concepts_required: Constructing a perpendicular at a point on a line
app_sections.strategy: Draw AB = 6 cm, construct a perpendicular at A, mark D 6 cm along it, then cut arcs of radius 6 cm from B and D to locate C.

guided_solution.instruction: Draw a base line and mark AB = 6 cm.
Construct a perpendicular to AB at A.
guided_solution.note: Arcs of equal radius each side of A on the line, then equal larger arcs from those two points crossing above A

guided_solution.instruction: Mark D on the perpendicular with AD = 6 cm.
guided_solution.note: Compasses set to 6 cm, centre A

guided_solution.instruction: Draw arcs of radius 6 cm from B and from D; call the crossing point C.
Join BC and DC, then check the figure.
guided_solution.note: All four sides 6 cm; each diagonal should measure 6√2 ≈ 8.5 cm

app_sections.final_answer: (i) A square ABCD with all four sides 6 cm and all angles 90°. Accuracy check: each diagonal measures 6√2 ≈ 8.5 cm.
app_sections.why_it_works: A quadrilateral with four equal sides and one right angle must be a square: the equal arcs guarantee the rhombus, and the constructed perpendicular upgrades it to a square. Because the construction uses only compasses and a straight edge, the right angle is exact rather than eyeballed.
common_mistakes: Using a protractor or set square instead of compasses.
Setting the compasses to slightly different radii for the two 6 cm arcs, so C is off.
Erasing construction arcs before the work is marked.
app_sections.exam_tip: Keep the compasses locked at 6 cm for every side arc — reopening them mid-construction is the commonest source of a lopsided square.

question.source_text: 16. Using a ruler, a pencil and a pair of compasses, construct triangle PQR with: • PQ = 8 cm • ∠PQR = 120° • QR = 5 cm
question.display_policy: Render verified structured mathematics when available; always retain the linked source visual for fidelity.
question.question_restated: Using a ruler, a pencil and a pair of compasses, construct triangle PQR with PQ = 8 cm, ∠PQR = 120° and QR = 5 cm.

app_sections.think_first: This is a side–angle–side construction, and 120° is simply 180° minus a constructed 60°.
concepts_required: Cosine rule as an accuracy check
app_sections.strategy: Draw PQ = 8 cm, construct 120° at Q by building 60° from the extension of PQ, mark R 5 cm along that arm, and join PR.

guided_solution.instruction: Draw PQ = 8 cm.
Extend PQ beyond Q to give a straight line through Q.
guided_solution.note: 120° is the supplement of 60°, so a 60° angle measured from the extension gives 120° with QP

guided_solution.instruction: Construct 60° at Q from the extension.
guided_solution.note: Centre Q, arc cutting the line; same radius from that intersection cuts the arc — join Q to the crossing

guided_solution.instruction: Mark R on that arm with QR = 5 cm.
guided_solution.note: Compasses set to 5 cm, centre Q

guided_solution.instruction: Join PR and check its length.

app_sections.final_answer: A correctly constructed triangle PQR with PQ = 8 cm, QR = 5 cm and the included angle ∠PQR = 120°. Accuracy check: PR ≈ 11.4 cm.
app_sections.why_it_works: Two sides and the angle between them fix a triangle uniquely, which is why side–angle–side works as a construction. Because 60° is the one angle compasses give directly (from an equilateral triangle), every multiple and supplement of 60° — 30°, 90°, 120° — is reachable by combining that construction with bisection or extension.
common_mistakes: Drawing the 60° on the wrong side of Q, producing 60° instead of 120°.
Marking QR = 5 cm along QP instead of along the new arm.
Checking with Pythagoras — the triangle is obtuse, not right-angled, so the cosine rule is the correct check.
app_sections.exam_tip: Remember the compass angle family: 60° direct, 30° by bisecting it, 90° by perpendicular, 120° as 180° − 60°. Recognising which one a question wants saves minutes.

question.source_text: 17. Using a ruler, a pencil and a pair of compasses, construct triangle ABC, such that: • AB = 8 cm • ∠BAC = 30° • AC = 10 cm
question.display_policy: Render verified structured mathematics when available; always retain the linked source visual for fidelity.
question.question_restated: Using a ruler, a pencil and a pair of compasses, construct triangle ABC such that AB = 8 cm, ∠BAC = 30° and AC = 10 cm.

app_sections.think_first: The 30° is not a direct compass angle — get it by constructing 60° and bisecting it.
app_sections.strategy: Draw AB = 8 cm, construct 60° at A and bisect it to get 30°, mark C 10 cm along that arm, then join BC.

guided_solution.instruction: Draw AB = 8 cm.
Construct a 60° angle at A.
guided_solution.note: Centre A, arc cutting AB at X; same radius centre X cuts the arc at Y; AY is at 60°

guided_solution.instruction: Bisect the 60° angle.
guided_solution.note: Equal arcs from X and Y crossing inside the angle; join A to the crossing

guided_solution.instruction: Mark C on the bisector with AC = 10 cm.
guided_solution.note: Compasses set to 10 cm, centre A

guided_solution.instruction: Join BC and check its length.

app_sections.final_answer: A correctly constructed triangle ABC with AB = 8 cm, AC = 10 cm and ∠BAC = 30°. Accuracy check: BC ≈ 5.0 cm.
app_sections.why_it_works: Angle bisection halves an angle exactly using only equal radii, so 30° comes from 60° with no protractor. Once the angle at A and both sides through A are set, the third vertex is determined, and the cosine rule gives the one length that verifies the whole drawing.
common_mistakes: Trying to construct 30° directly instead of bisecting 60°.
Bisecting with the compasses reset to a different radius between the two arcs.
Assuming BC must be long because the two given sides are long — here BC is the shortest side.
app_sections.exam_tip: When a construction asks for 30°, 45° or 15°, look for the bisection route first — those angles are never a single compass step.

quick_check.prompt: How would you construct a 45° angle with compasses only?
quick_check.answer: Construct a 90° perpendicular, then bisect it.

question.source_text: 18. Using a ruler, a pencil and a pair of compasses, construct the right-angled triangle ABC, such that: • AB = 5 cm • ∠ABC = 90° • ∠BAC = 60°
question.display_policy: Render verified structured mathematics when available; always retain the linked source visual for fidelity.
question.question_restated: Using a ruler, a pencil and a pair of compasses, construct the right-angled triangle ABC such that AB = 5 cm, ∠ABC = 90° and ∠BAC = 60°.

app_sections.think_first: Both required angles, 90° and 60°, are standard compass constructions built on the ends of AB.
concepts_required: Constructing a perpendicular at a point on a line
app_sections.strategy: Draw AB = 5 cm, construct 90° at B and 60° at A on the same side, and mark C where the two arms cross.

guided_solution.instruction: Draw AB = 5 cm.
Construct a perpendicular to AB at B.
guided_solution.note: Equal arcs each side of B along AB, then equal larger arcs from those points crossing above B

guided_solution.instruction: Construct a 60° angle at A on the same side of AB.
guided_solution.note: Centre A, arc cutting AB; same radius from that point cuts the arc; join A to it

guided_solution.instruction: Mark C where the two arms meet and join AC.
Check the drawing by calculation.

app_sections.final_answer: A correctly constructed right-angled triangle ABC with AB = 5 cm, ∠ABC = 90° and ∠BAC = 60°. Accuracy checks: BC ≈ 8.7 cm, AC = 10 cm and ∠ACB = 30°.
app_sections.why_it_works: Fixing a side and both angles at its ends (ASA) determines a triangle uniquely, so the two arms can only meet in one place. Because the triangle is right-angled, the tangent and cosine ratios give exact predicted lengths, turning an accuracy question into something you can verify numerically instead of trusting your eye.
common_mistakes: Building the 60° at B and the 90° at A, which reverses the triangle.
Drawing the two angles on opposite sides of AB, so the arms never meet.
Rounding 5√3 to 8 cm and then thinking the construction is wrong.
app_sections.exam_tip: Before drawing, sketch the triangle roughly and label the angles — it takes ten seconds and prevents the swapped-angle error that costs full marks.

quick_check.prompt: In a right-angled triangle with the right angle at B, AB = 4 cm and ∠BAC = 60°. Find AC.

question.source_text: 19. Using a ruler and a pair of compasses only, construct triangle NLM, in which: • LM = 12 cm • ∠MLN = 30° • ∠LMN = 90°
question.display_policy: Render verified structured mathematics when available; always retain the linked source visual for fidelity.
question.question_restated: Using a ruler and a pair of compasses only, construct triangle NLM in which LM = 12 cm, ∠MLN = 30° and ∠LMN = 90°.

app_sections.think_first: The 30° must come from bisecting a constructed 60°, since compasses cannot produce 30° in one step.
concepts_required: Constructing a perpendicular at a point on a line
app_sections.strategy: Draw LM = 12 cm, construct 60° at L and bisect it for 30°, construct the perpendicular at M, and mark N where the two arms meet.

guided_solution.instruction: Draw LM = 12 cm.
Construct 60° at L, then bisect it.
guided_solution.note: 60° arc construction, then equal arcs from the two arc points crossing inside

guided_solution.instruction: Construct a perpendicular to LM at M, on the same side as the 30° arm.
guided_solution.note: Equal arcs each side of M, then equal larger arcs crossing above M

guided_solution.instruction: Mark N where the two arms meet and join LN and MN.
Check the drawing by calculation.

app_sections.final_answer: A correctly constructed triangle NLM with LM = 12 cm, ∠MLN = 30° and ∠LMN = 90°. Accuracy checks: MN ≈ 6.9 cm, LN ≈ 13.9 cm and ∠LNM = 60°.
app_sections.why_it_works: Two angles at the ends of a known side determine the triangle, so no further measurement is needed. The construction is exact because 60° comes from an equilateral triangle and bisection halves it precisely; the perpendicular at M is likewise exact, so any error in the finished figure is drawing error, not method error.
common_mistakes: Using a protractor for the 30° when the question says ruler and compasses only.
Putting the perpendicular on the opposite side of LM from the 30° arm.
Misreading which vertex each angle belongs to — ∠MLN has its vertex at L.
app_sections.exam_tip: Read the vertex order in the angle name carefully: the middle letter is always the vertex, so ∠MLN puts the 30° at L.

question.source_text: 21. Using a ruler, a pencil and a pair of compasses, construct triangle XYZ, such that: • XY = 7 cm • YZ = 6 cm • XZ = 8 cm (i) Measure and state the size of angle XYZ. ∠XYZ = ______________________________
question.display_policy: Render verified structured mathematics when available; always retain the linked source visual for fidelity.
question.question_restated: Using a ruler, a pencil and a pair of compasses, construct triangle XYZ such that XY = 7 cm, YZ = 6 cm and XZ = 8 cm. (i) Measure and state the size of angle XYZ.

app_sections.think_first: Three given sides means a pure arc construction — no angles are drawn at all.
concepts_required: Cosine rule as an accuracy check
app_sections.strategy: Draw XY = 7 cm, swing an arc of radius 8 cm from X and one of radius 6 cm from Y; their intersection is Z. Then measure ∠XYZ.

guided_solution.instruction: Draw XY = 7 cm.
With centre X and radius 8 cm, draw an arc above XY.
guided_solution.note: This arc is every point at the correct distance XZ

guided_solution.instruction: With centre Y and radius 6 cm, draw a second arc cutting the first.
guided_solution.note: The crossing point is the only point at both correct distances

guided_solution.instruction: Join XZ and YZ, then measure ∠XYZ with a protractor.
Confirm with the cosine rule.

app_sections.why_it_works: Three sides fix a triangle completely — that is the SSS congruence condition — so the two arcs can only cross in one place on a given side of XY. The cosine rule is the algebraic form of the same fact: from three sides it returns one and only one value for each angle, which is why it can verify a measured construction.
common_mistakes: Drawing the arcs with the radii swapped (8 cm from Y, 6 cm from X), producing a mirror triangle.
Erasing the arcs, losing the construction marks.
Reading the outer scale of the protractor and writing 104.5° instead of 75.5°.
app_sections.exam_tip: After measuring an angle, check it against the side lengths: the largest angle must face the longest side. Here XZ = 8 cm is longest, so ∠XYZ must be the biggest angle — and it is.

question.source_text: 1. Several rays meet at O. The three angles above the horizontal straight line are (2x + 10)°, (x + 20)° and 3x°. [ a) Determine the value of x. b) Calculate the size of each of the three labelled angles above the line. c) The angle z is vertically opposite the angle (2x + 10)°. Determine z and state the relevant angle fact.
question.display_policy: Render verified structured mathematics when available; always retain the linked source visual for fidelity.
question.question_restated: Several rays meet at O on a horizontal straight line. The three angles above the line are (2x + 10)°, (x + 20)° and 3x°. a) Determine the value of x. b) Calculate the size of each of the three labelled angles above the line. c) The angle z is vertically opposite the angle (2x + 10)°. Determine z and state the relevant angle fact.

app_sections.think_first: Angles on one side of a straight line always add to 180°, and that single sentence gives you the equation.
concepts_required: Forming and solving a linear equation
app_sections.strategy: Set the three expressions equal to 180°, solve for x, substitute back for each angle, then use the vertically-opposite property for z.

guided_solution.instruction: Write the angle equation for the straight line.
Solve for x.
Substitute x = 25 into each expression.
Check the three angles.
Find z.
guided_solution.note: z is vertically opposite the 60° angle

app_sections.final_answer: (a) x = 25  (b) (2x + 10)° = 60°, (x + 20)° = 45°, 3x° = 75°  (c) z = 60°, because vertically opposite angles are equal
app_sections.why_it_works: Angles that sit side by side along a straight line make a half turn, which is 180°, so writing their sum as 180 is not a guess but a definition. When two straight lines cross, each pair of opposite angles is the supplement of the same neighbouring angle, so those opposite angles must be equal — that is the vertically opposite angle fact used for z.
common_mistakes: Setting the sum to 360° instead of 180°.
Finding x and stopping, without substituting back to give the actual angles.
Stating z = 60° without naming the angle fact, when the question explicitly asks for it.
app_sections.exam_tip: Always substitute your value of x back and check the angles add to the required total — it catches an arithmetic slip before you lose all the follow-on marks.
