question.source_text: 2. In trapezium ABCD, AB is parallel to DC and AD = BC. The angles at A and D are (3x + 10)° and (5x + 10)° respectively. a) Calculate the value of x. b) Calculate all four interior angles of ABCD, giving a reason for each pair of equal angles. c) State the most specific name of the trapezium.
question.display_policy: Render verified structured mathematics when available; always retain the linked source visual for fidelity.
question.question_restated: In trapezium ABCD, AB is parallel to DC and AD = BC. The angles at A and D are (3x + 10)° and (5x + 10)° respectively. a) Calculate the value of x. b) Calculate all four interior angles of ABCD, giving a reason for each pair of equal angles. c) State the most specific name of the trapezium.

app_sections.think_first: A and D are at the two ends of the same slanted side crossing a pair of parallel lines, so they are co-interior angles.
app_sections.strategy: Use the co-interior pair A and D to form an equation summing to 180°, solve for x, then use AD = BC to copy the angles across to B and C.

guided_solution.instruction: Identify the angle relationship at A and D.
guided_solution.note: AB is parallel to DC and AD is the transversal, so ∠A and ∠D are co-interior and add to 180°

guided_solution.instruction: Solve for x.
Evaluate the two given angles.
Use AD = BC to find the remaining angles.
guided_solution.note: The trapezium is isosceles, so the base angles on each parallel side are equal: ∠B = ∠A and ∠C = ∠D

guided_solution.instruction: Check the quadrilateral angle sum.

app_sections.final_answer: (a) x = 20  (b) ∠A = 70° and ∠B = 70° (equal base angles of an isosceles trapezium); ∠D = 110° and ∠C = 110° (equal base angles on DC, each co-interior with 70°)  (c) an isosceles trapezium
app_sections.why_it_works: When a transversal cuts two parallel lines, the two interior angles on the same side of it must total 180°, because together they wrap round from one parallel line to the other. The extra condition AD = BC makes the figure symmetrical about the perpendicular bisector of AB, and that mirror symmetry is what forces ∠A = ∠B and ∠D = ∠C.
common_mistakes: Treating ∠A and ∠D as equal (alternate) instead of supplementary (co-interior).
Assuming ∠A and ∠C are equal, as in a parallelogram — that is false here.
Answering 'trapezium' for part c when the equal sides make it specifically isosceles.
app_sections.exam_tip: Label which pair of parallel lines a transversal is crossing before deciding whether angles are equal or supplementary — the U-shape means add to 180°, the Z-shape means equal.

quick_check.prompt: In a trapezium PQRS with PQ parallel to SR, ∠P = 65°. Find ∠S.

question.source_text: 3. The diagram shows kite ABCD, where AB = AD, CB = CD, and diagonal AC is drawn. a) Prove that triangle ABC is congruent to triangle ADC. State the congruence case used. b) Hence show that AC bisects ∠BAD. c) If ∠ABC = 68°, determine ∠ADC.
question.display_policy: Render verified structured mathematics when available; always retain the linked source visual for fidelity.
question.question_restated: The diagram shows kite ABCD, where AB = AD, CB = CD, and the diagonal AC is drawn. a) Prove that triangle ABC is congruent to triangle ADC, stating the congruence case used. b) Hence show that AC bisects ∠BAD. c) If ∠ABC = 68°, determine ∠ADC.

app_sections.think_first: The diagonal AC belongs to both triangles, so it supplies the third pair of equal sides for free.
app_sections.strategy: List the three pairs of equal sides to establish SSS congruence, then read off the equal corresponding angles for parts b and c.

guided_solution.instruction: List the equal sides in triangles ABC and ADC.
guided_solution.note: AB = AD (given); CB = CD (given); AC = AC (common side)

guided_solution.instruction: State the congruence.
guided_solution.note: All three sides of one triangle equal all three sides of the other

guided_solution.instruction: Use corresponding angles at A.
guided_solution.note: ∠BAC and ∠DAC are corresponding angles of the congruent triangles, so they are equal

guided_solution.instruction: Conclude the bisection.
guided_solution.note: AC splits ∠BAD into two equal parts

guided_solution.instruction: Match the angles at B and D.
guided_solution.note: ∠ABC and ∠ADC are corresponding angles of the congruent triangles

app_sections.final_answer: (a) Triangle ABC ≅ triangle ADC by SSS (AB = AD, CB = CD, AC common)  (b) ∠BAC = ∠DAC as corresponding angles of congruent triangles, so AC bisects ∠BAD  (c) ∠ADC = 68°
app_sections.why_it_works: Congruence means the two triangles are identical copies, so every matched part — side, angle, area — is equal. Once SSS is established, no further calculation is needed for parts b and c: the equal angles are simply corresponding parts being read off. This is why a kite's axis of symmetry is exactly the diagonal joining the two vertices where equal sides meet.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to state AC = AC (common) — without it there is no third pair and no SSS.
Claiming SAS by using the angle at A, which is what you are trying to prove equal.
Writing the congruence with mismatched letter order, so the corresponding parts read off are the wrong ones.
app_sections.exam_tip: In a congruence proof, always write the two triangles with corresponding vertices in matching order (ABC ↔ ADC) — then every corresponding pair can be read straight off the naming.

quick_check.prompt: In kite PQRS, PQ = PS and RQ = RS. Which diagonal is the axis of symmetry?

question.source_text: 4. Line segments AC and BD intersect at O. It is given that AO = OC and BO = OD. a) Prove that triangle AOB is congruent to triangle COD. State the congruence case used. b) Hence prove that AB = CD. c) Use a pair of equal alternate angles to show that AB is parallel to CD.
question.display_policy: Render verified structured mathematics when available; always retain the linked source visual for fidelity.
question.question_restated: Line segments AC and BD intersect at O, with AO = OC and BO = OD. a) Prove that triangle AOB is congruent to triangle COD, stating the congruence case used. b) Hence prove that AB = CD. c) Use a pair of equal alternate angles to show that AB is parallel to CD.

app_sections.think_first: The crossing point O gives you a pair of vertically opposite angles, which is exactly the angle wedged between the two given equal sides.
concepts_required: Alternate angles and the test for parallel lines
app_sections.strategy: Pair the two given equal sides with the vertically opposite angle between them to get SAS, then read off equal corresponding sides and angles.

guided_solution.instruction: List the equal parts of triangles AOB and COD.
guided_solution.note: AO = OC (given); ∠AOB = ∠COD (vertically opposite angles); BO = OD (given)

guided_solution.instruction: State the congruence.
guided_solution.note: Two sides and the angle between them are equal

guided_solution.instruction: Read off the third pair of sides.
guided_solution.note: AB and CD are corresponding sides of the congruent triangles

guided_solution.instruction: Read off a pair of corresponding angles at A and C.
Interpret those angles for the line AC.
guided_solution.note: AC is a transversal cutting AB and CD, and ∠BAO and ∠DCO are alternate angles; equal alternate angles mean the lines are parallel

app_sections.final_answer: (a) Triangle AOB ≅ triangle COD by SAS (AO = OC, ∠AOB = ∠COD vertically opposite, BO = OD)  (b) AB = CD as corresponding sides of congruent triangles  (c) ∠BAO = ∠DCO are equal alternate angles for AB and CD with transversal AC, so AB is parallel to CD
app_sections.why_it_works: SAS works because fixing two sides and the angle wedged between them leaves no freedom in the third side. The vertically opposite angle is the key: it is equal automatically wherever two straight lines cross, so the diagram supplies the middle ingredient without it being stated. Part c then runs the alternate-angle rule backwards — equal alternate angles are not just a consequence of parallel lines, they are a test for them.
common_mistakes: Using ∠OAB and ∠OCD as the included angle — the included angle must be at O, between the two given sides.
Quoting SSA, which is not a valid congruence case.
Saying AB is parallel to CD because the diagram looks that way, instead of naming the equal alternate angles.
app_sections.exam_tip: Whenever two lines cross in a proof diagram, immediately mark the vertically opposite angles as equal — that free fact completes most SAS proofs.

question.question_restated: In triangle ABC, D lies on AB, E lies on AC and DE is parallel to BC, with AD = 6 cm, DB = 4 cm and AE = 7.5 cm. a) Explain why triangle ADE is similar to triangle ABC. b) Calculate the length of EC. c) The area of triangle ADE is 27 cm². Calculate the area of trapezium DBCE.

app_sections.think_first: DE parallel to BC creates equal corresponding angles, which is exactly what similarity needs — and remember the sides are compared to the whole triangle, not to the small piece.
concepts_required: Ratio of areas of similar figures
app_sections.strategy: Establish AA similarity from the parallel lines, use the ratio AD : AB to find AC and then EC, and square the length ratio to compare areas.

guided_solution.instruction: Match the angles of the two triangles.
guided_solution.note: ∠ADE = ∠ABC and ∠AED = ∠ACB (corresponding angles, DE parallel to BC); ∠A is common

guided_solution.instruction: Write the ratio of corresponding sides using the full side AB.
Find AC, then EC.
Convert the length ratio to an area ratio.
guided_solution.note: Area ADE : area ABC = 3² : 5² = 9 : 25, so area ABC = 27 × 25/9

guided_solution.instruction: Subtract to get the trapezium.
guided_solution.note: Area DBCE = area ABC − area ADE = 75 − 27

app_sections.final_answer: (a) ∠A is common and ∠ADE = ∠ABC, ∠AED = ∠ACB are corresponding angles because DE is parallel to BC, so the triangles are similar by AA  (b) EC = 5 cm  (c) area of trapezium DBCE = 48 cm²
app_sections.why_it_works: Parallel lines force corresponding angles to be equal, so the small triangle is an exact scaled copy of the large one sitting in the same corner. Under a scale factor k every length multiplies by k but every area multiplies by k², because area depends on two perpendicular directions at once. That is why a 3 : 5 length ratio becomes a 9 : 25 area ratio, and the trapezium is simply what is left when the small triangle is removed.
common_mistakes: Using AD : DB = 6 : 4 as the scale factor instead of AD : AB = 6 : 10.
Scaling the area by 3/5 rather than (3/5)².
Giving the area of the whole triangle ABC as the answer to part c instead of subtracting the small triangle.
app_sections.exam_tip: In a 'triangle within a triangle' similarity, always write out the full side of the large triangle first (AB = AD + DB) — the single most common error is comparing a part to a part.

quick_check.prompt: Two similar triangles have corresponding sides in the ratio 2 : 3. The smaller has area 12 cm². What is the area of the larger?

concepts_required: Comparing measurements to make a decision
app_sections.strategy: Apply Pythagoras to the 2.40 m and 0.90 m sides to get the diagonal, then compare that exact value with 2.55 m.

guided_solution.instruction: Identify the right-angled triangle.
guided_solution.note: The height and width meet at a corner at 90°, and the brace joins the opposite corners
guided_solution.result: legs 2.40 m and 0.90 m, hypotenuse = brace

guided_solution.instruction: Apply Pythagoras' theorem.
Take the square root.
guided_solution.result: brace = 2.56 m to the nearest centimetre

guided_solution.instruction: Compare the timber with the required length.
State the decision with the shortfall.

app_sections.final_answer: (a) The brace must be 2.56 m (to the nearest centimetre)  (b) No — the timber is 2.55 m but 2.5632 m is needed, so it falls short by about 0.013 m, roughly 1.3 cm
app_sections.why_it_works: The two sides of a rectangle meet at a right angle, so the diagonal is always the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle and Pythagoras applies directly. In part b the comparison must be made against the unrounded value: rounding to 2.56 m first still gives the right decision here, but rounding before comparing is the habit that produces wrong answers in borderline cases.
common_mistakes: Adding 2.40 and 0.90 instead of squaring, adding and square-rooting.
Rounding √6.57 to 2.6 m and then claiming 2.55 m is nowhere near.
Answering 'no' without a numerical justification, which the question specifically demands.

app_sections.strategy: Use Pythagoras on the 15 km and 8 km legs to get HR, compare it with the 16 km range, then subtract HR from the total travelled.

guided_solution.instruction: Note the right angle at Q.

guided_solution.instruction: Apply Pythagoras' theorem.
Take the square root.
Compare with the radio range.
guided_solution.result: the boat is out of range

guided_solution.instruction: Compare the two routes.
guided_solution.result: the direct route is 6 km shorter

app_sections.why_it_works: Compass directions that differ by 90° always produce a right-angled triangle, so Pythagoras converts two perpendicular legs into a single straight-line distance. Part c makes the triangle inequality concrete: any two sides of a triangle together exceed the third, which is exactly why going direct always beats going round two sides.
common_mistakes: Adding 15 and 8 to get a distance of 23 km for HR.
Deciding the boat is in range because 17 is 'close to' 16 — the comparison is strict.
Subtracting 16 from 17 in part c instead of comparing 23 with 17.

question.question_restated: A cuboid has length 12 cm, width 9 cm and height 8 cm. AC is a diagonal of the base and AG is a space diagonal. a) Calculate the length of AC. b) Hence calculate the length of AG. c) State why Pythagoras' theorem may be used twice in this problem.

app_sections.think_first: Get the flat base diagonal first — it becomes one leg of a second, upright right-angled triangle.
concepts_required: Identifying right angles in a solid
app_sections.strategy: Apply Pythagoras in the horizontal base to find AC, then again in the vertical triangle ACG using AC and the height.

guided_solution.instruction: Work in the rectangular base ABCD.
guided_solution.note: AB = 12 cm and BC = 9 cm meet at right angles

guided_solution.instruction: Apply Pythagoras to find AC.
Set up the upright triangle ACG.
guided_solution.note: CG is the vertical edge of 8 cm and it is perpendicular to the base, so ∠ACG = 90°
guided_solution.result: legs AC = 15 cm and CG = 8 cm

guided_solution.instruction: Apply Pythagoras again.
Explain the double use.
guided_solution.note: Two separate right-angled triangles exist: ABC lying flat in the base, and ACG standing upright because the vertical edge is perpendicular to every line in the base
guided_solution.result: two right angles, so two applications

app_sections.final_answer: (a) AC = 15 cm  (b) AG = 17 cm  (c) Because the solid contains two different right-angled triangles: ABC in the horizontal base (adjacent edges of a rectangle meet at 90°), and ACG in a vertical plane (the edge CG is perpendicular to the base, so it is perpendicular to AC). Pythagoras applies once in each.
app_sections.why_it_works: A vertical edge of a cuboid is perpendicular to every line drawn in the base, so pairing it with any base line automatically creates a right-angled triangle. That is what lets a three-dimensional length be reached in two flat steps: reduce the base to a single diagonal, then stand that diagonal up against the height. The same idea gives AG² = 12² + 9² + 8².
common_mistakes: Trying to use the height together with a single edge, skipping the base diagonal step.
Using 12 and 8 in the second step instead of AC = 15 and 8.
Treating AG as a face diagonal rather than a space diagonal.
app_sections.exam_tip: For any cuboid, the space diagonal is √(l² + w² + h²) — use the two-step method to show working, then use this formula to check your answer.

question.display_policy: Render verified structured mathematics when available; always retain the linked source visual for fidelity.
question.question_restated: A right-angled triangle has perpendicular sides a and b, hypotenuse c, and acute angle θ between the side b and the hypotenuse c, with a opposite θ. a) Express c in terms of a and b. b) Write an expression for sin θ + cos θ in terms of a, b and c. c) Given that a : b = 3 : 4, determine the exact value of sin θ + cos θ.

app_sections.think_first: Identify which side is opposite θ and which is adjacent before writing any ratio.
concepts_required: Sine and cosine ratios in a right-angled triangle
app_sections.strategy: Use Pythagoras for c, write the two ratios with respect to θ and add them, then substitute a = 3k, b = 4k to get a numerical value.

guided_solution.instruction: Apply Pythagoras to the two perpendicular sides.
Identify the sides relative to θ.
guided_solution.note: a is opposite θ and b is adjacent to θ, with c the hypotenuse
guided_solution.result: sin θ = a/c, cos θ = b/c

guided_solution.instruction: Add the two ratios.
Introduce the given ratio.
guided_solution.note: a : b = 3 : 4, so write a = 3k and b = 4k

guided_solution.instruction: Substitute into (a + b)/c.

app_sections.final_answer: (a) c = √(a² + b²)  (b) sin θ + cos θ = (a + b)/c  (c) sin θ + cos θ = 7/5 (= 1.4)
app_sections.why_it_works: Trigonometric ratios compare sides, so they depend only on the shape of the triangle and not on its size — which is why introducing the scale factor k and then cancelling it is legitimate. A 3 : 4 ratio of legs always produces the 3-4-5 triangle, so the exact value 7/5 holds for every triangle with those proportions, however large.
common_mistakes: Writing sin θ = b/c because b looks like the 'main' side — always check which side is opposite the angle.
Adding the ratios as (a + b)/(2c) or multiplying instead of adding.
Assuming a = 3 and b = 4 as actual lengths; using a = 3k, b = 4k shows the answer is independent of size.
app_sections.exam_tip: When a question gives a ratio rather than lengths, set the parts as multiples of k straight away — the k always cancels in a trigonometric ratio.

question.display_policy: Render verified structured mathematics when available; always retain the linked source visual for fidelity.
question.question_restated: A right-angled triangle ABC has the right angle at B, with BC = x, AB = x + 7 and hypotenuse AC = x + 8, where x is positive. The acute angle θ is at C. a) Use Pythagoras' theorem to form an equation in x. b) Solve the equation and state the three side lengths. c) Determine the exact values of sin θ, cos θ and tan θ.

app_sections.think_first: The longest expression, x + 8, must be the hypotenuse, so it is the one that stands alone on its side of the equation.
concepts_required: Forming and solving a quadratic equation
Trigonometric ratios in a right-angled triangle
app_sections.strategy: Square the two legs, set their sum equal to the square of the hypotenuse, solve the resulting quadratic and reject the negative root, then read off the ratios at C.

guided_solution.instruction: Write Pythagoras with the hypotenuse alone.
Expand both brackets.
Collect all terms on one side.
Factorise and solve, rejecting the negative root.
Write the ratios at C.
guided_solution.note: Opposite θ is AB = 12, adjacent is BC = 5, hypotenuse is AC = 13
guided_solution.result: sin θ = 12/13, cos θ = 5/13, tan θ = 12/5

app_sections.final_answer: (a) x² + (x + 7)² = (x + 8)²  (b) x = 5, so the sides are 5, 12 and 13  (c) sin θ = 12/13, cos θ = 5/13, tan θ = 12/5
app_sections.why_it_works: Pythagoras turns a geometric condition into an algebraic one, and because the unknown appears squared on both sides the x² terms partly cancel, leaving a quadratic that factorises cleanly. The negative root is rejected not by convention but because a side length cannot be negative. The result is the familiar 5-12-13 right triangle, whose ratios are exact fractions with no rounding at all.
common_mistakes: Setting x² + (x + 8)² = (x + 7)², i.e. choosing the wrong side as the hypotenuse.
Expanding (x + 7)² as x² + 49.
Keeping x = −3 as a second answer instead of rejecting it.
app_sections.exam_tip: In any Pythagoras equation, put the largest side by itself on one side — with algebraic sides the largest is the one with the biggest constant.

quick_check.prompt: A right-angled triangle has legs x and x + 2 and hypotenuse x + 4, with x positive. Form and solve the equation.
quick_check.answer: x² + (x + 2)² = (x + 4)² gives x² − 4x − 12 = 0, so x = 6 and the sides are 6, 8, 10.

question.source_text: 3. The right-angled triangle has side lengths 9, 12 and 15. The acute angles are θ and φ. a) Write the exact values of sin θ and cos φ. Hence state a relationship between them. b) Explain why θ + φ = 90°. c) Evaluate sin θ + cos θ exactly.
question.display_policy: Render verified structured mathematics when available; always retain the linked source visual for fidelity.
question.question_restated: A right-angled triangle has side lengths 9, 12 and 15, with the right angle between the sides 9 and 12. The acute angles are θ (between the 12-side and the hypotenuse) and φ (between the 9-side and the hypotenuse). a) Write the exact values of sin θ and cos φ, and hence state a relationship between them. b) Explain why θ + φ = 90°. c) Evaluate sin θ + cos θ exactly.

app_sections.think_first: θ and φ sit at opposite ends of the same hypotenuse, so what is 'opposite' for one is 'adjacent' for the other.
app_sections.strategy: Write each ratio from the triangle, notice the two fractions are identical, then use the angle sum to explain the complementary relationship.

guided_solution.instruction: Write sin θ.
guided_solution.note: The side opposite θ is 9 and the hypotenuse is 15

guided_solution.instruction: Write cos φ.
guided_solution.note: The side adjacent to φ is 9 and the hypotenuse is 15

guided_solution.instruction: State the relationship.
Use the angle sum for part b.
guided_solution.note: The three angles total 180° and one of them is the right angle: θ + φ + 90 = 180

guided_solution.instruction: Find cos θ and add.
guided_solution.note: The side adjacent to θ is 12, so cos θ = 12/15 = 4/5; then 3/5 + 4/5

app_sections.final_answer: (a) sin θ = 3/5 and cos φ = 3/5, so sin θ = cos φ  (b) The angles of a triangle sum to 180° and one angle is 90°, so θ + φ = 180° − 90° = 90°; the two acute angles are complementary  (c) sin θ + cos θ = 3/5 + 4/5 = 7/5
app_sections.why_it_works: In a right-angled triangle the two acute angles must be complementary, because the right angle already uses half of the 180°. The side opposite one acute angle is the side adjacent to the other, so their sine and cosine swap roles: sin θ = cos(90° − θ). That identity is not a coincidence of these numbers — it holds for every right-angled triangle.
common_mistakes: Using the hypotenuse 15 as one of the perpendicular sides.
Writing cos φ = 12/15 by taking the wrong side as adjacent to φ.
Giving sin θ + cos θ as a decimal such as 1.4 when the question asks for an exact value.
app_sections.exam_tip: Memorise sin θ = cos(90° − θ); it turns many 'find the relationship' questions into a one-line answer.

question.question_restated: The cross-section of a symmetrical roof is an isosceles triangle. Half the base is b, the vertical height is h, each sloping rafter has length s, and the base angle is θ. a) Express s in terms of b and h. b) Write sin θ + cos θ as a single fraction in terms of b, h and s. c) Given that tan θ = 3/4, show that s = 5b/4. d) Hence find the total length of the two sloping rafters in terms of b.

app_sections.think_first: The vertical height splits the isosceles triangle into two identical right-angled triangles with legs b and h and hypotenuse s.
concepts_required: Trigonometric ratios in a right-angled triangle
app_sections.strategy: Work inside one half-triangle: use Pythagoras for s, write the two ratios with respect to θ, then substitute h = 3b/4 from the given tangent.

guided_solution.instruction: Identify the right-angled half-triangle.
guided_solution.note: The height h is perpendicular to the base, giving legs b and h with hypotenuse s
guided_solution.result: right angle at the foot of h

guided_solution.instruction: Apply Pythagoras.
Write the two ratios at θ and add them.
guided_solution.note: sin θ = h/s (opposite over hypotenuse), cos θ = b/s (adjacent over hypotenuse)

guided_solution.instruction: Use tan θ = 3/4 to express h in terms of b.
Substitute into s = √(b² + h²) and double it.

app_sections.final_answer: (a) s = √(b² + h²)  (b) sin θ + cos θ = (h + b)/s  (c) tan θ = h/b = 3/4 gives h = 3b/4, so s² = b² + 9b²/16 = 25b²/16 and s = 5b/4  (d) total length of the two rafters = 2s = 5b/2
app_sections.why_it_works: Symmetry is what makes this work: the perpendicular height of an isosceles triangle bisects the base, creating two congruent right-angled triangles, so one of them carries all the information. Because tan θ fixes the ratio h : b rather than either value, every roof with tan θ = 3/4 is a scaled 3-4-5 triangle, and s always comes out as exactly 5/4 of the half-base.
common_mistakes: Using the full base instead of the half-base b in Pythagoras.
Writing tan θ = b/h instead of h/b — the opposite side is the height.
Giving the answer to part d as s rather than 2s, forgetting there are two rafters.
app_sections.exam_tip: In any isosceles triangle problem, draw the perpendicular height first — it converts the shape into two right-angled triangles you already know how to handle.

question.question_restated: P, Q and R lie on the same horizontal line with Q between P and R. A vertical mast RT is observed from P and from Q. PQ = 20 m, and the angles of elevation of T are 32° from P and 48° from Q. a) Let QR = x m and RT = h m, and write two equations for h using tangent. b) Hence show that x tan 48° = (x + 20) tan 32°. c) Calculate x and the height of the mast, giving each answer to 3 significant figures.

app_sections.think_first: Two right-angled triangles share the same vertical side h, so writing h twice and equating is the whole method.
concepts_required: Solving a linear equation with trigonometric coefficients
app_sections.strategy: Write h = x tan 48° from triangle QRT and h = (x + 20) tan 32° from triangle PRT, equate them and solve for x, then substitute back for h.

guided_solution.instruction: Use triangle QRT.
Use triangle PRT.
guided_solution.note: PR = PQ + QR = x + 20, and tan 32° = h ÷ (x + 20)

guided_solution.instruction: Equate the two expressions for h.
guided_solution.note: Both equal the same height h

guided_solution.instruction: Collect the x terms and solve.
Substitute back to find h.

app_sections.final_answer: (a) h = x tan 48° and h = (x + 20) tan 32°  (b) equating the two gives x tan 48° = (x + 20) tan 32°  (c) x = 25.7 m and the mast is 28.6 m high (both to 3 significant figures)
app_sections.why_it_works: The mast is the common side of two right-angled triangles standing on the same horizontal line, so expressing its height twice creates a single equation in the one unknown horizontal distance. The nearer observation point always gives the larger angle of elevation, which is why tan 48° − tan 32° is positive and x comes out positive. Only after x is known can the height be recovered.
common_mistakes: Using PR = 20 instead of PR = x + 20.
Rounding x to 25.7 before computing h, which shifts the height in the third significant figure.
Pairing 48° with the far point P and 32° with the near point Q.
app_sections.exam_tip: Keep the unrounded value of x in your calculator memory when substituting back — round only the final answers to the stated accuracy.

question.question_restated: A cliff AB is 36 m high, with B at sea level. From the top A, the angle of depression of a boat at C is 28°. a) Explain why the angle of elevation of A from C is also 28°. b) Calculate the horizontal distance BC. c) The boat moves 25 m directly towards B. Calculate the new angle of elevation of A, to the nearest degree.

app_sections.think_first: The horizontal at the cliff top and the sea surface are parallel, so the depression and elevation angles are alternate angles.
app_sections.strategy: Justify the equal angles from parallel horizontals, use tan 28° to get BC, subtract 25 m and use the inverse tangent for the new angle.

guided_solution.instruction: Compare the two horizontals.
guided_solution.note: The horizontal line at A and the sea-level line through B and C are parallel, and AC is a transversal
guided_solution.result: depression at A and elevation at C are alternate angles

guided_solution.instruction: State the conclusion for part a.
guided_solution.note: Alternate angles between parallel lines are equal
guided_solution.result: angle of elevation of A from C = 28°

guided_solution.instruction: Use the tangent ratio in triangle ABC.
Find the new horizontal distance.
Compute the new angle with inverse tangent.

app_sections.final_answer: (a) The horizontal at A is parallel to sea level, so the angle of depression at A and the angle of elevation at C are alternate angles between parallel lines and are therefore equal, both 28°  (b) BC ≈ 67.7 m  (c) the new angle of elevation is approximately 40°
app_sections.why_it_works: Angles of depression and elevation are always measured from a horizontal, and all horizontals in a vertical plane are parallel — so the alternate-angle rule makes the two angles equal every time. As the boat comes closer the same 36 m height is seen across a shorter base, so the tangent ratio grows and the angle of elevation increases, which is exactly what the calculation confirms.
common_mistakes: Measuring the angle of depression from the vertical cliff instead of the horizontal, giving 62°.
Adding 25 m rather than subtracting it, when the boat moves towards the cliff.
Rounding BC to 68 m before part c, which pushes the final angle to the wrong degree.
app_sections.exam_tip: Draw the dashed horizontal at the observer's eye every time a depression angle appears — the alternate-angle transfer to the ground point becomes obvious and saves a whole mark.

Total the four cables and add 2%.

app_sections.why_it_works: Because the mast stands at the centre and is perpendicular to the whole base, every corner is the same horizontal distance from M — half a diagonal — so all four cables are equal and only one needs calculating. The mast being vertical is what guarantees the right angle at M, letting Pythagoras carry a two-dimensional distance up into three dimensions. The 2% allowance is a multiplication by 1.02 applied after totalling.

Calculating AT for one corner and forgetting to multiply by four.
Adding 2 m instead of 2%, or applying the 2% to a single cable only.

question.question_restated: The quantities distance, displacement, speed, velocity, time and acceleration are used to describe the motion of a car. (a) State the THREE vector quantities. (b) State ONE feature that distinguishes a vector from a scalar.

app_sections.think_first: Ask of each quantity: does it need a direction to make sense?
app_sections.strategy: Test each quantity for whether a direction is part of its meaning, then state the defining difference.

guided_solution.instruction: Test each quantity for direction.
guided_solution.note: Distance, speed and time answer only 'how much'; displacement, velocity and acceleration all need 'in which direction'

guided_solution.instruction: List the vectors.
Name the remaining quantities as scalars.
guided_solution.note: Distance, speed and time have size only

guided_solution.instruction: State the distinguishing feature.
guided_solution.note: A vector has both magnitude and direction; a scalar has magnitude only

app_sections.final_answer: (a) The three vector quantities are displacement, velocity and acceleration  (b) A vector has both magnitude and direction, whereas a scalar has magnitude only
app_sections.why_it_works: The distinction is not about the numbers involved but about what the quantity describes. A speed of 60 km/h tells you nothing about where the car is heading; a velocity of 60 km/h due north does. Because vectors carry direction, they combine by the triangle or parallelogram law rather than by plain addition — which is why 3 km east then 4 km north gives a displacement of 5 km, not 7 km.
common_mistakes: Calling distance a vector by confusing it with displacement.
Listing speed as a vector because it has a numerical size.
Answering part b with 'a vector is bigger' or 'a vector is an arrow' rather than naming magnitude and direction.
app_sections.exam_tip: Pair each scalar with its vector partner — distance/displacement, speed/velocity — and the classification questions answer themselves.

quick_check.prompt: Is force a vector or a scalar? Give a reason.
quick_check.answer: A vector, because a force has both size and a direction in which it acts.

question.question_restated: The vector a is the column vector with components 6 and 8. (a) Calculate |a|, the magnitude of a. (b) Write down a unit vector in the direction of a.

app_sections.think_first: The two components are the legs of a right-angled triangle whose hypotenuse is the magnitude.
app_sections.strategy: Apply Pythagoras to the components for the magnitude, then divide the vector by that magnitude to get the unit vector.

guided_solution.instruction: Apply Pythagoras to the components.
Take the square root.
Divide the vector by its magnitude.
Check the unit vector.

app_sections.final_answer: (a) |a| = 10  (b) the unit vector is (1/10)(6, 8) = (0.6, 0.8), that is the column vector with components 3/5 and 4/5
app_sections.why_it_works: A column vector describes a horizontal step and a vertical step, which meet at a right angle, so its length is exactly the hypotenuse Pythagoras gives. Dividing every component by that length scales the arrow down to length 1 without turning it, so the direction is preserved while the size becomes the standard unit — which is why a unit vector is the pure statement of direction.
common_mistakes: Adding the components to get 14 instead of using Pythagoras.
Forgetting the square root and giving |a| = 100.
Dividing only one component by the magnitude.
app_sections.exam_tip: Always verify a unit vector by squaring and adding its components — the total must be exactly 1.

Solve the bottom equation.

So two vectors are equal only when both components agree, and a single vector equation is really a pair of separate equations — here one in x and one in y.

Matching the top of a with the bottom of b.

app_sections.why_it_works: Multiplying a vector by a scalar stretches it without changing the line it lies along, so any pair related by p = kq must be parallel. The magnitude is the straight-line distance between the points, so this is the distance formula in vector clothing. Dividing by that distance rescales the arrow to length 1 while leaving its direction untouched, which is what makes a unit vector the standard way to record 'this way' with no size attached.

Because only the start and finish matter, any route from A to C gives the same resultant — this path-independence is what makes vector addition useful for combining displacements, forces or velocities.

Assuming |AC| = |a| + |b|; the magnitudes only add when a and b point the same way.

That is why AC equals OB, and why the diagonal from the common vertex is the sum of the two sides meeting there: the parallelogram law and the triangle law are the same rule seen from two angles.

When they also share a point — here B is the end of AB and the start of BC — the only way for both to lie in the same direction from that shared point is for all three points to sit on one straight line. question.question_restated: In triangle OAB, OA = a and OB = b. The point P divides AB so that AP : PB = 2 : 1. (a) Express the vector AB in terms of a and b. (b) Express the vector AP in terms of a and b. (c) Hence show that OP = (1/3)a + (2/3)b.

app_sections.think_first: Convert the ratio into a fraction of the whole: AP : PB = 2 : 1 means AP is two-thirds of AB.
concepts_required: Dividing a line in a given ratio
app_sections.strategy: Write AB as a route through O, take two-thirds of it for AP, then travel O to A to P.

guided_solution.instruction: Write AB as a route through O.
Turn the ratio into a fraction.
guided_solution.note: AP : PB = 2 : 1, so AB is divided into 3 equal parts and AP is 2 of them

guided_solution.instruction: Substitute for AB.
Write OP as a route through A.
Simplify the coefficient of a.

app_sections.why_it_works: Any journey between two points can be rerouted through a third, which is why AB becomes AO + OB and turns into b − a. A ratio along a line is a fraction of the whole displacement, so P sits two-thirds of the way from A to B. Notice the coefficients of a and b in the final answer add to 1 — that is the signature of a point lying on the line AB, and a quick way to check this kind of result.
common_mistakes: Writing AB = a − b instead of b − a; the route runs from A, so AO = −a comes first.
Taking AP = (1/2)AB by treating the ratio as a fraction directly instead of 2 parts out of 3.
Stopping at OP = a + (2/3)(b − a) without simplifying to the required form.
app_sections.exam_tip: Check any 'point on a line' vector answer by adding the coefficients — if they do not total 1, the point is not on that line and you have slipped somewhere.

quick_check.prompt: In triangle OAB with OA = a and OB = b, M is the midpoint of AB. Express OM in terms of a and b.

(b) Given that 𝑀 is the midpoint of 𝑂𝐶, express 𝑂𝑀 ⃗⃗⃗⃗⃗⃗ in terms of 𝐚 and 𝐛. (c) Express 𝐴𝑀 ⃗⃗⃗⃗⃗⃗ in terms of 𝐚 and 𝐛. (d) Hence, show that 𝑀 is also the midpoint of 𝐴𝐵.

question.question_restated: OACB is a parallelogram whose diagonals OC and AB meet at M, with OA = a and OB = b. (a) Express OC in terms of a and b. (b) Given that M is the midpoint of OC, express OM in terms of a and b. (c) Express AM in terms of a and b. (d) Hence show that M is also the midpoint of AB.

app_sections.think_first: In the parallelogram OACB the two sides leaving O are a and b, so every other point can be reached by travelling along combinations of those two vectors.
concepts_required: Midpoint of a line segment in vector form
app_sections.strategy: Build OC as the sum of the two sides from O, halve it to reach M, then get AM as AO + OM and compare it with AB.

guided_solution.instruction: Travel from O to C along two sides of the parallelogram.
guided_solution.note: O to A is a, and A to C equals O to B because AC is parallel and equal to OB.

guided_solution.instruction: Take half of OC to reach the midpoint M.
Go from A to M by way of O.
Write AB in terms of a and b and compare it with AM.
guided_solution.note: AB = AO + OB = −a + b = b − a, so AM = ½ AB
guided_solution.result: AM = ½ AB, so M lies on AB halfway along it

app_sections.final_answer: (a) OC = a + b  (b) OM = ½(a + b)  (c) AM = ½(b − a)  (d) Since AB = b − a and AM = ½(b − a) = ½AB, the point M lies on AB and divides it equally, so M is the midpoint of AB.
app_sections.why_it_works: Any point in a plane can be written as a combination of two non-parallel vectors, and in a parallelogram the opposite sides are represented by identical vectors. Because OM came out as exactly half of OC, and AM came out as exactly half of AB, both diagonals are cut in the same place. That single point M is what the vector algebra proves the diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other.
common_mistakes: Writing OC = a − b instead of a + b by mixing up the direction of AC.
Forgetting that AO = −OA when routing a journey through O.
Concluding M is the midpoint of AB from the picture rather than from AM = ½AB.
app_sections.exam_tip: Turn every vector you need into a journey between named points, then insert O as a stopping point: XY = XO + OY always works.

quick_check.prompt: In the same parallelogram, express BM in terms of a and b.
quick_check.answer: BM = BO + OM = −b + ½(a + b) = ½(a − b)

question.source_text: 16. In triangle 𝑂𝐴𝐵, 𝑀 is the midpoint of 𝑂𝐴 and 𝑁 is the midpoint of 𝑂𝐵. 𝑂𝐴 ⃗⃗⃗⃗⃗ = 𝐚 and 𝑂𝐵 ⃗⃗⃗⃗⃗ = 𝐛. (a) Express 𝑂𝑀 ⃗⃗⃗⃗⃗⃗ and 𝑂𝑁 ⃗⃗⃗⃗⃗⃗ in terms of 𝐚 and 𝐛. (b) Show that 𝑀𝑁 ⃗⃗⃗⃗⃗⃗⃗ = 1 2 (𝐛−𝐚). (c) State TWO geometric relationships between 𝑀𝑁 and 𝐴𝐵.

question.question_restated: In triangle OAB, M is the midpoint of OA and N is the midpoint of OB, with OA = a and OB = b. (a) Express OM and ON in terms of a and b. (b) Show that MN = ½(b − a). (c) State TWO geometric relationships between MN and AB.

app_sections.think_first: Halving each side from O gives the two midpoints immediately, and the segment joining them is just the difference of those halves.
app_sections.strategy: Write OM and ON as halves of a and b, form MN = ON − OM, then compare the result with AB = b − a.

guided_solution.instruction: Halve OA and OB to reach the two midpoints.
guided_solution.note: M is halfway along OA and N is halfway along OB.

guided_solution.instruction: Route the journey from M to N through O.
Write AB in terms of a and b.
Compare MN with AB.
guided_solution.note: MN = ½AB, a scalar multiple, so the two segments point the same way.
guided_solution.result: MN is parallel to AB and half its length

app_sections.final_answer: (a) OM = ½a and ON = ½b  (b) MN = MO + ON = −½a + ½b = ½(b − a)  (c) MN is parallel to AB, and MN is half the length of AB.
app_sections.why_it_works: When one vector is a scalar multiple of another, the two line segments must be parallel, and the size of the scalar gives the ratio of their lengths. Here the scalar is ½, so MN is parallel to AB and exactly half as long. This is the midpoint theorem, proved by algebra rather than by congruent triangles.
common_mistakes: Writing MN = ½a − ½b by taking the journey in the wrong direction.
Saying MN equals AB because both are ½(b − a) in form, ignoring the factor.
Giving only one geometric relationship when two are asked for.
app_sections.exam_tip: Whenever a vector answer comes out as k times another vector, say the word 'parallel' — that is the mark the examiner is looking for.

quick_check.prompt: In the same triangle, P is the midpoint of AB. Express MP in terms of a and b.
quick_check.answer: OP = ½(a + b), so MP = OP − OM = ½(a + b) − ½a = ½b

question.question_restated: Three forces act successively as shown on the vector diagram, where F1 = (6, 2), F2 = (−1, 5) and F3 = (−5, −7) as column vectors. (a) Calculate F1 + F2. (b) Calculate F1 + F2 + F3. (c) State what the answer to (b) indicates about the three forces.

app_sections.think_first: Column vectors add component by component, so keep the top numbers with the top numbers and the bottom with the bottom.
app_sections.strategy: Add the x-components and the y-components separately for (a), add F3 to that result for (b), then interpret a zero resultant.

guided_solution.instruction: Add the top components and then the bottom components of F1 and F2.
Add F3 to the answer from step 1.
Interpret the zero resultant.
guided_solution.note: The three arrows drawn nose to tail return to the starting point, closing the triangle.

app_sections.final_answer: (a) F1 + F2 = (5, 7) as a column vector  (b) F1 + F2 + F3 = (0, 0), the zero vector  (c) The three forces have zero resultant, so they are in equilibrium; drawn nose to tail they form a closed triangle and produce no net movement.
app_sections.why_it_works: Adding vectors nose to tail traces a path, and the sum is the single arrow from the very start to the very end of that path. When the sum is the zero vector, the path has returned to where it began, so the closed figure on the diagram is not a coincidence. Physically, no net force acts on the object.
common_mistakes: Adding an x-component to a y-component when the columns are written across the page.
Losing a minus sign in (−5, −7) and getting a non-zero resultant.
Answering (c) with '0' instead of saying what zero means about the forces.
app_sections.exam_tip: After adding column vectors, glance back at the diagram: if the arrows close up into a polygon, your resultant must be zero.

question.source_text: 18. A boat moves due east at 8 km h−1 in still water. A current flows due north at 6 km h−1. (a) Write the resultant velocity as a column vector. (b) Calculate the magnitude of the resultant velocity. (c) Write a unit vector in the direction of the resultant velocity.
question.display_policy: Render verified structured mathematics when available; always retain the linked source visual for fidelity.
question.question_restated: A boat moves due east at 8 km/h in still water while a current flows due north at 6 km/h. (a) Write the resultant velocity as a column vector. (b) Calculate the magnitude of the resultant velocity. (c) Write a unit vector in the direction of the resultant velocity.

app_sections.think_first: East is the positive x-direction and north is the positive y-direction, so the two speeds slot straight into a column vector.
app_sections.strategy: Place 8 as the x-component and 6 as the y-component, use Pythagoras for the magnitude, then divide the vector by that magnitude.

guided_solution.instruction: Write the eastward speed as the x-component and the northward speed as the y-component.
Apply Pythagoras to the two components.
Divide each component of v by its magnitude.

app_sections.final_answer: (a) Resultant velocity = (8, 6) km/h  (b) Magnitude = √(8² + 6²) = √100 = 10 km/h  (c) Unit vector = (1/10)(8, 6) = (0.8, 0.6)
app_sections.why_it_works: East and north are perpendicular, so the two velocities form the legs of a right-angled triangle and the resultant is its hypotenuse. Dividing a vector by its own length keeps the direction but scales the length to exactly 1, which is what a unit vector means. Checking (0.8)² + (0.6)² = 1 confirms it.
common_mistakes: Adding the speeds to get 14 km/h instead of using Pythagoras.
Putting north in the x-slot and east in the y-slot.
Forgetting to divide both components when forming the unit vector.
app_sections.exam_tip: Always test a unit vector by squaring and adding its components — you should get exactly 1.

quick_check.prompt: Find the magnitude of the vector (5, 12) and a unit vector in its direction.

question.question_restated: The quadrilateral ABCD is drawn on a coordinate grid with A(1, 1), B(5, 3), C(9, 9) and D(5, 7). (a) Determine the vectors AB and DC. (b) Determine the vectors AD and BC. (c) Use your answers to show that ABCD is a parallelogram.

app_sections.think_first: Read the four coordinates off the grid first; after that every vector is just 'finish minus start'.
app_sections.strategy: Read A, B, C and D from the grid, subtract coordinates to get each vector, then show that the two pairs of opposite sides are equal vectors.

guided_solution.instruction: Read the four vertices from the grid.
Subtract the starting point from the finishing point for AB and for DC.
Do the same for AD and BC.
Compare the two pairs.
guided_solution.note: AB = DC and AD = BC, so both pairs of opposite sides are parallel and equal in length.

app_sections.final_answer: (a) AB = (4, 2) and DC = (4, 2)  (b) AD = (4, 6) and BC = (4, 6)  (c) AB = DC and AD = BC, so each pair of opposite sides is equal in magnitude and parallel in direction, which is exactly the condition for ABCD to be a parallelogram.
app_sections.why_it_works: Two vectors are equal only when they have both the same length and the same direction, so an equality like AB = DC packs both parallelogram conditions into one line. Coordinates make this checkable by pure arithmetic rather than by measuring the drawing. Showing one pair equal is already enough, but showing both makes the argument complete.
common_mistakes: Subtracting in the wrong order, e.g. computing CD instead of DC.
Misreading grid coordinates when the axis labels are spaced in twos.
Saying the shape 'looks like' a parallelogram instead of quoting AB = DC.
app_sections.exam_tip: Write vectors as finish minus start every time; the letters in the vector name tell you which point is which.

(a) Express 𝑂𝑃 ⃗⃗⃗⃗⃗ in terms of 𝐚 and 𝐛. (b) Express 𝑂𝑄 ⃗⃗⃗⃗⃗⃗ in terms of 𝐚 and 𝐛. (c) Show that 𝑂𝑀 ⃗⃗⃗⃗⃗⃗ = 2 3 (𝐚+ 𝐛). (d) Hence, prove that 𝑂, 𝑀 and 𝐶 are collinear and state 𝑂𝑀: 𝑀𝐶.

question.question_restated: OACB is a parallelogram with OA = a and OB = b. P divides AC so that AP : PC = 1 : 2, Q divides BC so that BQ : QC = 1 : 2, and M is the midpoint of PQ. (a) Express OP in terms of a and b. (b) Express OQ in terms of a and b. (c) Show that OM = (2/3)(a + b). (d) Hence prove that O, M and C are collinear and state OM : MC.

app_sections.think_first: AC runs in the same direction as OB and BC in the same direction as OA, so each ratio point is a whole side plus a fraction of the other.
concepts_required: Dividing a line in a given ratio
app_sections.strategy: Reach P and Q by going along one side then a third of the way along the other, average them to get M, then show OM is a scalar multiple of OC.

guided_solution.instruction: Identify the side vectors of the parallelogram.
guided_solution.note: AC is equal and parallel to OB, so AC = b; BC is equal and parallel to OA, so BC = a; and OC = a + b.
guided_solution.result: AC = b, BC = a, OC = a + b

guided_solution.instruction: Reach P by going O to A then one third of the way along AC.
Reach Q by going O to B then one third of the way along BC.
Average OP and OQ to reach the midpoint M of PQ.
Compare OM with OC and read off the ratio.
guided_solution.note: OC = a + b, so OM = (2/3)OC and MC = OC − OM = (1/3)OC
guided_solution.result: O, M, C are collinear with OM : MC = 2 : 1

app_sections.final_answer: (a) OP = a + (1/3)b  (b) OQ = b + (1/3)a  (c) OM = ½(OP + OQ) = ½((4/3)a + (4/3)b) = (2/3)(a + b)  (d) Since OC = a + b, OM = (2/3)OC; the two vectors are scalar multiples sharing the point O, so O, M and C lie on one straight line, and OM : MC = 2 : 1.
app_sections.why_it_works: A ratio like 1 : 2 means the first piece is one of three equal parts, which is why a third of a side appears rather than a half. The midpoint of a segment is the average of the position vectors of its ends, so averaging OP and OQ lands exactly on M. Finally, two vectors from the same point that are scalar multiples of each other must lie along the same line, and the scalar 2/3 fixes the division ratio.
common_mistakes: Reading AP : PC = 1 : 2 as AP = ½AC instead of (1/3)AC.
Using AC = a instead of AC = b by confusing which sides are parallel.
Stating OM : MC = 2 : 3 (comparing part to whole) instead of 2 : 1.
app_sections.exam_tip: For a ratio m : n along a segment, the first point sits m/(m+n) of the way along — add the parts before you take the fraction.

question.question_restated: The matrix A = (3 −1 5 / 0 4 2), a matrix whose first row is 3, −1, 5 and whose second row is 0, 4, 2. (a) State the order of A. (b) Write down the second row of A. (c) Write down the element in row 1, column 3. (d) State whether A is square or rectangular.

app_sections.think_first: Everything here is read straight off the matrix, so the only skill needed is counting rows and columns in the right order.
app_sections.strategy: Count the rows first and the columns second to give the order, then locate the requested row and element by position.

guided_solution.instruction: Count the horizontal rows, then the vertical columns.
guided_solution.note: Rows: (3 −1 5) and (0 4 2). Columns: the 3/0 column, the −1/4 column and the 5/2 column.
guided_solution.result: 2 rows, 3 columns, so the order is 2 × 3

guided_solution.instruction: Read off the lower of the two rows.
guided_solution.note: The second row is the one beginning with 0.

guided_solution.instruction: Go to row 1, then count across to the third column.
guided_solution.note: Row 1 is (3 −1 5); the third entry is 5.

guided_solution.instruction: Compare the number of rows with the number of columns.

app_sections.final_answer: (a) Order 2 × 3  (b) Second row = (0 4 2)  (c) The element in row 1, column 3 is 5  (d) A is rectangular, since it has 2 rows but 3 columns.
app_sections.why_it_works: The order of a matrix is always written rows first, columns second, and that convention is what makes element addresses unambiguous. An element referred to as row i, column j sits where those two lines cross. A matrix is square only when those two counts agree.
common_mistakes: Writing the order as 3 × 2 by counting columns before rows.
Reading the element in row 3, column 1 rather than row 1, column 3.
Calling any matrix with more than one row 'square'.
app_sections.exam_tip: Say 'rows before columns' to yourself every time you write an order or an element address — it removes most matrix slips.

question.source_text: 2. The matrices 𝐴, 𝐵 and 𝐶 are shown below. 𝐴= (1 0 0 1) 𝐵= (2 −1 4 3 0 5) 𝐶= ( 7 2 −3 6) (a) State which matrix is the identity matrix. (b) State which matrix is rectangular.

question.question_restated: Three matrices are given: A = (1 0 / 0 1), B = (2 −1 4 / 3 0 5) and C = (7 2 / −3 6). (a) State which matrix is the identity matrix. (b) State which matrix is rectangular. (c) State the order of EACH matrix.

app_sections.think_first: Identify each matrix by its shape and by the pattern of its entries — no arithmetic is needed at all.
app_sections.strategy: Look for the square matrix with 1s down the leading diagonal and 0s elsewhere, then count rows and columns for each matrix.

guided_solution.instruction: Look for 1s on the leading diagonal and 0s everywhere else.
guided_solution.note: A has 1, 1 down the diagonal from top left, with 0s off it.

guided_solution.instruction: Find the matrix whose row count differs from its column count.
Count rows then columns for each matrix.
guided_solution.note: A: 2 rows, 2 columns. B: 2 rows, 3 columns. C: 2 rows, 2 columns.
guided_solution.result: A is 2 × 2, B is 2 × 3, C is 2 × 2

app_sections.final_answer: (a) A is the identity matrix  (b) B is rectangular  (c) A is of order 2 × 2, B is of order 2 × 3, and C is of order 2 × 2.
app_sections.why_it_works: The identity matrix must be square and carry 1s only on the leading diagonal, because that is the pattern that leaves any conformable matrix unchanged when multiplied. C is square too, but its entries do not fit the pattern, so it is not the identity. Shape alone settles which matrix is rectangular.
common_mistakes: Calling C the identity because it is square.
Describing B as 3 × 2 by counting columns first.
Thinking a matrix of 0s is the identity — that is the zero matrix.
app_sections.exam_tip: The identity matrix is the matrix version of the number 1: square, with 1s on the diagonal, and it leaves other matrices unchanged under multiplication.

app_sections.strategy: Match the entry in row 1, column 1 and the entry in row 2, column 2, then solve the two resulting equations.

Solve for x.

Check the remaining entries agree.

guided_solution.instruction: Add the entries in matching positions.
Subtract each entry of A from the matching entry of B.

app_sections.why_it_works: Matrix addition and subtraction are done element by element, so they are only defined when the two matrices have exactly the same order. Order matters for subtraction: B − A is the negative of A − B. Careful handling of the minus signs in 6 − (−1) is where most of the marks are won or lost.
common_mistakes: Attempting to add matrices of different orders.
Computing A − B when B − A is asked for.
Getting 6 − (−1) = 5 instead of 7.
app_sections.exam_tip: Rewrite subtraction of a negative as addition before you calculate: 6 − (−1) becomes 6 + 1.

app_sections.strategy: Multiply each of the six entries by 3, then repeat with −2, keeping careful track of signs.

guided_solution.instruction: Multiply every entry of C by 3.
Multiply every entry of C by −2.
Check the order of each answer.
guided_solution.note: Scalar multiplication never changes the shape.

app_sections.why_it_works: A scalar multiplies each element independently, so it stretches every entry by the same factor and leaves the shape untouched. A negative scalar also flips the sign of every entry, which is why the two negative entries in C become positive in −2C. Zero entries stay zero whatever the scalar.

Getting −2 × −2 = −4 instead of 4.
Changing the order of the matrix in the answer.

app_sections.strategy: Double every entry of P, subtract the matching entry of Q, then recall what matrix leaves P unchanged under addition.

Subtract each entry of Q from the matching entry of 2P.
Decide what must be added to each entry of P to leave it unchanged.
guided_solution.note: Adding 0 to any number leaves it alone, so every entry of Z must be 0.

app_sections.why_it_works: Scalar multiplication is applied before addition or subtraction, just as with ordinary algebra. The zero matrix plays the same role for matrices that the number 0 plays for numbers: it is the additive identity, so adding it changes nothing. It must have the same order as P for the addition to be defined at all.

Slipping on 6 − (−1), which is 7, not 5.

question.question_restated: The matrices A and B satisfy A + B = C, where A = (2 −3 / 1 4) and C = (7 1 / −2 9). (a) Determine the matrix B. (b) Verify that B + A = C.

app_sections.think_first: Rearranging A + B = C gives B = C − A, exactly as you would with ordinary numbers.
app_sections.strategy: Make B the subject by subtracting A from C, then add A back to the answer to confirm it returns C.

guided_solution.instruction: Rearrange the equation to make B the subject.
guided_solution.note: A + B = C, so B = C − A.

guided_solution.instruction: Subtract each entry of A from the matching entry of C.
Add A to B and compare with C.

app_sections.final_answer: (a) B = C − A = (5 4 / −3 5)  (b) B + A = (5 + 2, 4 + (−3) / −3 + 1, 5 + 4) = (7 1 / −2 9), which is exactly C, so the answer checks out.
app_sections.why_it_works: Matrix addition is done entry by entry, so a matrix equation can be rearranged in the same way as a numerical one. Matrix addition is also commutative, which is why B + A gives the same result as A + B and makes the verification valid. The check catches sign errors, particularly at 1 − (−3).
common_mistakes: Computing A − C instead of C − A.
Mishandling 1 − (−3) and writing −2.
Skipping the verification, which is where an easy mark sits.
app_sections.exam_tip: When a question asks you to verify, actually write out the addition — the marks are for the working, not the agreement.

question.question_restated: Matrices P, Q and R have orders 2 × 3, 3 × 2 and 2 × 2 respectively. (a) State whether PQ is defined, and if so its order. (b) State whether QP is defined, and if so its order. (c) State whether PR is defined, giving a reason. (d) State the order of RP.

app_sections.think_first: Write the two orders side by side: the inner numbers decide whether the product exists, and the outer numbers give its order.
app_sections.strategy: For each product, line up the orders as (a × b)(c × d) and check b = c; if it holds, the product is a × d.

guided_solution.instruction: Line up the orders for PQ.
guided_solution.note: (2 × 3)(3 × 2): the inner numbers are 3 and 3, which match.

guided_solution.instruction: Line up the orders for QP.
guided_solution.note: (3 × 2)(2 × 3): the inner numbers are 2 and 2, which match.

guided_solution.instruction: Line up the orders for PR.
guided_solution.note: (2 × 3)(2 × 2): the inner numbers are 3 and 2, which do not match.

guided_solution.instruction: Line up the orders for RP.
guided_solution.note: (2 × 2)(2 × 3): the inner numbers are 2 and 2, which match.

app_sections.final_answer: (a) PQ is defined and has order 2 × 2  (b) QP is defined and has order 3 × 3  (c) PR is not defined, because the number of columns of P (3) does not equal the number of rows of R (2)  (d) RP has order 2 × 3
app_sections.why_it_works: A product row-by-column only makes sense when each row of the first matrix has exactly as many entries as each column of the second, which is the inner-numbers rule. The surviving outer numbers become the shape of the answer. Parts (a) and (b) also show why order matters: PQ and QP are not even the same size.
common_mistakes: Checking the outer numbers instead of the inner ones.
Assuming that if PQ exists then QP must have the same order.
Saying PR is defined because both matrices contain a 2.
app_sections.exam_tip: Write the orders next to each other, cover the outer numbers with your fingers, and check the two inner numbers match before doing any arithmetic.

app_sections.think_first: Multiplying a 2 × 2 matrix by a column vector gives another column vector: each row of A meets the single column of x.
app_sections.strategy: Multiply each row of A into the column x, adding the products, then read the order from the outer numbers 2 and 1.

guided_solution.instruction: Check the product is defined.
Multiply row 1 of A into the column x.
Multiply row 2 of A into the column x.
Assemble the answer as a column vector.

app_sections.final_answer: (a) Ax = (16 / 3), that is the column vector with entries 16 and 3  (b) The order of Ax is 2 × 1
app_sections.why_it_works: Each entry of the product comes from pairing a row of the first matrix with a column of the second, multiplying matched entries and adding. Because x has only one column, the answer also has only one column, so the shape 2 × 1 is forced by the rule that the outer numbers survive. This is exactly the structure that lets a matrix equation stand for simultaneous equations.

Using columns of A with rows of x instead of rows of A with the column of x.
Losing the sign in −1 × 5.

app_sections.strategy: Check the inner numbers agree, then form each of the four entries of MN by pairing one row of M with one column of N.

guided_solution.note: M is 2 × 3 and N is 3 × 2; both inner numbers are 3.

Pair row 2 of M with each column of N.
Write the completed product and state its order.

app_sections.why_it_works: Every entry of a product is a sum of products of matched pairs, so the row length of the first matrix must equal the column height of the second for the pairing to work. The entry in row i, column j of MN comes from row i of M and column j of N, which is a useful check if you lose your place. The 3s cancel out of the shape, leaving 2 × 2.

Placing an answer in the wrong position, e.g. putting the row-2, column-1 value in row 1.
Forgetting the middle term when a row entry is 0 and mis-adding the rest.

question.question_restated: A = (1 2 / 0 3) and B = (4 −1 / 2 5). (a) Calculate AB. (b) Calculate BA. (c) Hence show that matrix multiplication is not commutative for A and B.

app_sections.think_first: You must do the two multiplications separately — the order of the letters changes which rows meet which columns.
app_sections.strategy: Compute AB with rows of A into columns of B, compute BA with rows of B into columns of A, then compare the two results entry by entry.

guided_solution.instruction: Multiply the rows of A into the columns of B.
Now multiply the rows of B into the columns of A.
Compare the two products.
guided_solution.note: 8 ≠ 4 in the top-left position alone is enough.

app_sections.final_answer: (a) AB = (8 9 / 6 15)  (b) BA = (4 5 / 2 19)  (c) The two products differ — for example the entry in row 1, column 1 is 8 in AB but 4 in BA — so AB ≠ BA and matrix multiplication is not commutative for these matrices.
app_sections.why_it_works: In a product, the first matrix supplies the rows and the second supplies the columns, so swapping the letters changes every pairing. That is why AB and BA are generally different matrices even when both are defined and the same size. One mismatched entry is all that is needed to prove non-commutativity.
common_mistakes: Calculating AB and then writing the same answer for BA.
Mixing rows of A with rows of B.
Answering (c) with a general statement instead of pointing to the actual difference in the computed matrices.
app_sections.exam_tip: For a 'show that' part, quote the specific entries that differ — a bare 'they are not equal' rarely earns the mark.

app_sections.strategy: Write X = B − A, subtract corresponding entries carefully with signs, then add A back to verify.

guided_solution.instruction: Make X the subject of the equation.

guided_solution.instruction: Subtract each entry of A from the matching entry of B.
Add A back to X and compare with B.

app_sections.final_answer: (a) X = B − A = (6 −6 / 4 5)  (b) X + A = (6 + (−2), −6 + 5 / 4 + 3, 5 + 1) = (4 −1 / 7 6), which is B, so the answer is correct.
app_sections.why_it_works: Because matrix addition works entry by entry, the same rearrangement you use for numbers works for whole matrices, provided the orders match. The entry 4 − (−2) is the one that catches people: subtracting a negative adds. Substituting back is a complete check, since it reconstructs B exactly.
common_mistakes: Computing A − B rather than B − A.
Writing 4 − (−2) = 2.
Omitting the check in part (b).

app_sections.strategy: Add A to B to obtain 2X, then multiply that result by ½ to obtain X.

guided_solution.instruction: Add A to both sides to isolate 2X.
Add the matching entries of B and A.
Halve every entry of 2X.
Check by substituting back.
guided_solution.result: Equals B, so X is correct

app_sections.why_it_works: Matrix equations obey the same rearrangement rules as ordinary equations because addition and scalar multiplication act entry by entry. Halving a matrix means halving every element, not just the first one. Substituting the answer back reconstructs B exactly, which is a full verification.
common_mistakes: Computing B − A instead of B + A when moving A across.
Halving only some entries of 2X.
Dividing the entries of A or B by 2 as well as those of 2X.

question.question_restated: A = (1 2 / 3 1), x is the column vector (x / y) and b = (7 / 11), with Ax = b. (a) Write down the TWO simultaneous equations represented by the matrix equation. (b) Determine the values of x and y. (c) Check the solution by matrix multiplication.

app_sections.think_first: Each row of A multiplied into the column (x / y) produces one ordinary equation.
app_sections.strategy: Expand Ax row by row to get two equations, solve them by substitution, then multiply A by the solution vector to confirm it gives b.

Rearrange the second equation and substitute into the first.
Substitute x = 3 back to find y.

app_sections.why_it_works: The row-by-column rule turns each row of the coefficient matrix into the left-hand side of one equation, so a whole system can be packed into a single matrix statement. Solving is then ordinary algebra. Multiplying back is the fastest possible check because it re-derives both equations at once.

Sign slips when expanding 2(11 − 3x).
Finding x and forgetting to substitute back for y.

app_sections.strategy: Check that the 3 columns of Q match the 3 rows of p, multiply each day's row into the price column, then read the answers as money.

question.question_restated: A minibus company records adult and child passengers on three routes in R = (18 7 / 22 5 / 16 9), where column 1 is adults and column 2 is children, and the fare matrix f = (250 / 150) gives the adult and child fares in dollars. (a) Calculate Rf. (b) State what each element of Rf represents. (c) Determine which route earned the greatest fare revenue.

app_sections.think_first: Each row is one route, so multiplying that row into the fare column gives that route's takings in a single line of arithmetic.
concepts_required: Interpreting a product matrix in context
app_sections.strategy: Multiply each route row into the fare column, interpret the three results as revenue, then pick the largest.

guided_solution.instruction: Check the product is defined and find its shape.
guided_solution.note: R is 3 × 2 and f is 2 × 1; the inner 2s match.

guided_solution.instruction: Multiply route 1's row into the fare column.
Multiply route 2's row into the fare column.
Multiply route 3's row into the fare column.
Compare the three revenues.

app_sections.final_answer: (a) Rf = (5550 / 6250 / 5350)  (b) Each element is the total fare revenue, in dollars, collected on that route: $5550 on route 1, $6250 on route 2 and $5350 on route 3  (c) Route 2 earned the greatest fare revenue, $6250.
app_sections.why_it_works: Multiplying a row of passenger numbers by a column of fares pairs each passenger type with its own fare and adds the money, which is exactly the revenue calculation. Because there are three rows and one fare column, the answer is a 3 × 1 column with one revenue per route. The structure of the matrices does the bookkeeping for you.
common_mistakes: Multiplying adults by the child fare through careless pairing.
Attempting fR, which is not defined.
Choosing route 1 because it has the most adults, without comparing the totals.
app_sections.exam_tip: Check a revenue answer for plausibility: with fares of $250 and $150 and about 25 passengers, a few thousand dollars per route is the right size.

quick_check.prompt: A fourth route carries 20 adults and 10 children at the same fares. What is its revenue?

question.source_text: 19. A caterer prepares sandwiches, salads and fruit cups for two events. The order matrix 𝑂 and the unit-cost matrix 𝐜 are shown below. Costs are in dollars. 𝑂= (40 25 30 35 20 45) 𝐜= ( 12 18 8 ) (a) Calculate 𝑂𝐜. (b) Interpret the entries in 𝑂𝐜. (c)
question.display_policy: Render verified structured mathematics when available; always retain the linked source visual for fidelity.
question.question_restated: A caterer prepares sandwiches, salads and fruit cups for two events. The order matrix O = (40 25 30 / 35 20 45) has one row per event, and the unit-cost matrix c = (12 / 18 / 8) gives the cost in dollars of one sandwich, one salad and one fruit cup. (a) Calculate Oc. (b) Interpret the entries in Oc. (c) The caterer adds a delivery charge of $120 to each event. Write a column matrix showing the final cost of each event.

app_sections.think_first: Multiply first to get the food cost of each event, then add the fixed delivery charge to both entries at the end.
concepts_required: Interpreting a product matrix in context
app_sections.strategy: Multiply each event's row into the cost column, then add a column matrix of two 120s to include delivery.

guided_solution.instruction: Check the shapes match and find the order of the product.
guided_solution.note: O is 2 × 3 and c is 3 × 1; the inner 3s agree.

guided_solution.instruction: Multiply the first event's row into the cost column.
Multiply the second event's row into the cost column.
Add $120 to each entry for delivery.

app_sections.final_answer: (a) Oc = (1170 / 1140)  (b) The entries are the food costs in dollars: $1170 for the first event and $1140 for the second  (c) Adding the $120 delivery charge to each gives the final cost column matrix (1290 / 1260), that is $1290 for the first event and $1260 for the second.
app_sections.why_it_works: The row-by-column rule multiplies each quantity by the cost of that same item and adds the results, which is precisely how an order is priced. Placing the unit costs in a column is what aligns each cost with its own item. A fixed charge is added afterwards because it does not depend on quantity, so it belongs in an addition, not in the multiplication.
common_mistakes: Adding the $120 before multiplying, so it gets multiplied by quantities.
Pairing the salad quantity with the sandwich cost.
Giving the final costs as a row matrix when a column matrix is asked for.
app_sections.exam_tip: Fixed charges are added after the multiplication; only per-item amounts belong inside the cost column.

quick_check.prompt: A third event orders 20 sandwiches, 10 salads and 15 fruit cups. What is the food cost?

question.source_text: 20. Three branches sell Models A, B and C of a device. The sales matrix 𝑆 and the unit-price matrix 𝐩 are shown below. Prices are in dollars. 𝑆= ( 12 8 5 9 11 6 15 7 4 ) 𝐩= ( 450 600 750 )
question.display_policy: Render verified structured mathematics when available; always retain the linked source visual for fidelity.
question.question_restated: Three branches sell Models A, B and C of a device. The sales matrix S = (12 8 5 / 9 11 6 / 15 7 4) has one row per branch and one column per model, and the unit-price matrix p = (450 / 600 / 750) gives the price of each model in dollars. (a) Calculate Sp. (b) State what the entries of Sp represent. (c) A 5% commission is paid on the revenue of each branch; write the commission amounts as a column matrix. (d) Determine the total commission paid to the three branches.

app_sections.think_first: The product gives each branch's revenue; the commission is then just 5% of each of those numbers, which is a scalar multiplication.
concepts_required: Interpreting a product matrix in context
app_sections.strategy: Multiply each branch row into the price column to get revenues, take 5% of each to get commissions, then add the three commissions.

guided_solution.instruction: Multiply branch 1's row into the price column.
Multiply branch 2's row into the price column.
Multiply branch 3's row into the price column.
Take 5% of each revenue, that is multiply the column by 0.05.
Add the three commissions.

app_sections.final_answer: (a) Sp = (13950 / 15150 / 13950)  (b) Each entry is the total sales revenue in dollars of that branch: $13 950 for branch 1, $15 150 for branch 2 and $13 950 for branch 3  (c) Commission column matrix = 0.05 × Sp = (697.50 / 757.50 / 697.50)  (d) Total commission = $697.50 + $757.50 + $697.50 = $2152.50
app_sections.why_it_works: Each entry of Sp pairs the number of each model sold with the price of that same model and adds the money, so one multiplication prices three branches at once. Taking a percentage of every entry is a scalar multiplication, which is why the commission column has the same shape as the revenue column. Adding the commissions gives the same figure as 5% of the total revenue of $43 050, a useful cross-check.
common_mistakes: Pairing Model B sales with the Model A price.
Working out 5% as 0.5 and getting ten times too much.
Rounding revenue to the nearest dollar before taking the commission and losing the exact cents.
app_sections.exam_tip: When several percentages of a column are wanted, multiply the whole column by the decimal in one step rather than each entry separately.

quick_check.prompt: Find 5% of $8400.

Weight (kg) Tally Number of Bags 1–10 11–20 21–30 31–40 41–50 (h) For the class interval 21–30, state: (i) the upper-class boundary ________________________________ (ii) the class width ________________________________________ (iii) the class midpoint _____________________________________ (i) On the grid below , using a scale of 2 cm to represent 10 kgon the 𝑥-axis, and 1 cm to represent 1 bagon the 𝑦-axis, draw a histogram to represent the data contained in your frequency table above.

question.question_restated: Twenty bags of sugar were weighed to the nearest kg: 3, 38, 17, 33, 28, 12, 43, 38, 31, 30, 11, 8, 23, 18, 26, 50, 22, 35, 39, 5. (g) Complete a frequency table with class intervals 1–10, 11–20, 21–30, 31–40, 41–50. (h) For the class interval 21–30 state (i) the upper class boundary, (ii) the class width, (iii) the class midpoint. (i) Using 2 cm to 10 kg on the x-axis and 1 cm to 1 bag on the y-axis, draw a histogram of the frequency table.

app_sections.think_first: Tally each weight into its interval first, then check the five frequencies add back to 20 before you use them for anything else.
concepts_required: Class boundaries, class width and class midpoint
app_sections.strategy: Sort the twenty readings into the five classes and total them, then apply the boundary/width/midpoint definitions to 21–30 and use the frequencies as the bar heights of the histogram.

guided_solution.instruction: Tally the values into each class interval.
Check the frequencies against the number of bags.
guided_solution.result: 20 bags, so the table is complete

guided_solution.instruction: Find the upper class boundary of 21–30.
guided_solution.note: Weights are to the nearest kg, so the class stretches half a unit past 30

guided_solution.instruction: Find the class width as upper boundary minus lower boundary.
Find the class midpoint by averaging the class limits.
Draw the histogram with the class boundaries on the x-axis and frequency on the y-axis.

app_sections.final_answer: (g) 1–10: 3 bags; 11–20: 4 bags; 21–30: 5 bags; 31–40: 6 bags; 41–50: 2 bags (total 20).  (h)(i) 30.5 kg  (ii) 10 kg  (iii) 25.5 kg  (i) A histogram of five touching bars with heights 3, 4, 5, 6 and 2, drawn between the class boundaries 0.5, 10.5, 20.5, 30.5, 40.5 and 50.5.
app_sections.why_it_works: Weights recorded to the nearest kilogram are really intervals: a bag labelled 30 kg lies anywhere from 29.5 to 30.5 kg. That is why the class 21–30 actually runs from 20.5 to 30.5, giving a width of 10 and a boundary of 30.5, while the midpoint 25.5 is the value used to represent every bag in that class. A histogram uses those boundaries so the bars touch, showing that the data is continuous.
common_mistakes: Giving the class width as 30 − 21 = 9 instead of using the boundaries.
Quoting 30 as the upper class boundary — 30 is the upper class limit.
Leaving gaps between histogram bars, which is only correct for a bar chart of discrete categories.
Losing or double-counting a value in the tally; always check the frequencies sum to the stated total.
app_sections.exam_tip: Total your frequency column and compare it with the number given in the question before you go any further — one mis-tallied value ruins every later part.

quick_check.prompt: For the class interval 51–60 of data recorded to the nearest kg, state the lower class boundary and the class midpoint.
quick_check.answer: Lower class boundary 50.5 kg; midpoint 55.5 kg.
