Year 2010 2011 2012 2013 2014 2015 Production (tonnes) 150 275 100 40 125 210 (a) On the graph paper provided on page 21, draw a bar chart to represent the data given in the table above using a scale of 1 cm to represent 1 yearon the 𝑥-axis and 1 cmto represent 25 tonnes on the 𝑦-axis. (b) Determine the range of the number of bananas produced between 2010and 2015. (c) (i) During which year was there the greatest production of bananas? (i) How is this information shown on the bar chart?
question.display_policy: Render verified structured mathematics when available; always retain the linked source visual for fidelity.
question.question_restated: A farm's banana production, to the nearest tonne, was: 2010 → 150, 2011 → 275, 2012 → 100, 2013 → 40, 2014 → 125, 2015 → 210. (a) Draw a bar chart using 1 cm to 1 year on the x-axis and 1 cm to 25 tonnes on the y-axis. (b) Determine the range of the production between 2010 and 2015. (c)(i) In which year was production greatest, and (ii) how is that shown on the bar chart? (d)(i) Between which two consecutive years was the change in production greatest, and (ii) how is that shown on the bar chart?

app_sections.think_first: Every part here is read from the same six numbers, so work with the table and treat the bar chart as a picture of it.
app_sections.strategy: Plot one bar per year to the given scale, subtract the smallest production from the largest for the range, then compare the six values (and the differences between consecutive values) to answer the reading questions.

guided_solution.instruction: Set up the axes and draw one equal-width bar for each year.
guided_solution.note: Years along the x-axis (1 cm each); heights 150, 275, 100, 40, 125, 210 tonnes with 1 cm representing 25 tonnes, so 6 cm, 11 cm, 4 cm, 1.6 cm, 5 cm, 8.4 cm
guided_solution.result: Six separated bars of equal width

guided_solution.instruction: Find the range by subtracting the smallest value from the largest.
Identify the year with the greatest production.
Work out the change between each pair of consecutive years.
guided_solution.result: The largest change is 175 tonnes, between 2011 and 2012

app_sections.final_answer: (a) A bar chart with six equal, separated bars of heights 150, 275, 100, 40, 125 and 210 tonnes (1 cm = 25 tonnes).  (b) Range = 275 − 40 = 235 tonnes.  (c)(i) 2011  (ii) It is the tallest bar on the chart.  (d)(i) Between 2011 and 2012 (a fall of 175 tonnes)  (ii) It is the largest difference in height between two neighbouring bars.
app_sections.why_it_works: A bar chart converts each number into a length, so comparisons of size become comparisons of height. The range measures the spread of the data by using only the two extreme values, which on the chart are simply the tallest and shortest bars. Change between consecutive years is a difference, and a difference shows up as a step in height between adjacent bars.
common_mistakes: Giving the range as '40 to 275' instead of a single number, 235 tonnes.
Reading the greatest change as the change to or from the tallest bar, rather than comparing all five consecutive differences.
Drawing bars of unequal width, or joining them like a histogram.
app_sections.exam_tip: When a question says 'greatest change', list all the consecutive differences in a line before choosing — the biggest bar and the biggest change are usually not the same pair.

quick_check.prompt: Production over three years is 80, 210 and 150 tonnes. State the range and the greatest change between consecutive years.
quick_check.answer: Range = 130 tonnes; greatest change = 130 tonnes, between the first and second years.

question.source_text: 3. The table below shows the speeds, to the nearest km h−1, of 90 vehicles that pass a checkpoint. Speed (in km h−1) Frequency Cumulative Frequency 0–19 5 5 20–39 11 16 40–59 26 60–79 37 80–99 9 100–119
question.display_policy: Render verified structured mathematics when available; always retain the linked source visual for fidelity.
question.question_restated: The speeds, to the nearest km/h, of 90 vehicles passing a checkpoint are grouped as 0–19 (5), 20–39 (11), 40–59 (26), 60–79 (37), 80–99 (9), 100–119 (2). (a) For the class 20–39 state (i) the upper class limit, (ii) the class width, (iii) the speed at or below which 16 vehicles passed. (b) Complete the cumulative frequency column. (c) Draw the cumulative frequency curve using 2 cm to 20 km/h on the x-axis and 2 cm to 10 vehicles on the y-axis. (d)(i) Use the graph to estimate the speed at or below which 50% of the vehicles were driving.

app_sections.think_first: Cumulative frequency is a running total, and each running total belongs at the upper class boundary of its class, not at the middle.
concepts_required: Estimating the median from a cumulative frequency curve
app_sections.strategy: Add the frequencies in turn to complete the cumulative frequency column, plot each total against its upper class boundary, then read across from half the total frequency to estimate the median speed.

guided_solution.instruction: Read off the limits and width of the class 20–39.
guided_solution.note: Upper class limit is the larger number written in the class; boundaries are 19.5 and 39.5, so width = 39.5 − 19.5

guided_solution.instruction: Interpret the cumulative frequency of 16.
guided_solution.note: 5 + 11 = 16 vehicles fall in the classes 0–19 and 20–39, all with speeds up to the upper boundary 39.5
guided_solution.result: 16 vehicles travelled at 39.5 km/h or less (i.e. no more than 39 km/h as recorded)

guided_solution.instruction: Complete the cumulative frequency column by running totals.
Plot the cumulative frequencies against the upper class boundaries and join with a smooth curve.
guided_solution.result: A smooth S-shaped cumulative frequency curve

guided_solution.instruction: Read the median from the curve at half the total frequency.

app_sections.final_answer: (a)(i) 39  (ii) 20 km/h  (iii) 39.5 km/h (the upper class boundary of 20–39).  (b) Cumulative frequencies: 5, 16, 42, 79, 88, 90.  (c) Points (19.5, 5), (39.5, 16), (59.5, 42), (79.5, 79), (99.5, 88), (119.5, 90) joined by a smooth curve.  (d)(i) Reading across at a cumulative frequency of 45 gives a speed of about 61 km/h.
app_sections.why_it_works: A cumulative frequency curve answers the question 'how many are at most this value?', so each running total must be plotted at the top edge of its class — the only speed by which all of those vehicles have certainly been counted. Reading back from half the total frequency then gives the middle value of the whole distribution, which is the median.
common_mistakes: Plotting cumulative frequency against the class midpoint instead of the upper class boundary.
Giving the class width as 39 − 20 = 19.
Reading the median from the frequency column instead of the cumulative frequency curve.
Forgetting that the last cumulative frequency must equal the total, 90.
app_sections.exam_tip: Check your final cumulative frequency equals the total stated in the question — if it does not, one of your additions is wrong.

quick_check.prompt: Classes 0–9, 10–19, 20–29 have frequencies 4, 10 and 6. Write the cumulative frequencies and the point you would plot for the middle class.

question.source_text: 4. (a) The marks obtained by 10students in a test, scored out of 60, are shown below: For the data above, determine: (i) the range ____________________________________ (ii) the median ___________________________________ (iii) the interquartile range __________________________ (iv) the probability that a student chosen at random scores less than half the total marks in the test ________________________________________________________________________ (b) The frequency distribution below shows the masses, in kg, of 50adults prior to the start of a fitness programme. Mass (kg) Midpoint Frequency 60–64 62
question.display_policy: Render verified structured mathematics when available; always retain the linked source visual for fidelity.
question.question_restated: (a) Ten students scored the following marks out of 60: 29, 38, 26, 42, 38, 45, 35, 37, 38, 31. Determine (i) the range, (ii) the median, (iii) the interquartile range, (iv) the probability that a student chosen at random scored less than half the total marks. (b) A frequency distribution is then given for the masses, in kg, of 50 adults: 60–64 (midpoint 62, f = 8), 65–69 (67, 11), 70–74 (72, 15), 75–79 (77, 9), 80–84 (82, 5), 85–89 (87, 2); the instruction for part (b) continues past the bottom of this crop.

app_sections.think_first: Put the ten marks in order first — range, median and quartiles all read straight off an ordered list.
app_sections.strategy: Order the ten marks, then take the extremes for the range, the average of the 5th and 6th values for the median, the medians of the two halves for the quartiles, and count the qualifying marks for the probability.

guided_solution.instruction: Write the ten marks in ascending order.
Subtract the smallest mark from the largest for the range.
Average the two middle marks for the median.
guided_solution.note: With 10 values the median is the mean of the 5th and 6th: (37 + 38) ÷ 2

guided_solution.instruction: Find the quartiles as the medians of the lower and upper halves, then subtract.
guided_solution.note: Lower half 26, 29, 31, 35, 37 gives Q1 = 31; upper half 38, 38, 38, 42, 45 gives Q3 = 38; IQR = 38 − 31

guided_solution.instruction: Count the marks below half of 60 and divide by the number of students.
guided_solution.note: Half the total marks is 30; only 26 and 29 are below 30, so 2 out of 10

app_sections.final_answer: (a)(i) Range = 19  (ii) Median = 37.5  (iii) Interquartile range = 38 − 31 = 7  (iv) P(scores less than 30) = 2/10 = 1/5 = 0.2.  (b) The table of masses is given, but the wording of part (b) is not visible in this crop, so no answer is offered for it.
app_sections.why_it_works: The range uses only the two extreme marks, so it is easily distorted by one unusual score; the interquartile range instead measures the spread of the middle half of the data, which is why both are asked for. The median and quartiles are positions in an ordered list, so ordering the data is not optional — it is what makes those positions meaningful. The probability is just the proportion of the data that satisfies the condition.
common_mistakes: Finding the median without ordering the marks first.
Including the median value in both halves when finding the quartiles of an even-sized data set.
Reading 'less than half the total marks' as less than half the highest mark, or as 30 or less rather than below 30.
Giving the interquartile range as the pair 31 and 38 instead of their difference.
app_sections.exam_tip: Write the ordered list once, neatly, and mark Q1, the median and Q3 on it — nearly every part of a statistics question about spread is then just a subtraction.

quick_check.prompt: For 12, 15, 15, 18, 22, 27 find the median and the interquartile range.

question.source_text: 5. (a) Students in a group were asked to name their favourite sport. Their responses are shown on the pie chart below. (i) Calculate the value of 𝑥. (ii) What percentage of the students chose cricket? (iii) Given that 40students chose tennis, calculate the TOTAL number of students in the group.
question.display_policy: Render verified structured mathematics when available; always retain the linked source visual for fidelity.
question.question_restated: A pie chart shows the favourite sport of a group of students. The sector for cricket is 94°, the sector for tennis is 45° and the sector for football is x°. (i) Calculate the value of x. (ii) What percentage of the students chose cricket? (iii) Given that 40 students chose tennis, calculate the total number of students in the group.

app_sections.think_first: Every pie chart rests on one fact: the sector angles add up to 360°, and each angle is the same fraction of 360° as its group is of the total.
concepts_required: Percentages and scaling up from a part to a whole
app_sections.strategy: Subtract the two known sector angles from 360° to find x, then use the fraction angle/360 to convert cricket to a percentage and to scale the 40 tennis students up to the whole group.

guided_solution.instruction: Set the three sector angles equal to 360°.
Write cricket's angle as a fraction of the whole circle and convert to a percentage.
Use the tennis sector to find how many students one degree represents.
Scale up to the full 360°.

app_sections.final_answer: (i) x = 221  (ii) 94/360 × 100 = 26.1% (to 1 decimal place)  (iii) 320 students in the group.
app_sections.why_it_works: A pie chart shares out a whole turn of 360° in the same ratio as the data, so an angle and its group are two ways of writing the same fraction. Once you know that 45° corresponds to 40 students, the constant 'students per degree' unlocks every other sector, and the full 360° gives the whole group.
common_mistakes: Forgetting that the three sectors must fill the whole 360°, and solving 94 + 45 + x = 180.
Dividing 40 by 360 instead of by 45 when scaling up to the total.
Rounding 26.1% to 26% without being asked, or writing it as 26.1 students.
app_sections.exam_tip: On any pie chart question, first write 'total = 360°' and the value of one degree in real units — most parts then take one line.

quick_check.prompt: On a pie chart a 72° sector represents 18 people. How many people are in the whole survey?

question.source_text: 6. A group of 100students estimated the mass, 𝑚(grams), of a seed. The cumulative frequency curve below shows the results. (g) Using the cumulative frequency curve, estimate the: (i) Median (ii) upper quartile (iii) semi-interquartile range (iv) number of students whose estimate is 2.8grams or less
question.display_policy: Render verified structured mathematics when available; always retain the linked source visual for fidelity.
question.question_restated: A group of 100 students estimated the mass, m grams, of a seed; the results are shown on a cumulative frequency curve rising from 0 at m = 0 to 100 at about m = 8. Using the curve, estimate (i) the median, (ii) the upper quartile, (iii) the semi-interquartile range, (iv) the number of students whose estimate is 2.8 grams or less.

app_sections.think_first: Read from the cumulative frequency axis across to the curve and down for a mass; read up from the mass axis for a number of students.
concepts_required: Median and quartiles from a graph
app_sections.strategy: Convert each required statistic into a cumulative frequency (50, 75, 25 out of 100), read the matching mass off the curve, then combine the quartiles; for part (iv) read in the opposite direction, from m = 2.8 up to the curve.

guided_solution.instruction: Find the cumulative frequency that locates the median and read across.
guided_solution.note: Half of 100 is 50; draw a horizontal line from 50 to the curve and drop to the mass axis

guided_solution.instruction: Repeat at three-quarters of the total for the upper quartile.
Read the lower quartile the same way at one quarter of the total.
Halve the interquartile range for the semi-interquartile range.
For 2.8 g or less, read upward from the mass axis to the curve.
guided_solution.note: Go up from m = 2.8 to the curve, then across to the cumulative frequency axis

app_sections.final_answer: (i) Median ≈ 3.2 g  (ii) Upper quartile ≈ 4.3 g  (iii) Lower quartile ≈ 2.3 g, so semi-interquartile range ≈ (4.3 − 2.3)/2 ≈ 1.0 g  (iv) About 38 students. (These are graph readings, so answers within about ±0.2 g and ±2 students are acceptable.)
app_sections.why_it_works: On a cumulative frequency curve the vertical axis counts how many students gave an estimate at or below a mass, so a chosen count fixes a position in the ordered data and the curve converts it into a mass. That is exactly what the median and quartiles are: the values at the 50%, 25% and 75% positions. The semi-interquartile range halves the spread of the middle 50% of the data, giving a measure of spread that ignores extreme estimates.
common_mistakes: Using the number of students (100) as a mass, or reading the axes the wrong way round.
Taking the quartiles at 25 and 75 on the mass axis instead of the cumulative frequency axis.
Forgetting to halve the interquartile range for the semi-interquartile range.
Reading the median at the highest point of the curve instead of at half the total frequency.
app_sections.exam_tip: Always draw the dashed reference lines on the graph — examiners award marks for the correct construction lines even if your reading is slightly out.

quick_check.prompt: On a cumulative frequency curve for 80 students, which cumulative frequency do you use to find the lower quartile?

question.source_text: 9. Each of 75girls recorded the name of her favourite sport. The number of girls who chose track and cricket are shown on the bar chart below. (b) How many more girls chose cricket than track as their favourite sport? (c) Eleven girls recorded tennis as their favourite sport. For the remaining girls, the number who chose swimming compared to the number who chose football was in the ratio 2: 3. Use this information to complete the bar chart above. (d) Determine the modal sport.
question.display_policy: Render verified structured mathematics when available; always retain the linked source visual for fidelity.
question.question_restated: Each of 75 girls named her favourite sport. The bar chart shows only two bars so far: track = 12 girls and cricket = 17 girls. (b) How many more girls chose cricket than track? (c) Eleven girls chose tennis; for the remaining girls the number choosing swimming to the number choosing football is in the ratio 2 : 3 — use this to complete the bar chart. (d) Determine the modal sport.

app_sections.think_first: Read the two given bars off the chart, then treat the rest as a sharing-in-a-ratio problem on whatever girls are left.
concepts_required: Sharing a quantity in a given ratio
app_sections.strategy: Take track = 12 and cricket = 17 from the chart, subtract track, cricket and tennis from 75 to find the girls left, share that remainder in the ratio 2 : 3, then compare all five totals for the mode.

guided_solution.instruction: Read the two bars and subtract.
Find how many girls are left for swimming and football.
Share the 35 girls in the ratio 2 : 3.
Draw the three missing bars and compare all five frequencies.
guided_solution.note: Swimming 14, tennis 11, track 12, cricket 17, football 21 — total 75

app_sections.final_answer: (b) 5 more girls chose cricket than track.  (c) Remaining girls = 35, shared 2 : 3 gives swimming = 14 and football = 21, so bars of height 14 (swimming), 11 (tennis) and 21 (football) complete the chart.  (d) The modal sport is football (21 girls).
app_sections.why_it_works: The five bars must account for all 75 girls, so once three of the groups are known the rest is a fixed remainder. Sharing that remainder in the ratio 2 : 3 means splitting it into 5 equal parts and giving two parts to swimming and three to football. The mode is simply the category that occurs most often — on a bar chart, the tallest bar.
common_mistakes: Sharing all 75 girls in the ratio 2 : 3 instead of only the 35 who are left.
Forgetting to subtract the 11 tennis girls before sharing.
Naming the modal value as 21 rather than the sport, football.
Assuming the mode must be one of the bars already drawn.
app_sections.exam_tip: After filling in missing frequencies, add them all up and check against the total given in the stem — it catches ratio errors instantly.

question.question_restated: The marks out of 10 gained by 40 students on an essay writing test are: mark 4 (3 students), 6 (9), 7 (8), 8 (7), 9 (8), 10 (5). (i) Calculate the students' mean score. (ii) Determine (a) the modal mark and (b) the median mark.

app_sections.think_first: With a frequency table the mean needs Σfx, not the sum of the six different marks.
concepts_required: Median position in a frequency table
app_sections.strategy: Multiply each mark by its frequency and divide the total by 40 for the mean, take the mark with the largest frequency for the mode, and use a running total to locate the 20th and 21st marks for the median.

guided_solution.instruction: Multiply each mark by its frequency and add.
Divide by the total number of students.
Pick out the mark with the highest frequency.
Build a running total to find the 20th and 21st marks.

app_sections.why_it_works: A frequency table is a compressed list: the mark 6 appearing nine times contributes 6 × 9 to the total, which is why the mean is Σfx ÷ Σf. The mode is about how often a mark occurs, so it is the mark beside the largest frequency — not the largest frequency itself. The median is a position, and cumulative totals tell you which mark the 20th and 21st students in order actually scored.
common_mistakes: Dividing Σfx by 6 (the number of different marks) instead of by 40.
Giving the mode as 9, the frequency, rather than 6, the mark.
Taking the median as the middle row of the table instead of the middle student.
Forgetting that with 40 students the median averages the 20th and 21st values.

question.source_text: 1. A firm uses a combination of large and small boxes to package the items it produces. Large boxes can hold 8 items. Small boxes can hold 3 items. The firm wishes to package 84 or fewer items using no more than 18 boxes. Let 𝐿 represent the number of large boxes used and 𝑆 represent the number of small boxes used. (i) Write down two inequalities, other than 𝐿> 0and 𝑆> 0, to represent the information above. (ii) Using a scale of 2 cm to represent 5 units on both axes, draw the graphs to represent the inequalities in part (i) above and shade the UNWANTED region. (iii) A profit of $32 is made on a large box and $8 on a small box. Write down an expression to represent the total profit made on the boxes. (iv) From your graph, determine the number of large boxes, 𝐿, and small boxes, 𝑆, which will yield the maximum profit.
question.display_policy: Render verified structured mathematics when available; always retain the linked source visual for fidelity.
question.question_restated: A firm packs items in large boxes holding 8 items and small boxes holding 3 items. It wants to package 84 or fewer items using no more than 18 boxes. L is the number of large boxes and S the number of small boxes. (i) Write two inequalities other than L > 0 and S > 0. (ii) Draw the graphs (2 cm to 5 units on both axes) and shade the unwanted region. (iii) A profit of $32 is made on a large box and $8 on a small box — write an expression for the total profit. (iv) From the graph, find the L and S giving maximum profit. (v) Calculate that maximum profit.

app_sections.think_first: Translate each phrase into an inequality one at a time: 'holds 8 items each' becomes 8L, 'no more than 18 boxes' becomes L + S ≤ 18.
concepts_required: Forming linear inequalities from a word problem
Graphing linear inequalities and feasible regions
Objective function and optimisation at a vertex
app_sections.strategy: Write the item and box constraints, graph the two boundary lines, test the corners of the feasible region in the profit expression, and check that the best point uses whole numbers of boxes.

guided_solution.instruction: Turn the item limit and the box limit into inequalities.
guided_solution.note: Large boxes hold 8L items and small boxes 3S items, and at most 84 items; at most 18 boxes altogether

guided_solution.instruction: Draw the boundary lines and shade out the unwanted region.
guided_solution.note: 8L + 3S = 84 through (0, 28) and (10.5, 0); L + S = 18 through (0, 18) and (18, 0); keep the side containing the origin, with L ≥ 0 and S ≥ 0

guided_solution.instruction: Write the profit expression.
guided_solution.note: $32 per large box, $8 per small box

guided_solution.instruction: Find where the two lines cross, then test each corner in P.
Choose the best point with whole numbers of boxes, since half a box is impossible.
guided_solution.note: Nearby lattice points: (10, 0) gives 320; (10, 1) uses 8(10) + 3(1) = 83 items ≤ 84 and 11 boxes ≤ 18, giving 320 + 8

app_sections.final_answer: (i) 8L + 3S ≤ 84 and L + S ≤ 18  (ii) Graph the lines 8L + 3S = 84 and L + S = 18 and shade everything outside the region bounded by them and the axes  (iii) P = 32L + 8S  (iv) L = 10 large boxes and S = 1 small box (the corner (10.5, 0) is not usable because boxes are whole)  (v) Maximum profit = 32(10) + 8(1) = $328
app_sections.why_it_works: Each restriction in the wording is a straight-line boundary, and the set of points satisfying all of them at once is the feasible region. Because the profit expression is linear, its value increases steadily in one direction across that region, so the largest value is reached at an extreme point. Here profit weights a large box four times a small one, which pushes the optimum to the corner with as many large boxes as the item limit allows; because L and S count boxes, the answer must be a whole-number point inside the region.
common_mistakes: Writing L + S ≤ 84 or 8L + 3S ≤ 18 by mixing up items with boxes.
Shading the wanted region when the question asks for the unwanted region to be shaded.
Quoting L = 10.5 boxes as the answer.
Testing only one corner instead of comparing the profit at all of them.
app_sections.exam_tip: When the variables count physical objects, finish by checking your optimum is a whole-number point that still satisfies every inequality.

quick_check.prompt: If profit is P = 5x + 2y, which of the corners (0, 6) and (4, 1) gives the greater profit?

question.source_text: 2. A farmer grows 𝑥 acres of peas and 𝑦acres of tomatoes. He has 12 acres available to plant peas and tomatoes. (i) Write an inequality in 𝑥 and 𝑦 to satisfy this condition. The farmer must plant at least 2 acres of peas and at least 3 acres of tomatoes. (ii) Write two inequalities to satisfy these conditions. The number of acres of tomatoes planted must not be more than twice the number of acres of peas planted. (iii) Write an inequality in 𝑥 and 𝑦 to satisfy this condition. (iv) Using a scale of 1 cm to represent 1 acre on each axis, draw graphs of the inequalities written in parts (i), (ii), and (iii) above. (v) By shading the UNWANTED region, label as 𝑆the region which satisfies all four inequalities. (b) The farmer makes a profit of $75 on each acre of peas and $50 on each acre of tomatoes. (i)
question.display_policy: Render verified structured mathematics when available; always retain the linked source visual for fidelity.
question.question_restated: A farmer grows x acres of peas and y acres of tomatoes on 12 available acres. (i) Write an inequality for the land condition. He must plant at least 2 acres of peas and at least 3 acres of tomatoes. (ii) Write two inequalities for these. The acres of tomatoes must not be more than twice the acres of peas. (iii) Write an inequality for that. (iv) Draw the graphs (1 cm to 1 acre on each axis). (v) Shade the unwanted region and label as S the region satisfying all four inequalities. (b) Profit is $75 per acre of peas and $50 per acre of tomatoes: (i) write an expression for the total profit P, (ii) use the graph to find the acres of each that maximise profit, (iii) state the maximum profit.

app_sections.think_first: 'At least' means ≥, 'available' means the total cannot exceed 12, and 'not more than twice' compares y with 2x.
concepts_required: Maximising a linear objective function at a vertex
app_sections.strategy: Write the four inequalities, find the corner points of the region they define, then evaluate P = 75x + 50y at each corner and pick the largest.

guided_solution.instruction: Translate each condition into an inequality.
guided_solution.note: Total land: x + y ≤ 12; minimum plantings: x ≥ 2, y ≥ 3; tomatoes at most twice peas: y ≤ 2x

guided_solution.instruction: Draw the four boundary lines and identify the region satisfying all of them.
guided_solution.note: x + y = 12, x = 2, y = 3 and y = 2x, with 1 cm to 1 acre; shade out the unwanted side of each line
guided_solution.result: Region S bounded by the four lines

guided_solution.instruction: Find the corner points of S.
guided_solution.note: x = 2 meets y = 3 at (2, 3); x = 2 meets y = 2x at (2, 4); y = 2x meets x + y = 12 at 3x = 12, x = 4, y = 8; y = 3 meets x + y = 12 at (9, 3)

guided_solution.instruction: Write the profit expression and evaluate it at each corner.

app_sections.final_answer: (i) x + y ≤ 12  (ii) x ≥ 2 and y ≥ 3  (iii) y ≤ 2x  (iv)/(v) Region S has vertices (2, 3), (2, 4), (4, 8) and (9, 3)  (b)(i) P = 75x + 50y  (ii) 9 acres of peas and 3 acres of tomatoes  (iii) Maximum profit = $825
app_sections.why_it_works: Each inequality cuts the plane in half, and the region left over contains every planting plan the farmer could actually use. Since profit is linear, its contour lines are parallel straight lines sweeping across that region, so the last point they touch is a vertex. Peas earn more per acre than tomatoes, so the optimum uses all 12 acres with tomatoes cut back to their minimum of 3.
common_mistakes: Writing the tomato condition as y ≥ 2x or 2y ≤ x instead of y ≤ 2x.
Using x + y = 12 as an equation, so plans using less than 12 acres are wrongly excluded.
Testing points inside the region instead of at its corners.
Reversing the profit rates and computing 50x + 75y.
app_sections.exam_tip: Label each corner of your feasible region with its coordinates on the graph, then make a small table of P values — it is fast and shows the examiner your method.

quick_check.prompt: Where do the lines y = 2x and x + y = 12 intersect?

question.question_restated: A vendor buys x kg of peanuts and y kg of cashew nuts. (a)(i) She must buy a minimum of 10 kg of peanuts and a minimum of 5 kg of cashew nuts — write two inequalities. (ii) She buys no more than 60 kg of nuts in total; peanuts cost $4.00 per kg, cashews $8.00 per kg, and she spends at least $200 — write two inequalities. (b) Draw the graph of the four inequalities (2 cm to 10 kg on each axis) and shade only the region satisfying all four. (c) The profit is $2.00 per kg of peanuts and $5.00 per kg of cashews: (i) use the graph to find the number of kilograms of each nut for maximum profit, (ii) calculate the maximum profit.

app_sections.think_first: Two of these constraints are about weight and one is about money — keep the units apart as you write them.
app_sections.strategy: Write the four inequalities, simplify the cost one, find the corners of the region, then test P = 2x + 5y at each corner.

guided_solution.instruction: Write the two minimum-purchase inequalities.
guided_solution.note: At least 10 kg of peanuts, at least 5 kg of cashews

guided_solution.instruction: Write the weight limit and the spending condition, then simplify the cost inequality.
guided_solution.note: x + y ≤ 60; cost 4x + 8y ≥ 200, divide through by 4

guided_solution.instruction: Draw the four boundary lines and find the corners of the region satisfying all four.
guided_solution.note: x = 10 with x + 2y = 50 gives (10, 20); x = 10 with x + y = 60 gives (10, 50); y = 5 with x + 2y = 50 gives (40, 5); y = 5 with x + y = 60 gives (55, 5)

guided_solution.instruction: Write the profit function and evaluate it at each vertex.
Check the winning point against every condition.

app_sections.final_answer: (a)(i) x ≥ 10 and y ≥ 5  (ii) x + y ≤ 60 and 4x + 8y ≥ 200 (i.e. x + 2y ≥ 50)  (b) Region with vertices (10, 20), (10, 50), (55, 5) and (40, 5)  (c)(i) 10 kg of peanuts and 50 kg of cashew nuts  (ii) Maximum profit = 2(10) + 5(50) = $270
app_sections.why_it_works: Every constraint is linear, so the set of possible purchases is a polygon and a linear profit function reaches its greatest value at one of its corners. Cashews earn $5 per kg against $2 for peanuts, so profit rises fastest by loading up on cashews; the vendor therefore buys only the compulsory 10 kg of peanuts and fills the remaining allowance of the 60 kg limit with cashews.
common_mistakes: Writing the spending condition with ≤ instead of ≥ ('at least $200').
Mixing the cost per kg into the weight inequality, e.g. 4x + 8y ≤ 60.
Forgetting to check the corner also satisfies the constraints that were not used to create it.
Using the cost figures ($4 and $8) instead of the profit figures ($2 and $5) in the objective function.
app_sections.exam_tip: Simplify a money inequality by dividing through by a common factor before graphing — smaller numbers make the intercepts far easier to plot.

question.display_policy: Render verified structured mathematics when available; always retain the linked source visual for fidelity.
question.question_restated: A distance–time graph shows an athlete's 5-hour journey: distance rises steadily from 0 km to 12 km during the first 2 hours, stays at 12 km from 2 hours to 3.5 hours, then falls steadily back to 0 km at 5 hours. (i) Find the average speed during the first 2 hours. (ii) Say what the athlete did between 2 hours and 3 hours. (iii) Find the average speed on the return journey.

app_sections.think_first: On a distance–time graph the steepness of a line is the speed, and a flat line means no distance is being covered at all.
app_sections.strategy: Read the distance covered and the time taken for each straight section off the graph, then divide distance by time for the speeds.

guided_solution.instruction: Read the distance reached at the end of the first 2 hours.
guided_solution.note: The line climbs from 0 km at t = 0 to 12 km at t = 2

guided_solution.instruction: Divide that distance by the time.
Look at the shape of the graph between t = 2 and t = 3.
guided_solution.note: The graph is horizontal at 12 km, so the distance from the start does not change

guided_solution.instruction: Read off where the return journey starts and ends.
guided_solution.note: The line falls from 12 km at t = 3.5 h to 0 km at t = 5 h

guided_solution.instruction: Divide the return distance by the return time.

app_sections.final_answer: (i) 6 km/h  (ii) The athlete rested — he stayed 12 km from the start, covering no further distance.  (iii) 8 km/h
app_sections.why_it_works: Distance–time graphs turn motion into gradient. A steeper line covers more distance in the same time, so the gradient is the speed; a horizontal line has gradient zero, meaning the object is not moving. Because the return line falls, the athlete is moving back towards the start, but speed is still just the distance covered divided by the time taken.
common_mistakes: Reading the flat section as 'stopped for 1 hour' when the graph is flat from 2 h to 3.5 h — read the endpoints carefully.
Using the whole 5 hours instead of only the 1.5 hours of the return leg.
Calling the return speed negative — speed is never negative; only velocity has direction.
app_sections.exam_tip: Mark the coordinates of every corner of a travel graph before answering — most of the marks come from reading those points correctly.

app_sections.think_first: The temperature drops fast at first and then levels off, so the graph is a curve, not a straight line — and its steepness at a point is the rate of cooling there.

Choosing and using a given scale
Reading intermediate values from a curve
Gradient of a tangent as a rate of change
app_sections.strategy: Plot the seven points on the given scales, join them with a smooth curve, read the temperature at t = 15 directly off the curve, then draw a tangent at t = 30 and find its gradient.

guided_solution.instruction: Set up the axes on the stated scales.
guided_solution.note: Horizontal: 2 cm = 10 minutes, so mark 0 to 60. Vertical: 2 cm = 10 °C, so mark 0 to at least 90
guided_solution.result: axes t from 0 to 60 min, K from 0 to 90 °C

guided_solution.instruction: Plot the seven points from the table.
Join the points with one smooth curve, not a series of straight segments.
guided_solution.note: The curve falls steeply at first and then flattens towards about 25 °C

guided_solution.instruction: Read the curve at t = 15 minutes.
guided_solution.note: t = 15 lies midway between the points (10, 61) and (20, 40); the curve there sits just below the midpoint 50.5

guided_solution.instruction: Draw a tangent to the curve at t = 30 and take its gradient.
guided_solution.note: Using a tangent through roughly (20, 40) and (40, 27): gradient = (27 − 40) ÷ (40 − 20) = −13 ÷ 20

guided_solution.instruction: State the rate of cooling as a positive rate of decrease.
guided_solution.note: The negative gradient means temperature is falling

(iii) a) about 50 °C (accept 49–51 °C)  b) about 0.65 °C per minute (accept roughly 0.6–0.7 °C/min), i.e. the temperature is falling at that rate.
app_sections.why_it_works: A cooling liquid loses heat fastest when it is hottest, so equal time steps produce ever-smaller temperature drops and the graph must curve. Because the curve is smooth, values between plotted points can be read off directly. The instantaneous rate of change at a single instant is not the gradient of a chord but the gradient of the tangent at that point, which is why part (b) needs a tangent drawn at t = 30.
common_mistakes: Joining the points with straight lines instead of one smooth curve.
Ignoring the stated scale and inventing your own — the scale is worth marks.
Using a chord instead of a tangent for the rate at t = 30.
Giving the rate of cooling without units or without saying it is a decrease.

(i) For how many minutes was the train at rest at B? (ii) Determine the average speed of the train, in km/h, on its journey from A to B. The train continued its journey away from stations A and B to another station C, which is 50 km from B. The average speed on this journey was 60 km/h. (iii) Calculate the time, in minutes, taken for the train to travel from B to C. (iv) On your answer sheet, draw the line segment which describes the journey of the train from B to C.

question.question_restated: A distance–time graph shows a train's journey from station A to station B: the distance rises steadily from 0 km at 0 minutes to 100 km at B after 40 minutes, then stays at 100 km until 60 minutes. (i) For how many minutes was the train at rest at B? (ii) Determine the average speed in km/h from A to B. The train then travels on to station C, 50 km beyond B, at an average speed of 60 km/h. (iii) Calculate the time in minutes for the journey B to C. (iv) Draw the line segment describing the journey from B to C.

app_sections.think_first: Every flat section of a distance–time graph is a stop, and every sloping section is motion whose gradient gives the speed — watch the minutes-to-hours conversion.
app_sections.strategy: Read the endpoints of the flat section for the rest time, convert 40 minutes to hours for the A-to-B speed, use time = distance ÷ speed for B to C, and then plot the new segment from where the graph left off.

guided_solution.instruction: Read the start and end of the horizontal part of the graph.
guided_solution.note: The graph is flat at 100 km from t = 40 min to t = 60 min

guided_solution.instruction: Read the distance and time for the A-to-B leg.
Convert the time to hours, then divide.
Use time = distance ÷ speed for the B-to-C leg.
Fix the two endpoints of the new segment on the graph.
guided_solution.note: The train leaves B at t = 60 min at 100 km and arrives at C 50 km further on, 50 minutes later

guided_solution.instruction: Join those two points with a straight line.
guided_solution.note: Constant average speed means a straight segment
guided_solution.result: straight line from (60 min, 100 km) to (110 min, 150 km)

app_sections.final_answer: (i) 20 minutes  (ii) 150 km/h  (iii) 50 minutes  (iv) A straight line segment from (60 min, 100 km) to (110 min, 150 km).
app_sections.why_it_works: Average speed is total distance divided by total time, so the gradient of a distance–time line is exactly the speed of that leg. Since speed is asked in km/h, the time must be in hours before dividing — 40 minutes is two-thirds of an hour, not 0.40 of one. The final segment must begin where the graph stopped, at 60 minutes and 100 km, because the train has not moved during the rest.
common_mistakes: Dividing by 40 instead of by 2/3 of an hour, giving 2.5 instead of 150 km/h.
Writing 40 minutes as 0.4 hours.
Starting the B-to-C segment at t = 40 min instead of t = 60 min.
Drawing the B-to-C line ending at 50 km rather than 150 km — C is 50 km beyond B.
app_sections.exam_tip: Convert every time to hours the moment you see 'km/h' in the question, before any dividing happens.

question.question_restated: A speed–time graph shows an athlete's race: the speed rises steadily from 0 m/s at 0 s to 12 m/s at 6 s, stays at 12 m/s until 10 s, then falls steadily to 0 m/s at 13 s. (i) Determine a) the maximum speed, b) the number of seconds for which the speed was constant, c) the total distance covered. (ii) State the time-period during which a) the speed was increasing, b) the speed was decreasing, c) the acceleration was zero.

app_sections.think_first: On a speed–time graph the height is speed and the area underneath is distance — so the whole question is read off one trapezium.
concepts_required: Area under a speed–time graph as distance
app_sections.strategy: Read the maximum height and the flat section straight off the graph, then find the total distance as the area of the trapezium formed by the three straight sections.

guided_solution.instruction: Read the greatest height reached by the graph.
guided_solution.note: The graph levels off at the 12 line

guided_solution.instruction: Read where the horizontal section starts and ends.
guided_solution.note: Flat from t = 6 s to t = 10 s, so 10 − 6

guided_solution.instruction: Identify the shape under the graph.
guided_solution.note: A trapezium with parallel sides 13 s (whole base) and 4 s (the flat top), and height 12 m/s

guided_solution.instruction: Apply the trapezium area formula.
Match each section of the graph to the description asked for.
guided_solution.note: Rising line = speeding up, flat line = no change in speed, falling line = slowing down
guided_solution.result: 0–6 s rising, 6–10 s flat, 10–13 s falling

app_sections.final_answer: (i) a) 12 m/s  b) 4 seconds  c) 102 m  (ii) a) from 0 s to 6 s  b) from 10 s to 13 s  c) from 6 s to 10 s
app_sections.why_it_works: Distance is speed multiplied by time, and on a speed–time graph that product is exactly the area of the strip under the curve — so the whole distance is the area of the trapezium. Acceleration is the gradient of the graph, so a horizontal section means the gradient is zero and the athlete is neither speeding up nor slowing down, even though he is still running at 12 m/s.
common_mistakes: Confusing a speed–time graph with a distance–time graph and reading the flat part as 'at rest' — here the athlete is moving fastest.
Finding only the rectangle and missing the two triangles (or vice versa).
Using 12 as the base of the trapezium instead of the times 13 and 4.
Giving the acceleration-zero period as 'the whole race' because the acceleration graph looks flat.
app_sections.exam_tip: Write 'area under speed–time graph = distance' beside the graph before you start, and split the shape into a rectangle plus triangles if the trapezium formula feels risky.

question.question_restated: A distance–time graph shows a car's three-stage journey from Town A to Town C and back. Stage 1: 0 km at 06:00 rising to 40 km at 07:00; the car then stands still until 07:30. Stage 2: 40 km at 07:30 rising to 100 km (Town C) at 08:30; the car stands still until 08:45. Stage 3: 100 km at 08:45 falling to 0 km at 10:00. (i) State the time of day the car arrived at Town C. (ii) Calculate the total stopped time in minutes. (iii) Determine the constant speed during Stage 2. (iv) Calculate the average speed for the time the car was moving.

app_sections.think_first: Every horizontal piece of the graph is a stop, and 'average speed while moving' means you must take the stopped time out of the total before dividing.
concepts_required: Reading times of day from an axis
app_sections.strategy: Read the corner points off the graph, add the two flat sections for the stopped time, use the Stage 2 rise over its hour for the constant speed, then divide the whole 200 km by the moving time only.

guided_solution.instruction: Find where the graph first reaches its highest value, 100 km.
guided_solution.note: The graph tops out at 100 km, labelled C, at the 08:30 gridline

guided_solution.instruction: Add the lengths of the two horizontal sections.
Read the rise and the time for Stage 2.
guided_solution.note: From 40 km at 07:30 to 100 km at 08:30 — that is 60 km in 1 hour

guided_solution.instruction: Find the total distance travelled over the whole journey.
guided_solution.note: 100 km out to C plus 100 km back to A

guided_solution.instruction: Find the moving time by subtracting the stops from the total time.
Divide the total distance by the moving time.

app_sections.final_answer: (i) 08:30  (ii) 45 minutes  (iii) 60 km/h  (iv) about 61.5 km/h (200 km ÷ 3.25 h = 61.54 km/h)
app_sections.why_it_works: The car's distance from A is plotted, so a rising line means moving away, a falling line means returning, and a flat line means no change of position — a stop. The gradient of each sloping section is therefore the speed on that leg. The return leg still adds 100 km of travel even though the graph goes down, which is why the total distance is 200 km and not 0.
common_mistakes: Taking the total distance as 100 km and forgetting the return journey.
Dividing by the full 4 hours instead of the 3.25 hours of actual motion.
Reading times of day as plain numbers, so 08:45 becomes 8.45 hours.
Missing the shorter 15-minute stop at C because it spans only half a grid square.

A flat piece has gradient zero, meaning no movement. question.source_text: 1. The diagram below shows a circle where AC is a diameter. B and D are two other points on the circle and DCE is a straight line. Angle CAB = 28° and angle DBC = 46°. Calculate the value of each of the following angles. Show detailed working where necessary and give a reason to support your answers. (i) ∠DBA Reason: _______________________________________________________________________ (ii) ∠DAC Reason: _____________________________________________________________________ (iii) ∠BCE Reason: _____________________________________________________________________
question.display_policy: Render verified structured mathematics when available; always retain the linked source visual for fidelity.
question.question_restated: In a circle, AC is a diameter, B and D are two further points on the circle, and DCE is a straight line (E outside the circle). Angle CAB = 28° and angle DBC = 46°. Calculate, with a reason for each: (i) angle DBA, (ii) angle DAC, (iii) angle BCE.

app_sections.think_first: The word 'diameter' is the signal to look for a right angle at the circumference, and the two angles standing on chord DC are the key to the rest.
concepts_required: Cyclic quadrilateral: exterior angle equals interior opposite angle
app_sections.strategy: Use the diameter AC to get angle ABC = 90°, subtract the given 46° for angle DBA, match angles standing on chord DC for angle DAC, then use the exterior-angle property of cyclic quadrilateral ABCD at C.

guided_solution.instruction: Use the diameter to find the angle at B.
guided_solution.note: AC is a diameter, so angle ABC is the angle in a semicircle

guided_solution.instruction: Split angle ABC at B, since BD lies inside it.
Compare the two angles standing on chord DC.
guided_solution.note: ∠DAC and ∠DBC are both subtended by arc DC and both lie in the same segment

guided_solution.instruction: Find the whole angle at A of the cyclic quadrilateral ABCD.
Use the exterior angle of the cyclic quadrilateral at C, formed by extending DC to E.
guided_solution.note: The exterior angle equals the interior opposite angle, so ∠BCE = ∠BAD

app_sections.final_answer: (i) ∠DBA = 44° — the angle in a semicircle, ∠ABC, is 90°, and 90° − 46° = 44°.  (ii) ∠DAC = 46° — angles in the same segment, standing on the same chord DC, are equal.  (iii) ∠BCE = 74° — the exterior angle of cyclic quadrilateral ABCD equals the interior opposite angle ∠BAD = 28° + 46° = 74°.
app_sections.why_it_works: An angle drawn at the circumference on a diameter always measures 90°, because the diameter subtends a semicircular arc of 180° and the angle at the circumference is half the angle at the centre. The same halving rule makes every angle standing on chord DC in the same segment equal, which is why ∠DAC copies ∠DBC. And because opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add to 180°, the exterior angle at C — the supplement of the interior one — must equal the interior angle at A.
common_mistakes: Adding 46° to 90° instead of subtracting, because BD is inside angle ABC.
Pairing ∠DAC with the wrong angle — check which chord an angle stands on before calling them 'same segment'.
Using the exterior angle rule with the adjacent interior angle instead of the opposite one.
Giving answers with no reasons — the reasons carry marks in this question.
app_sections.exam_tip: Mark the diameter's right angle on the diagram the moment you spot it, then write each new angle on the figure as you find it so the next part is a simple read-off.

question.question_restated: A, B, C and D lie on a circle with centre O; AOC and BOD are straight lines through the centre. Angle CBD = 49° and angle OAB = 37°. Angle x is the angle AOB at the centre and angle y is the angle BDC at D. (i) Write down the mathematical names of the straight lines BC and OA. Then determine, with reasons: (a) angle x, (b) angle y.

app_sections.think_first: Two radii to the ends of a chord always make an isosceles triangle — that is what unlocks the angle at the centre here.
concepts_required: Isosceles triangle formed by two radii
app_sections.strategy: Name BC and OA from their positions in the circle, use the isosceles triangle OAB to get the angle at the centre, then use the right angle in the semicircle on diameter BD to finish triangle BCD.

guided_solution.instruction: Name the two lines from where their endpoints lie.
guided_solution.note: BC joins two points on the circumference; OA joins the centre to a point on the circumference
guided_solution.result: BC is a chord; OA is a radius

guided_solution.instruction: Note what kind of triangle OAB is.
guided_solution.note: OA and OB are both radii of the same circle, so OA = OB

guided_solution.instruction: Use the base angles of the isosceles triangle.
Apply the angle sum of triangle OAB.
Use the diameter BOD to find the angle at C in triangle BCD.
guided_solution.note: BD is a diameter, so ∠BCD is the angle in a semicircle

guided_solution.instruction: Apply the angle sum of triangle BCD.

app_sections.final_answer: (i) BC is a chord; OA is a radius.  (a) x = 106° — triangle OAB is isosceles (OA = OB, radii), so ∠OBA = 37° and x = 180° − 2(37°).  (b) y = 41° — BD is a diameter, so ∠BCD = 90° (angle in a semicircle), and y = 180° − 90° − 49°.
app_sections.why_it_works: Every radius of a circle has the same length, so any triangle with two radii as sides is automatically isosceles and its base angles are equal — this converts a single given angle into two. The right angle at C comes from BD being a diameter: an angle at the circumference standing on a diameter is half the straight angle of 180° at the centre, so it is always 90°.
common_mistakes: Calling OA a diameter or a chord instead of a radius.
Assuming ∠AOB = 2 × 37° by misapplying the angle-at-the-centre rule — that rule needs an angle at the circumference standing on the same arc.
Forgetting that BD passes through O and so is a diameter, and missing the right angle at C.
Using 49° at the wrong vertex of triangle BCD.
app_sections.exam_tip: Whenever a line in a circle passes through the centre, write 'diameter' beside it — that single word usually hands you a 90° angle somewhere on the circumference.

question.source_text: 9. In the diagram below, A, B, C and D are points on the circumference of a circle, with centre O. AOC and BOD are diameters of the circle. AB and DC are parallel. (i) State the reason why angle ABC is 90°. (ii) Determine the value of each of the following angles. Show detailed working where necessary and give a reason to support your answer. (a) Angle BAC Reason: _______________________________________________________________________ (b) Angle q Reason: ____________________________________________________________________ (iii) Calculate the value of angle r.
question.display_policy: Render verified structured mathematics when available; always retain the linked source visual for fidelity.
question.question_restated: A, B, C and D lie on a circle with centre O. AOC and BOD are diameters, and AB is parallel to DC. On the diagram angle BAC = 2p°, angle BCA = 3p°, angle BDC = q° and angle ACD = r°. (i) State why angle ABC = 90°. (ii) Determine, with reasons, (a) angle BAC and (b) angle q. (iii) Calculate the value of angle r.

app_sections.think_first: AC is a diameter, so the angle at B is 90° — that turns the two algebraic angles into a simple equation.
app_sections.strategy: Use the right angle at B to solve 2p + 3p + 90 = 180 for p, then get q as an angle in the same segment as ∠BAC and r as an alternate angle to ∠BAC across the parallel lines.

guided_solution.instruction: Explain the right angle at B.
guided_solution.note: AOC is a diameter and B is on the circumference, so ∠ABC stands on a semicircle

guided_solution.instruction: Write the angle sum of triangle ABC in terms of p.
Solve for p and hence for angle BAC.
Compare ∠BDC with ∠BAC.
guided_solution.note: Both angles stand on chord BC and both lie in the same segment

guided_solution.instruction: Use the parallel lines AB and DC with transversal AC.
guided_solution.note: ∠BAC and ∠ACD are alternate angles between the parallel lines

app_sections.final_answer: (i) ∠ABC = 90° because it is the angle in a semicircle — AOC is a diameter.  (ii) a) ∠BAC = 36° (from 2p + 3p + 90 = 180, so p = 18)  b) q = 36° — angles in the same segment, standing on chord BC, are equal.  (iii) r = 36° — alternate angles, since AB is parallel to DC and AC is a transversal.
app_sections.why_it_works: The angle in a semicircle is 90° because the diameter subtends a straight angle of 180° at the centre and the angle at the circumference is half of it. That fixed 90° leaves only 90° for the two algebraic angles, which is what makes p solvable. The same-segment rule then transfers ∠BAC to D without any new calculation, and the parallel lines transfer it again to r — one 36° angle appears three times in the figure.
common_mistakes: Writing 2p + 3p = 180 and forgetting the right angle.
Solving for p but then giving p = 18 as the answer for ∠BAC instead of 2p = 36°.
Matching ∠BDC with the wrong angle — it must stand on the same chord (BC) to be in the same segment.
Using corresponding instead of alternate angles across AB and DC.
app_sections.exam_tip: When angles are given as multiples of a letter, look for a right angle or a straight line first — it turns the diagram into a one-line equation.

question.source_text: 10. In the diagram below, E, C, G and F are points on the circumference of a circle. EG is a diameter of the circle. The tangent AEB is parallel to CD. Angle AEC = 68° and angle EFD = 106°. Determine the value of each of the following angles. Show detailed working where necessary and give a reason to support your answer. (i) ∠ECD Reason: _____________________________________________________________________ (ii) ∠CEG Reason: _____________________________________________________________________ (iii) ∠CGF Reason: _____________________________________________________________________
question.display_policy: Render verified structured mathematics when available; always retain the linked source visual for fidelity.
question.question_restated: E, C, G and F lie on a circle, EG is a diameter, the tangent AEB at E is parallel to the line CFD, angle AEC = 68° and angle EFD = 106°. Determine, with a reason for each: (i) angle ECD, (ii) angle CEG, (iii) angle CGF.

app_sections.think_first: Two facts do the work here: a tangent is perpendicular to the diameter through the point of contact, and the tangent–chord angle equals the angle in the alternate segment.
concepts_required: Tangent perpendicular to the diameter at the point of contact
app_sections.strategy: Use the parallel lines to move the 68° from E to C, use the perpendicular tangent to split the 90° at E, and add two equal angles at G to build angle CGF.

guided_solution.instruction: Compare angle AEC with angle ECD using the parallel lines.
guided_solution.note: AEB is parallel to CD and EC is a transversal, so angle AEC and angle ECD are alternate angles

guided_solution.instruction: Use the right angle between the tangent and the diameter at E.
guided_solution.note: ∠AEG = 90° because the tangent AEB is perpendicular to the diameter EG at the point of contact E; then ∠CEG = ∠AEG − ∠AEC = 90 − 68

guided_solution.instruction: Find angle CGE from the tangent–chord angle at E.
guided_solution.note: ∠AEC is the angle between the tangent and chord EC, so it equals the angle in the alternate segment, ∠EGC

guided_solution.instruction: Find angle EGF from angles in the same segment.
guided_solution.note: ∠EGF and ∠ECF stand on the same chord EF and lie in the same segment, and ∠ECF = ∠ECD = 68° because F lies on CD

guided_solution.instruction: Add the two angles at G.

app_sections.final_answer: (i) ∠ECD = 68° (alternate angles, AEB parallel to CD)  (ii) ∠CEG = 22° (the tangent is perpendicular to the diameter EG at E, so 90° − 68°)  (iii) ∠CGF = 136° (∠CGE = 68° by the alternate segment theorem and ∠EGF = ∠ECF = 68° as angles in the same segment). The 106° at F is not needed for these three parts.
app_sections.why_it_works: The alternate segment theorem links a direction outside the circle (the tangent) with an angle inside it, so the single given 68° can be carried right across the diagram. The parallel line CD repeats that 68° at C, and because angles standing on the same chord from the same side are equal, it reappears at G. Splitting the right angle between tangent and diameter converts the same 68° into the 22° at E.
common_mistakes: Matching the tangent–chord angle with an angle in the wrong segment (the one on the same side as the tangent ray).
Assuming angle CEG is 68° because it 'looks the same' — the diagram is not drawn to scale.
Trying to force every given number into every part; some data belongs to other parts of the question.
Quoting 'angles in a triangle' as a reason where a circle theorem is required.
app_sections.exam_tip: Write the reason beside each angle as you get it — in circle theorem questions the reasons carry as many marks as the numbers.

question.source_text: 11. The diagram below shows a circle, with the points P, Q, R and S lying on its circumference and centre marked O. RP is a diameter of the circle and AB is a tangent to the circle at P. Angle ATPQ = 3x°, angle QPR = 2x°, angle RPS = x° and angle QSP = 54°. Determine the value of each of the following angles. Show detailed working where possible and give a reason for your answer. (i) Angle x Reason: _______________________________________________________________ (ii) Angle y Reason: _______________________________________________________________ (iii) Angle z Reason: _______________________________________________________________
question.display_policy: Render verified structured mathematics when available; always retain the linked source visual for fidelity.
question.question_restated: P, Q, R and S lie on a circle with centre O; RP is a diameter and AB is a tangent at P. Angle APQ = 3x°, angle QPR = 2x°, angle RPS = x°, and angle QSP = 54°. Determine, with reasons: (i) the value of x, (ii) angle y = angle PRS, (iii) angle z = angle PQS.

app_sections.think_first: The tangent and the diameter meet at P at a right angle, and that single fact turns the labelled angles into an equation in x.
concepts_required: Tangent perpendicular to a diameter at the point of contact
app_sections.strategy: Add the angles between the tangent and the diameter to make 90° and solve for x, use the semicircle right angle at S to get y, then use the triangle PQS (or angles in the same segment) to get z.

guided_solution.instruction: Use the right angle between the tangent AB and the diameter RP at P.
Write down the angles at P that this gives.
Use the angle in a semicircle at S in triangle PRS.
guided_solution.note: RP is a diameter, so ∠RSP = 90°; then y = 180 − 90 − ∠RPS = 180 − 90 − 18

guided_solution.instruction: Find z from the angle sum of triangle PQS.
guided_solution.note: ∠QSP = 54° and ∠QPS = 54°, so z = 180 − 54 − 54 (equivalently z = ∠PRS = 72°, angles in the same segment on chord PS)

app_sections.final_answer: (i) x = 18 (tangent perpendicular to the diameter at P gives 3x + 2x = 90)  (ii) y = 72° (angle in a semicircle ∠RSP = 90°, then angle sum of triangle PRS)  (iii) z = 72° (angle sum of triangle PQS, or equally ∠PQS = ∠PRS as angles in the same segment on chord PS)
app_sections.why_it_works: Because the radius OP is perpendicular to the tangent, everything on the tangent side of P is measured from a right angle, which is what makes 3x + 2x = 90 legitimate. The diameter RP then forces a right angle at S, since any angle subtended by a diameter from the circumference is 90°. Finally, PS is a chord seen from Q and from R on the same side of it, so those two angles must be equal — a check that the 72° is right.
common_mistakes: Using 3x + 2x + x = 90 by including ∠RPS, which lies on the other side of the diameter.
Setting the angles at P equal to 180° without noticing which of them make the right angle.
Assuming ∠QSP = 54° is the angle in the alternate segment for 3x without checking which chord it stands on.
Confusing the angle at the centre with the angle at the circumference.
app_sections.exam_tip: Mark the 90° at the point of contact and at the end of any diameter before you start — most of these questions unlock from those two right angles.

question.question_restated: H, J, K, L and M lie on a circle with centre O. MK is a diameter and MK is parallel to HJ; MJ = JL and angle JMK = 38°. Explain, giving a reason, why (a) angle HJM = 38° and (b) angle MJK = 90°.

app_sections.think_first: Each answer needs one named theorem, not a calculation — say which lines or which theorem create the angle.
app_sections.strategy: Treat MJ as a transversal cutting the parallel lines MK and HJ for part (a), and use the diameter MK subtending an angle at J for part (b).

guided_solution.instruction: Identify the transversal joining the two parallel lines.
guided_solution.note: MK is parallel to HJ and the chord MJ crosses both of them
guided_solution.result: MJ is a transversal of two parallel lines

guided_solution.instruction: Name the relationship between angle JMK and angle HJM.
guided_solution.note: They lie on opposite sides of the transversal MJ and between the parallels MK and HJ, so they are alternate angles

guided_solution.instruction: Look at the angle that the diameter MK subtends at J.
guided_solution.note: J lies on the circumference and MK is a diameter, so MJK is an angle in a semicircle

app_sections.final_answer: (a) ∠HJM = 38° because MK is parallel to HJ and MJ is a transversal, so ∠HJM and ∠JMK are alternate angles (often called Z-angles), which are equal.  (b) ∠MJK = 90° because MK is a diameter and J lies on the circumference, so ∠MJK is the angle in a semicircle, which is a right angle.
app_sections.why_it_works: Parallel lines transfer an angle from one place in a figure to another without changing its size, which is why the 38° at M reappears at J. The semicircle result is really the angle-at-the-centre theorem in a special case: the diameter makes a straight angle of 180° at the centre, so the angle it makes at the circumference is half of that, 90°.
common_mistakes: Calling ∠HJM and ∠JMK corresponding angles or co-interior angles instead of alternate angles.
Giving 'angles in the same segment' as the reason for the right angle at J.
Using the given MJ = JL, which is not needed for these two parts.
Stating the answer without naming a theorem — the reason is what is being marked here.
app_sections.exam_tip: When a question says 'explain, giving a reason', a full-sentence theorem name earns the mark; a number on its own does not.

question.question_restated: W, X and U lie on a circle, TV is a tangent to the circle at U, UW is a diameter and triangle WXU is isosceles (WX = XU). Angle z is the angle between the chord UX and the tangent UV. Using appropriate theorems, state three reasons explaining why z = 45°.

app_sections.think_first: Build the 45° in three linked steps: a right angle from the diameter, equal base angles from the isosceles triangle, then the tangent–chord link.
concepts_required: Base angles of an isosceles triangle
app_sections.strategy: Get the right angle at X from the diameter, split the remaining 90° equally between the two base angles, then carry ∠XWU across to the tangent using the alternate segment theorem.

guided_solution.instruction: Use the diameter to fix the angle at X.
guided_solution.note: UW is a diameter and X is on the circumference, so ∠WXU is the angle in a semicircle

guided_solution.instruction: Share the remaining angle sum between the two equal base angles.
guided_solution.note: Triangle WXU is isosceles with WX = XU, so ∠XWU = ∠XUW = (180 − 90) ÷ 2

guided_solution.instruction: Transfer the base angle to the tangent using the alternate segment theorem.
guided_solution.note: z is the angle between the tangent UV and the chord UX, so it equals the angle subtended by UX in the alternate segment, ∠XWU

app_sections.final_answer: Reason 1: ∠WXU = 90°, the angle in a semicircle, because UW is a diameter.  Reason 2: triangle WXU is isosceles with WX = XU, so the base angles are equal and ∠XUW = ∠XWU = (180 − 90) ÷ 2 = 45°.  Reason 3: z = ∠XUV is the angle between the tangent TV and the chord UX, which equals the angle in the alternate segment, ∠XWU = 45°. (Equivalently, the tangent is perpendicular to the diameter UW, so z = 90° − ∠XUW = 45°.)
app_sections.why_it_works: The diameter guarantees a right angle at X, which leaves exactly 90° to be shared between the two base angles; equal sides force them to be equal, so each is 45°. The alternate segment theorem then says the tangent makes the same angle with a chord as that chord subtends from the far arc, so the 45° found inside the triangle is repeated between the tangent and UX.
common_mistakes: Assuming the triangle is isosceles about the wrong pair of sides, giving base angles at the wrong vertices.
Using the tangent–radius right angle but forgetting to subtract the 45°.
Stating the answer as '45° because the diagram looks symmetrical' with no theorem named.
Naming only two reasons when the question explicitly asks for three.
app_sections.exam_tip: Number your reasons 1, 2, 3 to match the spaces given — the mark scheme awards one mark per distinct theorem.
