question.source_text: 14. L, M, N and R are points on the circumference of a circle, with centre O. PQ is a tangent to the circle at R. Angle PRL = 48° and angle RON = 156°. Find the value of each of the following angles, giving reasons for each of your answers. Show ALL working where appropriate. (i) Angle r (ii) Angle e (iii) Angle a
question.display_policy: Render verified structured mathematics when available; always retain the linked source visual for fidelity.
question.question_restated: L, M, N and R lie on a circle with centre O, and PQ is a tangent to the circle at R. Angle PRL = 48° and angle RON = 156°. In the diagram r = angle NLR (at L), e = angle NRQ (between the chord RN and the tangent ray RQ) and a = angle NML (at M). Find r, e and a, giving reasons.

app_sections.think_first: The 156° is an angle at the centre, so the matching angle at the circumference is half of it.
concepts_required: Angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference
app_sections.strategy: Halve the central angle to get r, use the alternate segment theorem for e, then find angle NRL on the straight tangent line and use the cyclic quadrilateral NMLR to get a.

guided_solution.instruction: Halve the angle at the centre to get the angle at the circumference on chord NR.
guided_solution.note: ∠RON = 156° at the centre, and L is on the major arc, so ∠NLR = 156 ÷ 2

guided_solution.instruction: Apply the alternate segment theorem to the tangent and chord RN.
guided_solution.note: e is the angle between the tangent RQ and the chord RN, so it equals the angle subtended by RN in the alternate segment, ∠NLR

guided_solution.instruction: Use the straight tangent line to find angle NRL.
Use the cyclic quadrilateral NMLR, in which angles at M and R are opposite.

app_sections.final_answer: (i) r = ∠NLR = 78° (angle at the centre, 156°, is twice the angle at the circumference on the same chord NR)  (ii) e = ∠NRQ = 78° (tangent–chord angle equals the angle in the alternate segment, ∠NLR)  (iii) a = ∠NML = 126° (angles on the straight line PRQ give ∠NRL = 180 − 78 − 48 = 54°, and NMLR is a cyclic quadrilateral, so ∠NML = 180 − 54)
app_sections.why_it_works: Chord NR is the hinge of the whole diagram: the centre sees it at 156°, so every point on the major arc sees it at 78°, and the tangent at R makes that same 78° with it. Once the three angles at R are known, the tangent being a straight line pins down angle NRL, and the cyclic quadrilateral rule converts that into the angle at the opposite vertex M.
common_mistakes: Doubling instead of halving the angle at the centre.
Matching the tangent–chord angle with the angle on the same side of the chord as the tangent ray.
Forgetting that P, R and Q are collinear, so the three angles at R total 180°, not 360°.
Using 'angles in the same segment' where opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are needed.
app_sections.exam_tip: Mark the centre angle and its half on the diagram immediately — most tangent-and-centre questions are then a chain of one-line steps.

quick_check.prompt: An angle at the centre standing on chord AB is 130°. What is the angle AB subtends at a point on the major arc?

question.source_text: 15. K, L, M and N are points on the circumference of a circle with centre O. XT is a tangent to the circle at K. Angle LKY = 48°, MKO = 12° and angle XKM = 56°. (i) Find the value of angle KOL, giving reasons for each step of your working. (ii) Find the value of each of the following angles: (b) ∠LMN
question.display_policy: Render verified structured mathematics when available; always retain the linked source visual for fidelity.
question.question_restated: K, L, M and N lie on a circle with centre O, and XY is a tangent to the circle at K. In the diagram the tangent–chord angle to KN is 56° (marked between KX and KN), angle MKO = 12° and angle LKY = 48°. (i) Find angle KOL, giving reasons for each step. (ii)(b) Find angle LMN.

app_sections.think_first: Two radii to the ends of a chord always make an isosceles triangle — that is the route to an angle at the centre.
concepts_required: Tangent perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact
Isosceles triangle formed by two radii
app_sections.strategy: Subtract the 48° from the tangent–radius right angle to get angle OKL, use OK = OL to get the other base angle, then find angle KOL; for angle LMN use the angles on the straight tangent line at K and the cyclic quadrilateral KNML.

guided_solution.instruction: Use the right angle between the tangent and the radius OK.
guided_solution.note: ∠OKY = 90° (tangent perpendicular to radius at the point of contact), so ∠OKL = 90 − 48

guided_solution.instruction: Use the isosceles triangle formed by the two radii.
guided_solution.note: OK = OL (radii of the same circle), so ∠OLK = ∠OKL = 42°

guided_solution.instruction: Apply the angle sum of triangle KOL.
Find angle NKL from the angles on the straight tangent line XKY.
Use the cyclic quadrilateral KNML, in which K and M are opposite vertices.

app_sections.final_answer: (i) ∠KOL = 96°: the tangent is perpendicular to the radius OK, so ∠OKL = 90° − 48° = 42°; OK = OL are radii, so ∠OLK = 42°; the angle sum of triangle KOL then gives 180 − 42 − 42 = 96°.  (ii)(b) ∠LMN = 104°: the angles on the straight line XKY give ∠NKL = 180 − 56 − 48 = 76°, and KNML is a cyclic quadrilateral, so ∠LMN = 180 − 76 = 104°. (A check: the tangent–chord angle of 48° gives ∠KNL = 48°, so the centre angle ∠KOL = 96° as found.)
app_sections.why_it_works: Every radius meets the tangent at 90°, so angles measured from the tangent can always be converted into angles measured from a radius. Because two radii to the same chord are equal, the triangle they form is isosceles and its apex angle at the centre follows from the angle sum. The angles at K along the tangent line add to a straight angle, giving the interior angle of the cyclic quadrilateral, and opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary.
common_mistakes: Treating ∠OKL as 48° instead of 90° − 48°.
Forgetting that OK = OL makes triangle KOL isosceles and assuming it is equilateral or right-angled.
Adding the angles at K to 360° rather than 180° along the straight tangent.
Pairing the wrong vertices of the cyclic quadrilateral (K with N rather than K with M).
app_sections.exam_tip: Draw in the radii to both ends of a chord whenever a centre angle is wanted — the isosceles triangle is nearly always the quickest route.

quick_check.prompt: A tangent at K makes an angle of 30° with chord KL. What is the angle KOL at the centre?

question.source_text: 16. The diagram below, not drawn to scale, shows a circle with centre 𝑂. 𝐸𝐻and 𝐸𝐹are tangents to the circle. 𝐹𝑂𝐺and 𝐽𝑂𝐻are straight lines. The measure of ∠𝐹𝐸𝐻= 44∘. Calculate, giving reasons for your answer, the measure of: (i) ∠𝐸𝐻𝐹 (ii) ∠𝐹𝐺𝐻 (iii)∠𝐽𝐻𝐸 (iv) ∠𝐽𝐺𝐻
question.display_policy: Render verified structured mathematics when available; always retain the linked source visual for fidelity.
question.question_restated: A circle has centre O; EH and EF are tangents to the circle from the external point E, FOG and JOH are straight lines (diameters), and angle FEH = 44°. Calculate, giving reasons, (i) angle EHF, (ii) angle FGH, (iii) angle JHE, (iv) angle JGH.

app_sections.think_first: Two tangents from the same external point are equal in length, so triangle EFH is isosceles — that gives the first angle and the rest follows.
concepts_required: Equal tangents from an external point
Base angles of an isosceles triangle
Tangent perpendicular to radius; angle in a semicircle
app_sections.strategy: Use the isosceles tangent triangle for angle EHF, carry that angle into the circle with the alternate segment theorem for angle FGH, then use the tangent–radius right angle and the semicircle right angle for the last two.

guided_solution.instruction: Use the equal tangents to make triangle EFH isosceles.
guided_solution.note: EH = EF (tangents from an external point are equal), so ∠EHF = ∠EFH = (180 − 44) ÷ 2

guided_solution.instruction: Apply the alternate segment theorem at F.
guided_solution.note: ∠EFH is the angle between the tangent EF and the chord FH, so it equals the angle subtended by FH in the alternate segment, ∠FGH

guided_solution.instruction: Use the tangent–radius right angle at H, remembering J, O, H are collinear.
guided_solution.note: EH is a tangent and OH is a radius, so ∠OHE = 90°; since JOH is a straight line, ∠JHE is the same angle

guided_solution.instruction: Use the diameter JH to find the angle it subtends at G.
guided_solution.note: JOH is a diameter and G lies on the circumference, so ∠JGH is an angle in a semicircle

app_sections.final_answer: (i) ∠EHF = 68° (EH = EF, tangents from an external point are equal, so triangle EFH is isosceles: (180 − 44) ÷ 2)  (ii) ∠FGH = 68° (tangent–chord angle ∠EFH equals the angle in the alternate segment)  (iii) ∠JHE = 90° (the tangent EH is perpendicular to the radius OH, and J, O, H lie on a straight line)  (iv) ∠JGH = 90° (angle in a semicircle, since JOH is a diameter)
app_sections.why_it_works: The two tangents from E are mirror images in the line OE, so the triangle they form with the chord FH is isosceles and the 44° at E splits the remaining 136° evenly. The alternate segment theorem then converts the tangent–chord angle at F into an angle standing on FH inside the circle. The last two parts use the two right angles that circles hand you free: tangent-to-radius, and any angle subtended by a diameter.
common_mistakes: Halving 44° instead of halving 180° − 44°.
Matching the tangent–chord angle to the angle in the wrong segment.
Missing that JOH being a straight line makes ∠JHE the same as ∠OHE.
Assuming ∠FGH and ∠JGH must be different simply because they are different parts of the question.
app_sections.exam_tip: With two tangents from one point, immediately mark the equal lengths and the two right angles at the points of contact — most of the working then falls out of one isosceles triangle.

quick_check.prompt: Two tangents from a point A touch a circle at B and C, and angle BAC = 50°. Find angle ABC.

question.source_text: 17. The diagram below, not drawn to scale, shows a circle with centre 𝑂. The points 𝐴, 𝐵, 𝐶, and 𝐷lie on the circumference of the circle. 𝐸𝐴𝐹and 𝐸𝐷𝐺are tangents to the circle at 𝐴and 𝐷respectively. ∠𝐴𝑂𝐷= 114∘and ∠𝐶𝐷𝐺= 18∘. Calculate, giving reasons for EACH step of your answer, the measure of: (i) ∠𝐴𝐶𝐷 (ii) ∠𝐴𝐸𝐷 (iii)∠𝑂𝐴𝐶 (iv) ∠𝐴𝐵𝐶
question.display_policy: Render verified structured mathematics when available; always retain the linked source visual for fidelity.
question.question_restated: A circle has centre O with A, B, C and D on its circumference. EAF and EDG are tangents to the circle at A and D respectively, angle AOD = 114° and angle CDG = 18°. Calculate, giving reasons for each step, (i) angle ACD, (ii) angle AED, (iii) angle OAC, (iv) angle ABC.

app_sections.think_first: Start from the 114° at the centre — it gives the angle at the circumference and, through the tangent quadrilateral OAED, the angle at E.
concepts_required: Angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference
Tangent perpendicular to radius; angle sum of a quadrilateral
app_sections.strategy: Halve the central angle for angle ACD, use the quadrilateral OAED with its two right angles for angle AED, combine the isosceles triangle OAD with the alternate segment angle for angle OAC, then use the cyclic quadrilateral ABCD for angle ABC.

guided_solution.instruction: Halve the angle at the centre standing on chord AD.
guided_solution.note: ∠AOD = 114° and C lies on the major arc, so ∠ACD = 114 ÷ 2

guided_solution.instruction: Work in the quadrilateral OAED, using the tangent–radius right angles.
guided_solution.note: ∠OAE = ∠ODE = 90°, and the angles of a quadrilateral total 360°: ∠AED = 360 − 90 − 90 − 114

guided_solution.instruction: Use the isosceles triangle OAD to find angle OAD.
Use the alternate segment theorem on the tangent DG and chord DC, then subtract.
guided_solution.note: ∠CDG = 18° equals ∠CAD in the alternate segment; AC lies between AO and AD, so ∠OAC = ∠OAD − ∠CAD = 33 − 18

guided_solution.instruction: Build angle ADC and use the cyclic quadrilateral ABCD.

app_sections.final_answer: (i) ∠ACD = 57° (angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference on chord AD)  (ii) ∠AED = 66° (in quadrilateral OAED, ∠OAE = ∠ODE = 90° as tangent–radius angles, so 360 − 90 − 90 − 114)  (iii) ∠OAC = 15° (OA = OD gives ∠OAD = (180 − 114) ÷ 2 = 33°, and the tangent–chord angle ∠CDG = 18° = ∠CAD, so 33 − 18)  (iv) ∠ABC = 75° (∠ODC = 90 − 18 = 72°, so ∠ADC = 33 + 72 = 105°, and ABCD is cyclic, so ∠ABC = 180 − 105)
app_sections.why_it_works: The central angle of 114° fixes the arc AD, so every point on the major arc sees AD at 57°, and the two right angles where the tangents meet their radii turn OAED into a quadrilateral whose fourth angle is forced. The alternate segment theorem moves the 18° from outside the circle at D to inside at A, which is what allows angle OAC to be found as a difference. Finally, the opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary, so the angle at D determines the angle at B.
common_mistakes: Using 114° directly as an angle at the circumference instead of halving it.
Forgetting that OAED has two right angles and trying to use a triangle instead.
Adding ∠CAD to ∠OAD instead of subtracting, which puts C on the wrong side of AO.
Pairing B with C rather than with D when applying the cyclic quadrilateral rule.
app_sections.exam_tip: With two tangents and the centre in one diagram, look for the quadrilateral containing the two right angles — its angle sum of 360° gives the angle at the external point in one line.

quick_check.prompt: Tangents from E touch a circle at A and D, and ∠AOD = 130°. Find ∠AED.

question.source_text: 14. The graph below shows a triangle ABC and its image A'B'C' after undergoing a single transformation. (i) Write down the coordinates of the vertices of ΔABC. (ii) Write down the coordinates of the vertices of ΔA'B'C'. (iii) Describe FULLY the transformation that maps triangle ABC onto triangle A'B'C'. .............................................................................................................................. ..............................................................................................................................
question.display_policy: Render verified structured mathematics when available; always retain the linked source visual for fidelity.
question.question_restated: A graph shows triangle ABC with the right angle at A, and its image A'B'C' after a single transformation. (i) Write down the coordinates of the vertices of triangle ABC. (ii) Write down the coordinates of the vertices of triangle A'B'C'. (iii) Describe fully the transformation that maps triangle ABC onto triangle A'B'C'.

app_sections.think_first: Compare the two triangles first: same size but turned, with the horizontal side becoming vertical — that points to a rotation, not a reflection or translation.
concepts_required: Describing a transformation fully (type, angle, direction, centre)
app_sections.strategy: Read the six vertices off the grid, notice the sides swap between horizontal and vertical with the shape unchanged in size, then find the rotation angle and locate the centre by testing a candidate point on all three vertices.

guided_solution.instruction: Read the coordinates of the object.
guided_solution.note: The right angle is at A, with AC vertical and AB horizontal

guided_solution.instruction: Read the coordinates of the image.
guided_solution.note: A'B' is now vertical of length 3 and A'C' horizontal of length 2

guided_solution.instruction: Decide the type of transformation from the side lengths and orientation.
guided_solution.note: Lengths are unchanged (3 and 2), so it is not an enlargement; the horizontal side AB becomes the vertical side A'B', so the shape has been turned through 90°, clockwise

guided_solution.instruction: Find the centre by using the fact that it is equidistant from each point and its image.
guided_solution.note: Test (0.5, −0.5): A(3, 2) is at (2.5, 2.5) from it and A'(3, −3) is at (2.5, −2.5), a quarter turn clockwise; the same works for B → B' and C → C'

app_sections.final_answer: (i) A(3, 2), B(6, 2), C(3, 4)  (ii) A'(3, −3), B'(3, −6), C'(5, −3)  (iii) A rotation through 90° clockwise (that is, 270° anticlockwise) about the centre (0.5, −0.5).
app_sections.why_it_works: A rotation keeps every length and angle the same but turns the whole figure about a fixed point, so equal side lengths with swapped directions identify it at once. The centre is the one point that does not move: it is the same distance from each object point as from its image, which is why testing a candidate on all three vertices confirms it.
common_mistakes: Describing the transformation as a reflection because the image looks 'flipped'.
Giving the angle without the direction, or the direction without a centre — a full description needs type, angle, direction and centre.
Reading the image coordinates with the signs of the negative y-values wrong.
Assuming the centre must be the origin.
app_sections.exam_tip: To locate a rotation centre, join each point to its image, draw the perpendicular bisectors of two of those segments, and take their crossing point.

quick_check.prompt: Rotate the point (4, 1) through 90° clockwise about the origin.

question.source_text: 15. The letter A and a point C (6, 6) are shown on the grid below. On the diagram, draw accurately each of the following transformations: (i) The enlargement of letter A by scale factor 2, about centre C (6, 6). (ii) The translation of letter A using the vector (−3 2 )
question.display_policy: Render verified structured mathematics when available; always retain the linked source visual for fidelity.
question.question_restated: On a grid the letter A is drawn with apex (4, 4), feet (3, 2) and (5, 2) and a crossbar from (3.5, 3) to (4.5, 3); the point C(6, 6) is marked. Draw accurately (i) the enlargement of letter A by scale factor 2 about centre C(6, 6), and (ii) the translation of letter A by the vector (−3, 2).

app_sections.think_first: Transform the key points of the letter one at a time, then join them up in the same order as the original.
concepts_required: Image coordinates under a scale factor
app_sections.strategy: For the enlargement use image = C + 2 × (point − C) for each key point; for the translation add −3 to every x-coordinate and 2 to every y-coordinate.

guided_solution.instruction: List the key points of the letter A.
guided_solution.note: Apex, two feet and the two ends of the crossbar

guided_solution.instruction: Apply the enlargement rule about C(6, 6) with scale factor 2.
guided_solution.result: Enlarged letter with apex (2, 2) and feet (0, −2) and (4, −2)

guided_solution.instruction: Check the enlargement by comparing a length.
guided_solution.note: The distance between the feet was 2 units and is now 4 units, and every image point lies on the line from C through its object point

guided_solution.instruction: Apply the translation by adding the vector to each point.
guided_solution.result: Translated letter with apex (1, 6) and feet (0, 4) and (2, 4)

app_sections.final_answer: (i) The enlargement has apex (2, 2), feet (0, −2) and (4, −2), and a crossbar from (1, 0) to (3, 0) — twice the size of the original and on the far side of C(6, 6) from it.  (ii) The translated letter has apex (1, 6), feet (0, 4) and (2, 4), and a crossbar from (0.5, 5) to (1.5, 5) — the same size, moved 3 units left and 2 units up.
app_sections.why_it_works: An enlargement multiplies the displacement from the centre by the scale factor, so every image point lies on the ray from C through the object point at twice the distance, and every length doubles while the shape is unchanged. A translation adds the same vector to every point, so nothing about the shape, size or orientation changes — only its position.
common_mistakes: Multiplying the coordinates by 2 instead of multiplying the distance from the centre C by 2.
Translating with the vector components swapped, moving 3 up and 2 left.
Enlarging only the outline and forgetting the crossbar, so the image is not the same letter.
Drawing the image without joining the points in the original order.
app_sections.exam_tip: Draw a faint ray from the centre through one object point and past its image — if the image is not on that ray, your enlargement is wrong.

quick_check.prompt: Enlarge the point (5, 4) by scale factor 2 about centre (1, 2).

(ii) Describe fully the transformation which maps triangle X onto triangle Z. ________________________________________________________________________ ________________________________________________________________________ (iii) On the diagram, translate triangle Y using the vector (−7 1 ) Label this image V. question.question_restated: Three triangles are drawn on a square grid: X with vertices (0, 2), (6, 2), (4, 4); Y with vertices (0, −2), (6, −2), (4, −4); Z with vertices (−2, 0), (−2, 6), (−4, 4). (i) X is mapped onto Y by a reflection — state the equation of the mirror line. (ii) Describe fully the transformation which maps X onto Z. (iii) Translate Y using the vector (−7, 1) and label the image V. (iv) Enlarge X about the centre C(0, 0) by scale factor 1/2 and label the image W.

app_sections.think_first: Write down the vertices of all three triangles first; every part is then a comparison of coordinates.
concepts_required: Enlargement with a fractional scale factor
app_sections.strategy: Match each vertex of X with its partner in Y and in Z to identify the mirror line and the rotation, then apply the given vector and scale factor to produce V and W.

guided_solution.instruction: Compare X with Y vertex by vertex.

Check the enlargement forwards on one vertex.
guided_solution.note: From (5, 1) to X(1, 4) is (−4, 3); doubling gives (−8, 6), landing on (−3, 7) = X' ✓

guided_solution.instruction: Find the mirror line by taking the midpoint of a point and its image.
guided_solution.note: X'(−3, 7) and X"(7, 7): midpoint x = (−3 + 7)/2 = 2; Y'(−1, 7) and Y"(5, 7): midpoint x = 2; y-coordinates are unchanged, so the mirror is vertical

app_sections.why_it_works: An enlargement of scale factor 2 puts every image point twice as far from the centre as its object, so reversing it means halving that displacement — which is exactly an enlargement of scale factor 1/2 about the same centre. A reflection leaves every point at the same perpendicular distance from the mirror on the opposite side, so the mirror passes through the midpoint of each point and its image; because only the x-coordinates change here, that mirror is a vertical line.
common_mistakes: Halving the coordinates themselves rather than the distances from the centre (5, 1).
Writing the mirror line as y = 2 instead of x = 2.
Giving the mirror as 'halfway between the triangles' with no equation.
Enlarging forwards by 2 again, producing a triangle even larger than X'Y'Z'.

app_sections.think_first: Both transformations act on the four vertices one at a time, so find the image of each corner and then join them in the same order.
app_sections.strategy: Read the four vertices of P off the grid, apply the rule (x, y) -> (x + 10, y - 4) for the translation, then the rule (x, y) -> (x, -y) for the reflection in y = 0, and plot each image.

app_sections.why_it_works: A translation slides every point of a shape by the same displacement, so adding the column vector to each coordinate pair moves the whole figure without turning or resizing it. A reflection in y = 0 sends each point to the point the same perpendicular distance on the other side of the x-axis, which leaves x unchanged and reverses the sign of y. Both are isometries, so the image is always congruent to the object.

Subtracting instead of adding the top component of the translation vector.
Reflecting in x = 0 (the y-axis) instead of y = 0, changing the sign of x instead of y.
Joining the image points in a different order, which distorts the shape.

app_sections.why_it_works: A transformation is identified by what it does to corresponding points. When every image point is the object point plus the same fixed displacement, the transformation must be a translation, and the vector is that displacement. When corresponding points sit at equal distances on opposite sides of a fixed line with everything on that line fixed, the transformation is a reflection, and the mirror line is the perpendicular bisector of any object-image segment.
common_mistakes: Giving a translation vector with the components the wrong way round.
Saying 'reflection' without stating the equation of the mirror line, which loses marks for an incomplete description.
Assuming the mirror is the y-axis because both triangles straddle it, instead of finding the midpoint x = 1.
app_sections.exam_tip: 'Describe fully' means state the type of transformation AND all of its data: vector for a translation; mirror line for a reflection; centre, angle and direction for a rotation; centre and scale factor for an enlargement.

app_sections.why_it_works: Reflection in y = x interchanges the roles of the two axes, so a point a units along and b units up becomes b units along and a units up. Because a reflection reverses the sense in which the vertices are traced, checking orientation is a quick way to distinguish a reflection from a rotation when the two could otherwise be confused. guided_solution.instruction: Find the centre C using image = 2 x object - C, so C = 2 x object - image.
Confirm the centre with a second pair of vertices.
guided_solution.note: Using (4, 4) -> (5, 1):  C = (2(4) - 5, 2(4) - 1) = (3, 7). The other two pairs give the same point.

guided_solution.instruction: State the transformation fully.
guided_solution.note: Positive scale factor, so the image is on the same side of the centre as the object and the same way up.

app_sections.final_answer: An enlargement with centre (3, 7) and scale factor 2.
app_sections.why_it_works: An enlargement multiplies the displacement of every point from a fixed centre by the same scale factor, so all lengths are multiplied by k while all angles are unchanged. That is why the image is similar to the object, and why the vector equation image - centre = k(object - centre) rearranges to centre = (k x object - image)/(k - 1); with k = 2 this simplifies to centre = 2 x object - image. Any two corresponding pairs must give the same centre, which is a built-in check.
common_mistakes: Giving the scale factor as the ratio of areas (4) instead of the ratio of lengths (2).
Describing it as 'enlargement scale factor 2' with no centre, which is not a full description.
Pairing the wrong vertices, for example matching a top-left vertex to a bottom-right one.
app_sections.exam_tip: To locate a centre of enlargement quickly, draw straight lines through two pairs of corresponding vertices and extend them until they cross; the crossing point is the centre.

question.question_restated: Quadrilateral O has vertices (1, 1), (2, 3), (4, 1) and (3, 0). Quadrilateral M has vertices (1, 3), (3, 7), (7, 3) and (5, 1), and quadrilateral N has vertices (-1, -1), (-2, -3), (-4, -1) and (-3, 0). M and N are the images of O under two different transformations; describe each of those single transformations fully.

app_sections.think_first: Check the sizes first: if the image is bigger it must be an enlargement, and if it is the same size but turned round, look for a rotation.
concepts_required: Rotation of 180 degrees about the origin
app_sections.strategy: Match corresponding vertices of O with those of M and N. For M compare side lengths to get a scale factor and then solve for the centre; for N spot the coordinate rule and name the rotation.

guided_solution.instruction: Read the vertices of the three quadrilaterals from the grid and pair them up.
Compare a side of O with the matching side of M.
guided_solution.note: In O the step from (1, 1) to (2, 3) is (1, 2); in M the step from (1, 3) to (3, 7) is (2, 4), which is twice as long. Every side of M is twice the matching side of O.

guided_solution.instruction: Find the centre of the enlargement using centre = 2 x object - image.
Now compare O with N vertex by vertex.
Name the transformation with that rule.
guided_solution.note: Changing the sign of both coordinates turns every point through a half turn about the origin; for a half turn the direction of turning does not need to be stated.
guided_solution.result: Rotation of 180 degrees about the origin (0, 0)

app_sections.final_answer: O onto M: an enlargement with centre (1, -1) and scale factor 2.  O onto N: a rotation of 180 degrees about the origin (0, 0).
app_sections.why_it_works: An enlargement multiplies every displacement from a fixed centre by the scale factor, so lengths double while angles stay the same and the image is similar to the object. A rotation of 180 degrees about the origin sends the position vector v to -v, which is exactly the rule (x, y) -> (-x, -y); it preserves both size and orientation, so N is congruent to O and not a mirror image of it.
common_mistakes: Describing O onto N as a reflection, since a half turn also looks 'flipped' at a glance but preserves orientation.
Giving the enlargement without its centre.
Assuming the centre of enlargement is the origin because the shapes are near it.
app_sections.exam_tip: For a half turn, test the rule (x, y) -> (-x, -y) on every vertex. If it works for all of them the centre is the origin; if not, the centre is elsewhere and you must find it.

question.source_text: 1. The diagram below shows a quadrilateral 𝑃𝑄𝑅𝑆where 𝑃𝑄and 𝑆𝑅are parallel. 𝑆𝑄= 8cm, ∠𝑆𝑃𝑄= 90∘, ∠𝑆𝑄𝑅= 82∘and ∠𝑄𝑆𝑅= 30∘. Determine: (i) The length 𝑃𝑆. (ii) The length 𝑃𝑄. (iii)The area of 𝑃𝑄𝑅𝑆.
question.display_policy: Render verified structured mathematics when available; always retain the linked source visual for fidelity.
question.question_restated: In quadrilateral PQRS, PQ is parallel to SR. The diagonal SQ = 8 cm, angle SPQ = 90 degrees, angle SQR = 82 degrees and angle QSR = 30 degrees. Determine (i) the length PS, (ii) the length PQ, and (iii) the area of PQRS.

app_sections.think_first: The diagonal SQ splits the quadrilateral into a right-angled triangle and a non-right-angled triangle, and the parallel sides hand you the missing angle in the right-angled one.
concepts_required: Trigonometric ratios in a right-angled triangle
Area of a triangle = (1/2)ab sin C
app_sections.strategy: Use the parallel sides to transfer the 30 degrees into triangle PQS, solve that right-angled triangle for PS and PQ, then find SR by the sine rule in triangle QSR and add the two triangle areas.

guided_solution.instruction: Use the parallel lines to find angle PQS.
guided_solution.note: PQ is parallel to SR and SQ is a transversal, so angle PQS = angle QSR (alternate angles) = 30 degrees.

guided_solution.instruction: In right-angled triangle PQS, use SQ as the hypotenuse to find PS.
guided_solution.note: PS is opposite the 30 degree angle: PS = SQ x sin 30 = 8 x 0.5

guided_solution.instruction: Find PQ in the same triangle.
guided_solution.note: PQ is adjacent to the 30 degree angle: PQ = SQ x cos 30 = 8 x 0.8660

guided_solution.instruction: Work out the third angle of triangle QSR and use the sine rule to find SR.
guided_solution.note: angle SRQ = 180 - 82 - 30 = 68 degrees, so SR / sin 82 = 8 / sin 68, giving SR = 8 x sin 82 / sin 68

guided_solution.instruction: Find the area of each triangle and add them.
guided_solution.note: Area PQS = (1/2)(4)(6.928) = 13.86 cm squared;  Area QSR = (1/2)(8)(8.544) sin 30 = 17.09 cm squared

app_sections.final_answer: (i) PS = 4 cm  (ii) PQ = 6.93 cm (3 s.f.)  (iii) Area of PQRS = 30.9 cm squared (3 s.f.)
app_sections.why_it_works: A diagonal turns any quadrilateral into two triangles, so its area is always the sum of the two triangle areas. The parallel sides let you move a known angle from one triangle into the other by the alternate-angle property, which is what makes the right-angled triangle solvable from a single length. Once two angles and a side of the second triangle are known, the sine rule fixes the remaining sides, and the formula (1/2)ab sin C gives the area without needing a perpendicular height.
common_mistakes: Using the 82 degree angle as the angle in triangle PQS instead of the alternate 30 degrees.
Taking SQ as a shorter side rather than the hypotenuse of the right-angled triangle.
Forgetting to add the second triangle's area, or double counting the diagonal.
Rounding PQ to 6.9 too early and then losing accuracy in the area.
app_sections.exam_tip: When a quadrilateral question gives you a diagonal, split it at once and label every angle you can deduce before choosing a rule.

app_sections.think_first: Two equal angles in a triangle tell you something about its sides straight away, and the third angle then comes from the angle sum.
app_sections.strategy: Recognise the two equal base angles to name the triangle, then subtract their total from 180 degrees to get the remaining angle.

guided_solution.instruction: Compare the two given angles.
guided_solution.note: angle MPN = angle PMN = 52 degrees, so two angles of the triangle are equal.

guided_solution.instruction: Name the triangle from that property.
guided_solution.note: A triangle with two equal angles has the two sides opposite them equal, so NP = NM.

guided_solution.instruction: Use the angle sum of a triangle to find the third angle.

app_sections.why_it_works: The base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal, and the converse holds too: equal angles force the sides opposite them to be equal. Since the three interior angles of any triangle always add to 180 degrees, knowing two of them determines the third exactly, with no need for the given length of 12.5 cm.

Dividing 180 by 3 instead of subtracting the two known angles.
Trying to use the 12.5 cm in a trigonometric calculation when it is not needed for either part.

question.question_restated: In triangle PQR, angle QPR = 62 degrees, angle PQR = 90 degrees and PR = 11 cm. Calculate (i) the size of angle PRQ and (ii) the length of side RQ.

app_sections.think_first: The right angle sits at Q, so PR is the hypotenuse and the whole triangle can be solved with the basic ratios.
concepts_required: Sine ratio in a right-angled triangle
app_sections.strategy: Subtract the two known angles from 180 degrees for part (i), then use the sine ratio with the hypotenuse PR to find the side opposite the 62 degree angle.

guided_solution.instruction: Use the angle sum of the triangle.
Identify the hypotenuse.
guided_solution.note: The right angle is at Q, so the hypotenuse is the side facing it, which is PR = 11 cm.

guided_solution.instruction: Decide which ratio links RQ to PR.
guided_solution.note: RQ is opposite the 62 degree angle at P, so sin 62 = RQ / PR.

guided_solution.instruction: Evaluate.

app_sections.final_answer: (i) angle PRQ = 28 degrees  (ii) RQ = 9.71 cm (3 s.f.)
app_sections.why_it_works: In a right-angled triangle the hypotenuse is always opposite the right angle, and sine relates the hypotenuse to the side opposite a chosen acute angle. Because the two acute angles of a right-angled triangle add to 90 degrees, finding one immediately gives the other, and you can then choose whichever ratio uses the length you already have.
common_mistakes: Treating RQ as the hypotenuse and dividing by sin 62 instead of multiplying.
Using the 28 degree angle with the sine ratio for RQ, which gives PQ instead.
Leaving the calculator in radian mode.
app_sections.exam_tip: Mark the hypotenuse first, then label the other two sides opposite and adjacent relative to the angle you are using. The correct ratio then chooses itself.

question.source_text: 4. From a harbour 𝐻, the bearing of two ships, 𝑄and 𝑅, are 069∘and 151∘respectively. 𝑄is 175 km from 𝐻while 𝑅is 242 km from 𝐻. (i) Complete the diagram above to show the information given. (ii) Calculate 𝑄𝑅, the distance between the two ships, to the nearest km. (iii)Calculate how far due south ship 𝑅is from harbour 𝐻.

question.question_restated: From a harbour H the bearing of ship Q is 069 degrees and the bearing of ship R is 151 degrees. Q is 175 km from H and R is 242 km from H. (i) Complete the diagram to show this information. (ii) Calculate QR, the distance between the two ships, to the nearest km. (iii) Calculate how far due south of H ship R is.

app_sections.think_first: The two bearings are both measured from the same north line at H, so the angle between the ships at H is simply the difference of the bearings.
concepts_required: Resolving a distance into a north-south component
app_sections.strategy: Find angle QHR as the difference of the bearings, apply the cosine rule in triangle QHR to get QR, then drop a perpendicular from R to the north-south line through H and use the cosine ratio for the southward distance.

guided_solution.instruction: Label the diagram: mark HQ = 175 km, HR = 242 km, the bearing 069 degrees to Q and the bearing 151 degrees to R, both measured clockwise from the north line at H.
guided_solution.note: The 069 degree angle is already shown; add the 151 degree angle and the two distances.

guided_solution.instruction: Find the angle at H inside the triangle.
Apply the cosine rule in triangle QHR.
Take the square root and round.
For the southward distance, note that the bearing 151 degrees makes an angle of 180 - 151 = 29 degrees with the due-south direction from H.
guided_solution.result: 211.7 km, i.e. about 212 km due south

app_sections.final_answer: (i) HQ = 175 km on a bearing of 069 degrees and HR = 242 km on a bearing of 151 degrees, both measured clockwise from north at H.  (ii) QR = 278 km  (iii) R is 211.7 km (about 212 km) due south of H.
app_sections.why_it_works: Bearings are all measured clockwise from the same north direction, so subtracting one from the other gives the true angle between the two paths at the observation point. With two sides and the included angle known, the cosine rule is the only rule that fits, and it returns the third side directly. For part (iii) the southward displacement is the component of HR along the north-south line, and since the bearing is 29 degrees away from due south that component is 242 cos 29.
common_mistakes: Adding the bearings instead of subtracting them.
Using the sine rule when only two sides and the included angle are known.
Using sin 29 instead of cos 29, which gives the east-west distance rather than the southward one.
Forgetting to take the square root at the end of the cosine rule.
app_sections.exam_tip: Always sketch the north line at the point the bearing is measured from; the included angle in the triangle then becomes obvious rather than guessed.

question.source_text: 5. The diagram below shows straight roads connecting the towns L, M, N and R. LR = 18 km, LN = 12 km and MN = 10 km. Angle RLN = 25° and angle LMN = 88°. (i) Calculate angle MLN. (ii) Calculate the distance NR. (iii) Determine the bearing of town R from town L.
question.display_policy: Render verified structured mathematics when available; always retain the linked source visual for fidelity.
question.question_restated: Straight roads join the towns L, M, N and R. LR = 18 km, LN = 12 km, MN = 10 km, angle RLN = 25 degrees and angle LMN = 88 degrees. The diagram also shows that the bearing of M from L is 050 degrees. (i) Calculate angle MLN. (ii) Calculate the distance NR. (iii) Determine the bearing of R from L.

app_sections.think_first: Triangle LMN has two sides and a non-included angle, which is a sine-rule situation; triangle LNR has two sides and the angle between them, which is a cosine-rule situation.
concepts_required: Adding angles at a point to build a bearing
app_sections.strategy: Use the sine rule in triangle LMN to find angle MLN, the cosine rule in triangle LNR to find NR, then add the 50 degree bearing of M, angle MLN and angle NLR to get the bearing of R from L.

guided_solution.instruction: In triangle LMN write the sine rule with the side and angle pairs you know.
guided_solution.note: MN / sin(MLN) = LN / sin(LMN), so sin(MLN) = MN x sin(LMN) / LN = 10 x sin 88 / 12

guided_solution.instruction: Take the inverse sine.
guided_solution.note: The obtuse alternative is impossible because angle LMN is already 88 degrees.

guided_solution.instruction: In triangle LNR apply the cosine rule with LN = 12, LR = 18 and the included angle 25 degrees.
Take the square root.
Build the bearing of R from L by adding angles clockwise from north at L.
guided_solution.note: Bearing of M from L = 050 degrees; then add angle MLN = 56.4 degrees to reach LN, and add angle NLR = 25 degrees to reach LR:  50 + 56.4 + 25 = 131.4
guided_solution.result: Bearing of R from L = 131 degrees (to the nearest degree)

app_sections.final_answer: (i) angle MLN = 56.4 degrees  (ii) NR = 8.75 km (3 s.f.)  (iii) The bearing of R from L is 131 degrees.
app_sections.why_it_works: The sine rule pairs each side with the angle opposite it, so it is the right tool when you know a side, its opposite angle and one more side. The cosine rule is the right tool when the known angle lies between the two known sides, because no side-angle pair is complete. A bearing is just a total turn measured clockwise from north, so once the roads are in order around L you can accumulate the angles between them to reach any direction.
common_mistakes: Using the cosine rule in triangle LMN, where the 88 degree angle is not between the two known sides.
Choosing the obtuse solution 123.6 degrees for angle MLN, which would make the angle sum exceed 180 degrees.
Forgetting the initial 050 degrees and quoting the bearing of R as 81.4 degrees.
Rounding angle MLN to 56 degrees before adding, which shifts the final bearing.
app_sections.exam_tip: Before choosing a rule, mark on the diagram which angle is opposite which side. Complete side-angle pair means sine rule; angle sandwiched between two sides means cosine rule.

question.source_text: 6. From a port L, ship R is 250 kilometres on a bearing of 065°. Ship T is 180 kilometres from L on a bearing of 148°. This information is illustrated in the diagram below. (i) Complete the diagram above by inserting the value of angle RLT. (ii) Calculate RT, the distance between the two ships. (iii) Determine the bearing of T from R.
question.display_policy: Render verified structured mathematics when available; always retain the linked source visual for fidelity.
question.question_restated: From a port L, ship R is 250 km away on a bearing of 065 degrees and ship T is 180 km away on a bearing of 148 degrees. (i) Insert the value of angle RLT on the diagram. (ii) Calculate RT, the distance between the two ships. (iii) Determine the bearing of T from R.

app_sections.think_first: Both bearings start at L, so the angle at L is the difference between them, and the triangle is then a straightforward cosine-rule problem.
app_sections.strategy: Find angle RLT by subtracting the bearings, use the cosine rule for RT, then find angle LRT by the sine rule and combine it with the back bearing of L from R.

guided_solution.instruction: Subtract the two bearings to get the angle at L.
Apply the cosine rule in triangle RLT with LR = 250, LT = 180 and the included angle 83 degrees.
Take the square root.
Use the sine rule to find angle LRT, the angle at R in the triangle.
guided_solution.note: sin(LRT) / LT = sin(RLT) / RT, so sin(LRT) = 180 x sin 83 / 289.71 = 0.6167

guided_solution.instruction: Find the bearing of L from R (the back bearing) and turn through angle LRT towards T.
guided_solution.note: Bearing of R from L is 065, so the bearing of L from R is 065 + 180 = 245 degrees. T lies anticlockwise from L as seen from R, so the bearing of T from R is 245 - 38.1.
guided_solution.result: Bearing of T from R = 206.9, i.e. 207 degrees

app_sections.final_answer: (i) angle RLT = 83 degrees  (ii) RT = 290 km (3 s.f.)  (iii) The bearing of T from R is 207 degrees (to the nearest degree).
app_sections.why_it_works: Because both bearings are measured from the same north line at L, their difference is the true angle of the triangle at L. With two sides and that included angle, the cosine rule gives the third side, and the sine rule then gives a second angle. A back bearing differs from the forward bearing by exactly 180 degrees because the north lines at the two points are parallel, which is what lets you convert an interior angle of the triangle into a compass direction.
common_mistakes: Adding the bearings to get 213 degrees for the angle at L.
Forgetting to square root at the end of the cosine rule.
Adding angle LRT to the back bearing instead of subtracting it, giving 283 degrees.
Quoting a bearing with fewer than three figures.
app_sections.exam_tip: Draw a short north arrow at every point you take a bearing from. Back bearing = forward bearing plus or minus 180 degrees, whichever keeps the answer between 000 and 360.

question.source_text: 7. The diagram below shows a triangular field LMP on horizontal ground. (i) Calculate the value of angle MLP. (ii) The bearing of P from L is 210°. (a) Find the bearing of M from L. (b) Calculate the value of angle NLP and hence find the bearing of L from P.
question.display_policy: Render verified structured mathematics when available; always retain the linked source visual for fidelity.
question.question_restated: A triangular field LMP on horizontal ground has LM = 120 m, LP = 150 m and PM = 180 m, with a north line drawn at L. (i) Calculate angle MLP. (ii) The bearing of P from L is 210 degrees. (a) Find the bearing of M from L. (b) Calculate angle NLP and hence find the bearing of L from P.

app_sections.think_first: All three sides are known, so the angle at L comes from the cosine rule; after that the whole question is about turning angles into compass directions.
concepts_required: Back bearings and parallel north lines
app_sections.strategy: Rearrange the cosine rule to find angle MLP from the three sides, then subtract that angle from the bearing of P to reach M, and use the fact that the north lines at L and P are parallel to get the back bearing.

guided_solution.instruction: Write the cosine rule for the angle at L using the three sides.
guided_solution.note: cos(MLP) = (LP squared + LM squared - PM squared) / (2 x LP x LM) = (22500 + 14400 - 32400) / (2 x 150 x 120)

guided_solution.instruction: Take the inverse cosine.
guided_solution.note: The positive cosine tells you the angle is acute.

guided_solution.instruction: For (ii)(a), start from the bearing of P and turn back towards M.
guided_solution.note: In the diagram M lies clockwise of north but anticlockwise of P, so the bearing of M from L = 210 - 82.8
guided_solution.result: Bearing of M from L = 127.2, i.e. 127 degrees

guided_solution.instruction: For (ii)(b), find the geometric angle NLP between the north line at L and the line LP.
guided_solution.note: A bearing of 210 degrees is measured clockwise from north, so the angle you actually draw from the north ray round to LP is 360 - 210 = 150 degrees on the anticlockwise side.

guided_solution.instruction: Use the parallel north lines at L and P to get the back bearing.
guided_solution.note: The north line at P is parallel to the north line at L, so the bearing of L from P = 210 - 180.
guided_solution.result: Bearing of L from P = 030 degrees

app_sections.final_answer: (i) angle MLP = 82.8 degrees  (ii)(a) The bearing of M from L is 127 degrees  (ii)(b) angle NLP = 150 degrees and the bearing of L from P is 030 degrees.
app_sections.why_it_works: The cosine rule is the only rule that connects three sides to an angle, and rearranging it isolates the cosine of the angle you want. Bearings are directions measured clockwise from north, so any two directions from the same point differ by the angle between them; that is why subtracting angle MLP from the bearing of P gives the bearing of M. Back bearings differ by 180 degrees because the north lines at any two points on a plan are parallel, so the two bearings are co-interior angles across the line joining them.
common_mistakes: Putting the side opposite the required angle in the wrong place in the cosine rule.
Adding angle MLP to 210 degrees, which would put M in the wrong quadrant.
Writing angle NLP as 210 degrees, confusing the bearing with the drawn angle.
Giving the back bearing as 390 degrees instead of subtracting 180.
app_sections.exam_tip: Bearings are always written with three figures, so 30 degrees must be recorded as 030 degrees.

app_sections.why_it_works: An angle of elevation is measured from the horizontal, so the sight line, the horizontal ground distance and the vertical height always form a right-angled triangle in which tangent links the height to the ground distance. For the perimeter, the diagonal QS splits the quadrilateral into two triangles; the one containing the unknown side has two sides and the angle between them, which is precisely the cosine rule case.
common_mistakes: Using sin 21 or cos 21 instead of tan 21, which needs the slant distance QT rather than the ground distance.

app_sections.exam_tip: Angle of elevation problems almost always reduce to tan = opposite over adjacent, because the given distance is a horizontal ground distance and the unknown is a vertical height.

question.source_text: 9. Points E, F, G and H are on level ground. The diagram below gives information on the distances and angles between the points. The angle of elevation of the top of the tower, 𝑇, from the point 𝐹is 31∘. What length of wire was used to secure point 𝑇to point 𝐹? (iii)The bearing of 𝐸from 𝐻is 228∘. Find the bearing of: a) 𝐻 from 𝐸 b) 𝐺 from 𝐻.

question.question_restated: E, F, G and H are on level ground. In the diagram HG = 5.3 m, HF = 11 m, GF = 6.9 m, angle EHG = 54° and x = angle GHF. (i) Show that x = 29.5°, correct to 1 decimal place. (ii) A vertical tower GT stands at G and is secured by wire to E, F and H. The angle of elevation of the top T from F is 31°. Find the length of wire from T to F. (iii) The bearing of E from H is 228°. Find the bearing of (a) H from E, (b) G from H.

app_sections.think_first: Every part here is either a cosine-rule triangle, a right-angled triangle standing on the ground, or a bearing turned through a known angle — sort out which before you start.
app_sections.strategy: Use the cosine rule in triangle HGF (all three sides known) to find x. For the wire FT, note the tower is vertical at G so triangle FGT is right-angled at G with FG = 6.9 m and elevation 31°. For the bearings, use the back-bearing rule and add or subtract the 54° at H.

guided_solution.instruction: In triangle HGF write the cosine rule for the angle x at H, opposite side GF.
guided_solution.note: cos x = (HG² + HF² − GF²) / (2 × HG × HF)

guided_solution.instruction: Evaluate the numerator and denominator, then take the inverse cosine.
For the wire, use right-angled triangle FGT with the right angle at G, base FG = 6.9 m and angle of elevation 31° at F.
guided_solution.note: cos 31° = FG / FT, so FT = 6.9 ÷ cos 31°

guided_solution.instruction: Find the bearing of H from E by taking the back bearing of 228°.
Find the bearing of G from H by turning 54° from HE towards HG, which is the anticlockwise (decreasing) direction.

app_sections.final_answer: (i) cos x = 0.8703 so x = 29.5° (1 d.p.)  (ii) FT = 8.05 m of wire  (iii) a) 048°  b) 174°
app_sections.why_it_works: The cosine rule links all three sides of a triangle to one angle, so knowing HG, HF and GF fixes the angle between HG and HF completely. The tower is vertical, so the wire FT, the ground distance FG and the tower GT form a right-angled triangle in which the elevation angle at F ties the hypotenuse to the known base. Bearings are directions measured clockwise from north, so reversing a direction changes it by exactly 180°, and rotating from one ray to another at the same point changes the bearing by the angle between them.
common_mistakes: Using HF or the wrong pair of sides as the 'included' sides for angle x.
Taking GT rather than FT as the wire length — the wire is the slant, not the tower.
Adding 180° to 228° instead of subtracting, giving an impossible bearing of 408°.
Adding the 54° to 228° when the diagram shows G lies clockwise-back from E.
app_sections.exam_tip: Write the cosine rule already rearranged for the angle before substituting; it stops you dividing by the wrong product.

question.question_restated: PQRS is a quadrilateral made of triangles PQS and QRS. In triangle QRS, SQ = 18 m, SR = 16 m and angle QSR = 25°. (iii) Calculate the length of QR. (ii) The bearing of P from S is 205°; with angle PSQ = 72° and angle QSR = 25°, determine the bearing of (a) R from S and (b) S from P.

app_sections.think_first: QR sits opposite a known angle with both of its arms given, so this is a cosine-rule question; the bearings then come from rotating away from SP by the marked angles at S.
concepts_required: Angles at a point in a diagram
app_sections.strategy: Apply the cosine rule in triangle QRS using SQ, SR and the included angle QSR. For bearings, start at the given bearing of SP and subtract the angles PSQ and QSR to swing round to SR, then use the back-bearing rule for S from P.

guided_solution.instruction: Write the cosine rule for QR in triangle QRS, with angle QSR between the two known sides.
Evaluate each term and take the square root.
Find the bearing of Q from S by turning 72° from SP towards SQ, which reduces the bearing.
Turn a further 25° from SQ to reach SR.
Take the back bearing of SP to get the bearing of S from P.

app_sections.final_answer: (iii) QR = 7.6 m  (ii) (a) bearing of R from S = 108°  (b) bearing of S from P = 025°
app_sections.why_it_works: The cosine rule is the only triangle rule that works from two sides and the angle between them, which is exactly the information triangle QRS supplies. Bearings at a single point behave like a protractor reading: each marked angle at S is the turn between two rays, so the bearings of SP, SQ and SR differ by those marked angles. Reversing a direction always changes the bearing by 180°.
common_mistakes: Trying the sine rule when the angle given lies between the two known sides.
Adding 72° and 25° to 205° instead of subtracting, ignoring which side of SP the points lie.
Forgetting that a bearing must be written with three figures, e.g. 025° not 25°.
Rounding cos 25° too early and losing the first decimal place.
app_sections.exam_tip: Sketch the north line at the point you are measuring from and mark the given bearing first; the direction of the turn then becomes obvious.

question.question_restated: From a harbour H the bearing of buoy S is 185° and the bearing of buoy Q is 311°. HQ = 5.4 km and HS = 3.5 km. (i) State the value of angle QHS. (ii) Calculate QS, the distance between the buoys. (iv) Calculate the bearing of S from Q.

app_sections.think_first: The two bearings are measured from the same point H, so the angle between them is just their difference — and that angle sits between the two known sides.
app_sections.strategy: Subtract the bearings to get angle QHS, use the cosine rule with HQ, HS and that angle to find QS, then use the sine rule to find angle HQS and combine it with the back bearing of HQ to get the bearing of S from Q.

guided_solution.instruction: Subtract the two bearings measured at H.
Apply the cosine rule in triangle QHS.
Use the sine rule to find angle HQS, opposite the known side HS.
Find the bearing of H from Q as the back bearing of 311°.
Add angle HQS, since S lies clockwise of QH as seen from Q.

app_sections.final_answer: (i) angle QHS = 126°  (ii) QS = 7.98 km (about 8.0 km)  (iv) bearing of S from Q = 151.8°, i.e. about 152°
app_sections.why_it_works: Bearings from a common point are directions on the same protractor, so their difference is the true angle of the triangle at that point. With two sides and the included angle, the cosine rule gives the third side; the sine rule then unlocks a second angle. Finally, a bearing at Q must be measured from Q's own north line, which is why you start from the back bearing of HQ and turn by the triangle's angle at Q.
common_mistakes: Using 360° − 126° = 234° as the triangle angle; a triangle angle can never exceed 180°.
Forgetting that cos 126° is negative, which makes the two squares be added to, not subtracted from, the total.
Measuring the final bearing from H's north line instead of Q's.
Adding instead of subtracting when forming the back bearing 311° − 180°.
app_sections.exam_tip: Draw a fresh north arrow at every point you are asked to take a bearing from — bearings are always measured at the point named after the word 'from'.

question.question_restated: In the diagram (not drawn to scale) R, S and T lie on a straight line with S between R and T. ST = 6 m, WR = 11.2 m, WT = 14.8 m and angle WRS = 90°. Giving answers to 1 decimal place, calculate (ii) the length RS and (iii) the measure of angle RTW.

app_sections.think_first: The right angle at R makes WRT a right-angled triangle with WT as its hypotenuse, so Pythagoras gives the whole base RT before you strip off the 6 m.
app_sections.strategy: Use Pythagoras in triangle WRT to find RT, subtract ST to get RS, then use the sine ratio (opposite WR over hypotenuse WT) to find angle RTW.

guided_solution.instruction: Apply Pythagoras in right-angled triangle WRT, where WT is the hypotenuse.
Subtract ST from RT, since S lies between R and T.
In triangle WRT, identify WR as opposite angle RTW and WT as the hypotenuse.
Take the inverse sine.

app_sections.why_it_works: Because angle WRS is 90° and R, S, T are collinear, angle WRT is also 90°, so the whole triangle WRT is right-angled with WT as hypotenuse. That lets Pythagoras give the full base RT in one step, and RS is simply what is left of that base after the 6 m section ST. The angle at T then follows from the sine ratio, which needs only the side opposite the angle and the hypotenuse — both already known.
common_mistakes: Adding the squares instead of subtracting; WT is the hypotenuse, so its square is the largest.
Finding RT and quoting it as RS without removing the 6 m.
Using tan with RT instead of sin with WT and picking up rounding error from RT.
Rounding RT to 9.7 before subtracting, which shifts RS to 3.7 only by luck.
app_sections.exam_tip: Keep the unrounded value in your calculator memory and round only the final answer — the question asks for 1 decimal place at the end, not at every stage.

question.display_policy: Render verified structured mathematics when available; always retain the linked source visual for fidelity.
question.question_restated: OPQL is a parallelogram with OP = r and OL = s. T is the point such that vector PQ = vector QT. M divides PL in the ratio 2 : 1. (i) Find, in terms of r and s, a) vector PL and b) vector OM. (ii) Prove that O, M and T are collinear.

app_sections.think_first: In a parallelogram opposite sides are equal vectors, so PQ is just s — that single fact unlocks both T and M.
concepts_required: Vector addition and the triangle law
Dividing a line in a given ratio
app_sections.strategy: Use PQ = OL = s to place Q and T, build PL by going P → O → L, take two-thirds of PL to reach M from P, then show OT is a scalar multiple of OM.

guided_solution.instruction: Travel from P to L through O using the triangle law.
Find PM, remembering M divides PL in the ratio 2 : 1 so PM is two-thirds of PL.
Add OP and PM to reach M from O.
Express OT. Since OPQL is a parallelogram, PQ = OL = s, and QT = PQ = s as well.
guided_solution.note: OT = OP + PQ + QT = r + s + s

guided_solution.instruction: Compare OT with OM.
guided_solution.result: OT = 3 OM, so OT is parallel to OM and they share the point O — hence O, M and T are collinear

app_sections.final_answer: (i) a) PL = s − r  b) OM = (1/3)(r + 2s) = (1/3)r + (2/3)s.  (ii) OT = r + 2s = 3 OM; since OT is a scalar multiple of OM and both start at O, the points O, M and T lie on the same straight line.
app_sections.why_it_works: A vector route between two points can be built from any chain of known vectors, so P → O → L gives PL without needing coordinates. A ratio along a line converts directly into a fraction of the whole vector, which is why PM = (2/3)PL. Collinearity is proved when one vector equals a number times another and the two vectors share a starting point — parallel plus a common point forces a single straight line.
common_mistakes: Writing PL = r − s by going the wrong way round; PL starts at P, so the r term must be negative.
Taking PM as (1/2)PL or (2/1)PL instead of (2/3)PL.
Assuming PQ = r; in parallelogram OPQL the side PQ matches OL, not OP.
Stopping after showing OT and OM are parallel without mentioning the common point O.
app_sections.exam_tip: For a collinearity proof, always end with the sentence naming the shared point — 'parallel and share point O, therefore collinear' — because that is where the mark sits.

The point 𝐴lies on 𝐿𝑀such that 𝐿𝐴: 𝐴𝑀= 1: 2, and the point 𝐵on 𝑀𝑁 such that 𝑀𝐵: 𝐵𝑁= 2: 1. (vi) Express, in its simplest form, 𝑀𝑁 ⃗⃗⃗⃗⃗⃗⃗ in terms of 𝐱and 𝐳. (vii) a) Find, in terms of 𝐱and 𝐲, in its simplest form, an expression for 𝐿𝑁 ⃗⃗⃗⃗⃗ . b) Show that 𝐴𝐵 ⃗⃗⃗⃗⃗ = 2 3 (2𝐱−4𝐲). (viii) Based on your results in part (ii), state TWO geometric properties relating 𝐿𝑁to 𝐴𝐵. ________________________________________________________________________

question.question_restated: OLMN is a quadrilateral with O the origin, OL = 4y, OM = 6z and ON = 2x. A lies on LM with LA : AM = 1 : 2, and B lies on MN with MB : BN = 2 : 1. (vi) Express MN in terms of x and z. (vii) a) Find LN in terms of x and y. b) Show that AB = (2/3)(2x − 4y). (viii) State TWO geometric properties relating LN to AB.

app_sections.think_first: Everything is measured from the origin O, so any vector PQ is simply OQ − OP — build each answer that way before touching the ratios.
concepts_required: Dividing a line in a given ratio
app_sections.strategy: Get MN and LN by subtracting position vectors, then reach B by travelling A → M → B, using AM = (2/3)LM and MB = (2/3)MN, and finally compare AB with LN.

guided_solution.instruction: Subtract the position vectors of M and N.
Do the same for L and N.
Find LM, then take the part of it from A to M. Since LA : AM = 1 : 2, AM is two-thirds of LM.
Find MB, which is two-thirds of MN since MB : BN = 2 : 1.
Add AM and MB to travel from A to B, and factor the result.
Compare AB with LN.
guided_solution.result: AB is parallel to LN and AB is two-thirds the length of LN

app_sections.final_answer: (vi) MN = 2x − 6z  (vii) a) LN = 2x − 4y  b) AB = AM + MB = (4z − (8/3)y) + ((4/3)x − 4z) = (4/3)x − (8/3)y = (2/3)(2x − 4y)  (viii) AB is parallel to LN (same direction), and AB is two-thirds the length of LN, i.e. |AB| : |LN| = 2 : 3.
app_sections.why_it_works: With O as origin every point has a position vector, so the vector from one point to another is always 'finish minus start'. A ratio along a segment converts into a fraction of that segment's vector, letting you land exactly on A and B. When the final expression for AB turns out to be a number times LN, that number carries both facts at once: the direction is unchanged (parallel) and the length is scaled by that number.
common_mistakes: Writing MN = OM − ON, reversing the direction.
Using LA = (2/3)LM instead of AM = (2/3)LM — the ratio 1 : 2 puts A nearer L.
Forgetting to simplify and so missing the factor (2/3) that reveals the parallel property.
Giving only one geometric property when TWO are asked for.
app_sections.exam_tip: When a 'show that' answer is given to you in factored form, aim your simplification at that exact form — it tells you what to factor out.

question.question_restated: (a) Vector PQ = (5, −4) (column vector). If P is the point (−2, 3), determine the coordinates of Q. (b) In pentagon OABCD, OA is parallel to DC and AB is parallel to OD, with OD = 2AB and OA = 2DC. Given OA = a and AB = b, find in terms of a and b, in simplest form: (vi) AD, (vii) BC, and (viii) state the conclusion about AD and BC that follows.

app_sections.think_first: A column vector tells you how far to move, so Q is P shifted by (5, −4); the pentagon then needs OD and DC written in terms of a and b before any route is built.
concepts_required: Column vectors and translation of a point
app_sections.strategy: Add the column vector to the coordinates of P for part (a). For (b), turn the parallel/length statements into OD = 2b and DC = (1/2)a, then build AD and BC as chains of known vectors and compare them.

guided_solution.instruction: Add the components of PQ to the coordinates of P.
Translate the two given conditions into vectors. AB is parallel to OD with OD = 2AB, and OA is parallel to DC with OA = 2DC.
Travel from A to D through O.
Travel from B to C through A, O and D.
guided_solution.note: BC = BA + AO + OD + DC = −b − a + 2b + (1/2)a

guided_solution.instruction: Compare the two results.
guided_solution.result: AD and BC are parallel, with AD twice the length of BC

app_sections.final_answer: (a) Q = (3, −1)  (b) (vi) AD = 2b − a  (vii) BC = b − (1/2)a = (1/2)(2b − a)  (viii) BC = (1/2)AD, so AD and BC are parallel and AD is twice as long as BC.
app_sections.why_it_works: A column vector is a pure displacement: adding it to a point's coordinates moves that point without changing anything else, which is why Q = P + PQ. In the pentagon, 'parallel' means one vector is a scalar multiple of the other, and the length statements fix the scalar, so OD and DC can be written entirely in a and b. Once both AD and BC are expressed in the same two vectors, one being a multiple of the other proves the parallel relationship and the length ratio in a single line.
common_mistakes: Subtracting the column vector from P instead of adding it, giving (−7, 7).
Setting DC = 2a instead of (1/2)a — read carefully which is twice which.
Losing a sign when reversing a vector, e.g. writing BA as +b.
Stating only that the two are parallel and omitting the length relationship.
app_sections.exam_tip: Convert every worded condition ('X is parallel to Y and twice as long') into an equation in vectors before you start any route — the algebra then does itself.

question.question_restated: O is the origin, E lies on OF with OE = 2EF, and M is the midpoint of EG. Given OG = c and OF = d, find in terms of c and d, in simplest form: (i) FG, (ii) EG, (iii) OM.

app_sections.think_first: OE = 2EF splits OF into three equal parts, so E is two-thirds of the way from O to F — write OE = (2/3)d before anything else.
concepts_required: Dividing a line in a given ratio
Midpoint of a line in vectors
app_sections.strategy: Convert OE = 2EF into OE = (2/3)OF, then get FG and EG by subtracting position vectors, and reach M by going O → E → halfway along EG.

guided_solution.instruction: Use OE = 2EF to split OF into three equal parts.
Find FG by subtracting the position vectors of F and G.
Find EG the same way, using the position vector of E.
Reach M by adding half of EG to OE, since M is the midpoint of EG.

app_sections.final_answer: (i) FG = c − d  (ii) EG = c − (2/3)d  (iii) OM = (1/2)c + (1/3)d
app_sections.why_it_works: The condition OE = 2EF says OE is twice EF, so OF is cut into three equal pieces and E sits at the two-thirds mark; that turns a worded ratio into the vector (2/3)d. From there every vector between two points is 'position of finish minus position of start'. A midpoint is exactly halfway, so adding half of EG to the position vector of E lands precisely on M.
common_mistakes: Reading OE = 2EF as OE = 2OF and writing OE = 2d.
Writing FG = d − c by reversing start and finish.
Using OM = (1/2)(OE + OG) but substituting OF for OE.
Failing to collect the d terms: (2/3)d − (1/3)d is (1/3)d, not (1/3)d subtracted.
app_sections.exam_tip: The midpoint of PQ always has position vector (1/2)(OP + OQ) — check your route answer against that formula as a free verification.

question.question_restated: Given the column vectors WX = (5, −1), XY = (−3, 7) and ZY = (8, −7), determine each of the following: (i) a vector other than (5, −1) that is parallel to WX, (ii) WY, (iii) XZ, (iv) |XY|.

app_sections.think_first: Column vectors add and subtract component by component, and the only trap here is that ZY points the wrong way for the route you need in part (iii).
concepts_required: Vector addition using the triangle law
app_sections.strategy: Multiply WX by any convenient scalar for (i); add WX and XY for WY; for XZ go X → Y → Z, using YZ = −ZY; then apply Pythagoras to the components of XY.

guided_solution.instruction: Multiply WX by any scalar other than 1 to produce a parallel vector.
guided_solution.note: 2 × (5, −1) = (10, −2); any multiple such as (15, −3) or (−5, 1) also works

guided_solution.instruction: Add WX and XY component by component to get WY.
Reverse ZY to get YZ, since the route X → Y → Z needs YZ.
Add XY and YZ.
Apply Pythagoras to the components of XY.

app_sections.final_answer: (i) (10, −2) — any non-zero multiple of (5, −1) other than itself  (ii) WY = (2, 6)  (iii) XZ = (−11, 14)  (iv) |XY| = √58 ≈ 7.62 units
app_sections.why_it_works: Two vectors are parallel exactly when one is a scalar multiple of the other, so scaling the components keeps the direction and only changes the length. Adding vectors nose-to-tail cancels the middle letter — WX + XY leaves WY — which is why the components simply add. Reversing a vector flips the sign of both components, so ZY becomes YZ, and the magnitude is just the hypotenuse of the right triangle whose legs are the two components.
common_mistakes: Giving (5, −1) itself, or the zero vector, as the parallel vector.
Using ZY directly in the chain X → Y → Z instead of reversing it to YZ.
Adding an x-component to a y-component when the columns are written horizontally.
Squaring −3 as −9 when finding the magnitude.
app_sections.exam_tip: Write column-vector chains with the letters lined up (WX + XY = WY) and check that the inner letters match before you compute anything.

quick_check.prompt: If AB = (4, −3) and BC = (−1, 8), find AC and |AB|.

question.question_restated: OPQ is a triangle in which ARB and AOQ are straight lines. B is the midpoint of PQ, R is the midpoint of AB, R lies on OP with OR : RP = 1 : 3, OP = 4a and OQ = 8b. Find, in terms of a and/or b in simplest form: (iv) PQ, (v) PR, (vi) RB.

app_sections.think_first: Take O as origin: once you have the position vectors of P, Q, R and B, every answer is a subtraction.
concepts_required: Dividing a line in a given ratio
app_sections.strategy: Write PQ as OQ − OP, use OR : RP = 1 : 3 to get OR = (1/4)OP = a, find B as the midpoint of PQ, then subtract to get RB.

guided_solution.instruction: Subtract the position vectors of P and Q.
Use the ratio OR : RP = 1 : 3 to locate R on OP.
guided_solution.note: OR is one of four equal parts of OP, so OR = (1/4)(4a)

guided_solution.instruction: Find PR by subtracting the position vectors of P and R.
Find B, the midpoint of PQ, using the midpoint rule.
Subtract OR from OB to get RB.

app_sections.why_it_works: Choosing O as the origin turns every point into a position vector, and the vector from one point to another is always 'position of the finish minus position of the start'. A ratio of 1 : 3 along OP means OP is cut into four equal pieces, so OR is a quarter of OP. The midpoint rule is simply the average of the two end position vectors, which places B exactly halfway along PQ.
common_mistakes: Reading OR : RP = 1 : 3 as OR = (1/3)OP instead of (1/4)OP.
Writing PQ = OP − OQ and getting the sign of every term wrong.
Giving PR as 3a and forgetting the direction is from P back towards O.
Trying to find A first when B and R are enough to reach RB.

question.question_restated: O is the origin, OX = u and OY = v. OX and OY are extended so that X and Y are the midpoints of OA and OB respectively. (i) Express BX in terms of u and v. (ii) YA and BX intersect at M with BM = 2MX. (a) Express BM in terms of u and v. (b) Use a vector method to establish the ratio in which M divides YA.

app_sections.think_first: Because X and Y are midpoints, OA = 2u and OB = 2v — write those down first, and every other vector follows.
concepts_required: Dividing a line in a given ratio
Proving points lie on a line using parallel vectors
app_sections.strategy: Use OA = 2u and OB = 2v, build BX by subtraction, take two-thirds of it for BM, add to OB to get the position vector of M, then compare YM with YA.

guided_solution.instruction: Use the midpoint information to write OA and OB.
guided_solution.note: X is the midpoint of OA, so OA = 2 OX; Y is the midpoint of OB, so OB = 2 OY

guided_solution.instruction: Find BX by subtracting the position vectors of B and X.
Convert BM = 2MX into a fraction of BX. It means BM : MX = 2 : 1, so BM is two-thirds of BX.
Add BM to OB to reach M.
Find YM and YA and compare them.
guided_solution.note: YM = OM − OY = (2/3)u − (1/3)v; YA = OA − OY = 2u − v; so YM = (1/3)(2u − v)

guided_solution.instruction: Read off the division of YA. Since YM is one third of the whole of YA, the remaining part MA is two thirds.
guided_solution.result: M divides YA with YM : YA = 1 : 3, i.e. YM : MA = 1 : 2

app_sections.final_answer: (i) BX = u − 2v  (ii)(a) BM = (2/3)(u − 2v) = (2/3)u − (4/3)v  (b) OM = (2/3)u + (2/3)v, so YM = (2/3)u − (1/3)v = (1/3)(2u − v) = (1/3)YA. M therefore lies on YA with YM equal to one third of the whole line YA, that is YM : YA = 1 : 3 and YM : MA = 1 : 2.
app_sections.why_it_works: The midpoint conditions double u and v to reach A and B, so every point in the figure can be written with just those two vectors. Splitting BX in the ratio 2 : 1 fixes M as a single point, and its position vector then lets you test whether M lies on YA: because YM comes out as a pure scalar multiple of YA, M is on that line and the scalar is exactly the fraction of YA covered. Note carefully whether a ratio compares a part to the whole (YM : YA) or a part to the remaining part (YM : MA) — they are different statements of the same fact.
common_mistakes: Taking BM = (1/2)BX instead of (2/3)BX from BM = 2MX.
Writing BX = 2v − u by reversing the direction.
Confusing the part-to-whole ratio YM : YA = 1 : 3 with the part-to-part ratio YM : MA = 1 : 2.
Forgetting that X and Y are midpoints and using OA = u, OB = v.
app_sections.exam_tip: After finding a point's position vector, always test collinearity by writing one vector as a multiple of another — the multiple itself tells you the ratio.

quick_check.prompt: If BM = 3MX, what fraction of BX is BM?

answer_validation.independent_check_note: The vectors are right (YM = (1/3)YA so YM:MA = 1:2), but question_restated silently rewords printed part (b), which demands a proof that YM:MA = 1:3 - a false claim the answer quietly corrects rather than flags.

question.source_text: 8. Three points, 𝑂, 𝑃 and 𝑅, are shown on the grid below. 𝑂 is the origin. (iii) Write the position vector of 𝑅, 𝑂𝑅 ⃗⃗⃗⃗⃗ , in the form (𝑎 𝑏). (iv) Another point, 𝑄, is located in such a way that 𝑄𝑅 ⃗⃗⃗⃗⃗ = ( 2 −4). Using this information, plot the point 𝑄 on the graph. (v) Determine ∣𝑄𝑅 ⃗⃗⃗⃗⃗ ∣, the magnitude of 𝑄𝑅 ⃗⃗⃗⃗⃗ . (vi) Show, by calculation, that 𝑂𝑃𝑄𝑅 is a parallelogram.

question.question_restated: On the grid, O is the origin, P is the point (−2, 4) and R is the point (5, 1). (iii) Write the position vector OR as a column vector. (iv) Q is such that QR = (2, −4); plot Q. (v) Determine |QR|. (vi) Show by calculation that OPQR is a parallelogram.

app_sections.think_first: Read the coordinates straight off the grid, then remember that QR runs from Q to R — so to find Q you go backwards from R.
app_sections.strategy: Read OR from the grid, subtract QR from R's coordinates to locate Q, apply Pythagoras for the magnitude, then show a pair of opposite sides are equal vectors.

guided_solution.instruction: Read the coordinates of R from the grid and write them as a column vector.
guided_solution.note: R is 5 units right and 1 unit up from O

guided_solution.instruction: Since QR = OR − OQ, rearrange to OQ = OR − QR and substitute.
guided_solution.result: Q = (3, 5); plot the point 3 right and 5 up

guided_solution.instruction: Apply Pythagoras to the components of QR.
Write the vectors of one pair of opposite sides of OPQR.
State the conclusion. Equal vectors mean the sides are both parallel and of equal length.
guided_solution.note: Check the other pair too: PQ = (3, 5) − (−2, 4) = (5, 1) = OR
guided_solution.result: Both pairs of opposite sides are equal and parallel, so OPQR is a parallelogram

app_sections.final_answer: (iii) OR = (5, 1)  (iv) Q = (3, 5)  (v) |QR| = √20 = 2√5 ≈ 4.47 units  (vi) OP = (−2, 4) and RQ = (−2, 4), so OP = RQ; also PQ = (5, 1) = OR. Both pairs of opposite sides are equal in length and parallel, therefore OPQR is a parallelogram.
app_sections.why_it_works: A position vector is just the point's coordinates written as a column, so reading the grid gives OR directly. The vector QR is the displacement from Q to R, so undoing it from R lands you back on Q. Two sides of a quadrilateral being represented by identical column vectors means they have the same direction and the same length — and that is precisely the definition of a parallelogram.
common_mistakes: Adding QR to R instead of subtracting it, plotting Q at (7, −3).
Writing |QR| as 2 + (−4) or as √(2 − 4) instead of using squares.
Comparing OP with QR (which gives the negative) and concluding the sides are not equal — compare OP with RQ, or state that OP = −QR.
Leaving the answer as √20 when the question expects a simplified surd or a decimal.
app_sections.exam_tip: When testing a parallelogram with vectors, always take the two opposite sides in the same rotational direction round the shape, or the signs will fight you.

quick_check.prompt: A(1, 2), B(4, 3), C(6, 7), D(3, 6). Is ABCD a parallelogram?
quick_check.answer: AB = (3, 1) and DC = (3, 1), so AB = DC — yes, it is a parallelogram.
