question.question_restated: In the diagram O, M and N lie on a straight line with M the midpoint of ON, and P is a point above the line with OP = r and PM = s. (a)(i) Sketch the diagram and insert X on OM such that OX = (1/3)OM. (ii) Produce PX to Q such that PX = 4XQ. (b) Write in terms of r and s: (i) OM, (ii) PX, (iii) QM. (c) Show that PN = 2PM + OP.

app_sections.think_first: Only two vectors are given, r along OP and s along PM, so build the position vector of every other point out of those two before answering anything.
concepts_required: Vector addition and the triangle law
Dividing and extending a line in a given ratio
app_sections.strategy: Get OM = r + s from the route O → P → M, place X one third of the way along OM, extend PX by a quarter of its length to reach Q, and use MN = OM to prove the result in (c).

guided_solution.instruction: For the sketch, mark X on OM one third of the way from O to M, and extend the line from P through X to Q so that XQ is a quarter of PX.
guided_solution.note: OX : XM = 1 : 2, and Q lies beyond X on the same straight line as P and X
guided_solution.result: X and Q correctly placed on the sketch

guided_solution.instruction: Travel from O to M through P.
Find OX, then PX by going P → O → X.
Find XQ as a quarter of PX, then add it to OX to reach Q.
Subtract OQ from OM to obtain QM.
For part (c), use the fact that M is the midpoint of ON, so MN = OM = r + s.
guided_solution.note: PN = PM + MN = s + (r + s) = r + 2s, while 2PM + OP = 2s + r

app_sections.why_it_works: Because M is the midpoint of ON, the vector MN is identical to OM — same length, same direction — which is what makes part (c) collapse so neatly. Everything else is built by nose-to-tail addition: a route from one point to another can pass through any points whose vectors you already know, and the middle letters cancel. Splitting a segment in a ratio just means taking that fraction of the whole vector, and 'producing' a line means continuing in the same direction, so XQ keeps the direction of PX.
common_mistakes: Treating OM as r or as s alone instead of the sum r + s.
Reading PX = 4XQ as XQ = 4PX and stretching the line the wrong way.
Writing MN as −OM; M is the midpoint of ON, so MN points the same way as OM.
Slipping on the fraction arithmetic in QM — keep a common denominator of 12.
app_sections.exam_tip: When a question later says 'show that', work out both sides independently and finish by writing that they are equal — do not start by assuming the result.

quick_check.prompt: M is the midpoint of ON and OM = a + b. Write ON in terms of a and b.

question.question_restated: In triangle OAB, OA = r and OB = s. E is the midpoint of CD, OC = (3/4)OA and AD = (2/3)AB. Write, in terms of r and s in simplest form, an expression for (i) CD and (ii) OE.

app_sections.think_first: C is on OA and D is on AB, so find the position vector of each before attempting CD.
concepts_required: Dividing a line in a given ratio
app_sections.strategy: Write OC = (3/4)r, find AB then take two-thirds of it to locate D, subtract to get CD, and average OC and OD to get OE.

guided_solution.instruction: Write the position vector of C using OC = (3/4)OA.
Find AB, then AD as two-thirds of it, and add to OA to reach D.
Subtract OC from OD to get CD.
Use the midpoint rule on C and D to find OE.

app_sections.why_it_works: Taking O as origin means every named point has a position vector, and a vector between two points is always the difference of their position vectors. The fractions OC = (3/4)OA and AD = (2/3)AB place C and D exactly, and once both are in terms of r and s the subtraction is pure algebra. A midpoint is the average of the two ends, so OE follows immediately without needing to travel through C.
common_mistakes: Using AD = (2/3)OB instead of (2/3)AB — the fraction is of AB, not of a side from O.
Writing OD = (2/3)(s − r) and forgetting to add OA.
Careless fraction work: 1/3 − 3/4 is −5/12, not 5/12 or −2/12.
Taking OE as half of CD rather than the average of OC and OD.
app_sections.exam_tip: Convert every ratio or fraction into a position vector from the origin as soon as you read it; the rest of the question then becomes subtraction.

question.question_restated: In triangle OPQ, OP = 3u and OQ = v. Q is the midpoint of OR and M is the midpoint of PQ. L lies on OP with OL = (2/3)OP. (i) Write, in terms of u and v, an expression for a) LM and b) PR. (ii) Prove that L, M and R are collinear.

app_sections.think_first: Q being the midpoint of OR means OR = 2v — that single line makes the collinearity fall out at the end.
concepts_required: Dividing a line in a given ratio
app_sections.strategy: Write OL = 2u and OR = 2v, find M as the midpoint of PQ, then form LM and LR and show one is a multiple of the other.

guided_solution.instruction: Write OL and OR from the given conditions.
guided_solution.note: OL = (2/3)(3u) = 2u; Q is the midpoint of OR so OR = 2 OQ = 2v

guided_solution.instruction: Find OM using the midpoint rule on P and Q.
Subtract OL from OM to get LM.
Subtract OP from OR to get PR.
Form LR and compare it with LM.
State the conclusion.
guided_solution.note: LR is a scalar multiple of LM and both start at L
guided_solution.result: L, M and R are collinear

app_sections.final_answer: (i) a) LM = (1/2)(v − u) = (1/2)v − (1/2)u  b) PR = 2v − 3u  (ii) LR = 2v − 2u = 4 × (1/2)(v − u) = 4 LM. Since LR is a scalar multiple of LM and the two vectors share the point L, the points L, M and R lie on one straight line.
app_sections.why_it_works: Two vectors that are scalar multiples of each other point along the same direction; if they also start at the same point, that direction is a single straight line through all three points. The rest is bookkeeping: the midpoint rule places M, the fraction 2/3 places L, and the midpoint condition on OR doubles v to reach R.
common_mistakes: Using OR = v instead of 2v — Q is the midpoint of OR, not of OQ.
Writing OL = (2/3)u instead of (2/3)(3u) = 2u.
Comparing LM with MR but not tying the two vectors to a common point.
Stating 'parallel' as the conclusion instead of 'collinear'.
app_sections.exam_tip: For collinearity, pick the two vectors that share a vertex (here LM and LR) — comparing LM with MR works too but the shared-point wording is cleaner.

quick_check.answer: AC = 4 AB, and both start at A, so A, B and C are collinear.

question.question_restated: PQRS is a parallelogram with PQ = u and PS = v. M lies on QS with QM : MS = 1 : 2. (i) Write, in terms of u and v, an expression for a) QS and b) QM. (ii) Show that MR = (1/3)(u + 2v). (iii) T is the midpoint of PQ. Prove that R, M and T are collinear.

app_sections.think_first: In a parallelogram QR equals PS, so the diagonal PR is simply u + v — that is the key to reaching R.
concepts_required: Dividing a line in a given ratio
app_sections.strategy: Build QS by the route Q → P → S, take one third of it for QM, use PR = u + v to reach R, then subtract position vectors to get MR and MT and compare them.

guided_solution.instruction: Travel from Q to S through P.
Take one third of QS, since QM : MS = 1 : 2 splits QS into three equal parts.
Find the position vectors of M and R relative to P. In the parallelogram QR = PS = v, so PR = PQ + QR.
Subtract PM from PR to obtain MR.
Find MT, using PT = (1/2)u since T is the midpoint of PQ.
Compare MR and MT.
guided_solution.result: MR = −2 MT, so R, M and T are collinear (with RM : MT = 2 : 1)

app_sections.final_answer: (i) a) QS = v − u  b) QM = (1/3)(v − u)  (ii) PM = (2/3)u + (1/3)v and PR = u + v, so MR = PR − PM = (1/3)u + (2/3)v = (1/3)(u + 2v)  (iii) MT = −(1/6)(u + 2v) = −(1/2)MR, so MR = −2 MT. The vectors MR and MT are parallel and share the point M, therefore R, M and T are collinear, with RM : MT = 2 : 1.
app_sections.why_it_works: In a parallelogram opposite sides are equal vectors, so QR = PS = v and the diagonal PR is just the sum of the two side vectors. Once every point is expressed from the single origin P, each required vector is a difference of position vectors. The negative scalar linking MR and MT simply means M lies between R and T on the line — the vectors point in opposite directions from M, which is exactly what collinearity through an interior point looks like.
common_mistakes: Writing QS = u − v by going S to Q instead of Q to S.
Taking QM = (1/2)QS because the ratio 1 : 2 was misread as a half.
Using QR = u instead of v — in PQRS the side QR matches PS.
Being thrown by the minus sign in MR = −2MT and concluding the points are not collinear.
app_sections.exam_tip: Pick one point as your origin (here P) and write every other point's position vector from it; almost all parallelogram vector questions then reduce to subtraction.

app_sections.why_it_works: Each entry of a matrix product is the sum of products of a row of the first matrix with the column of the second, so setting a product equal to the zero matrix gives one ordinary equation per entry. For simultaneous equations, writing them as AX = B lets you undo the multiplication by A: multiplying both sides on the left by A inverse leaves X on its own, and the inverse exists exactly when the determinant is not zero.

question.question_restated: W = (3  6 / -2  5). (a)(i) Find the 2x2 matrix L such that W + L is the zero matrix. (ii) Find the 2x2 matrix P such that WP is the identity matrix. (b) A right-angled triangle M has vertices X(1, 1), Y(3, 1) and Z(3, 4). M is transformed by the matrix N = (0  1 / 1  0) to give the image M'. Find the coordinates of the vertices of M'.

app_sections.think_first: L is the additive inverse of W and P is the multiplicative inverse of W, so one part needs sign changes and the other needs a determinant.
app_sections.strategy: Write L as the negative of W, compute the inverse of W for P using the determinant and adjugate, then multiply N by each vertex written as a column matrix.

guided_solution.instruction: For L, change the sign of every element of W so that each pair adds to zero.
For P, note that WP = I means P is the inverse of W, so first find det W.
Swap the leading diagonal entries, change the sign of the other two, and divide by the determinant.
For (b), write each vertex as a column matrix and multiply on the left by N.
State the image triangle.
guided_solution.note: N = (0  1 / 1  0) swaps the two coordinates, which is a reflection in the line y = x.

app_sections.why_it_works: Adding matrices works entry by entry, so the matrix that cancels W must be the one whose entries are the negatives of W's. Multiplication is different: WP = I says P undoes W, and for a 2x2 matrix that inverse is the adjugate divided by the determinant. Transforming a point means multiplying its position vector, written as a column, by the transformation matrix, which is why the image coordinates come out one vertex at a time.
common_mistakes: Confusing the additive inverse with the multiplicative inverse and giving L as the inverse of W.
Dividing by the wrong determinant, for example 15 - 12 = 3 instead of 15 + 12 = 27.
Writing the vertices as row matrices and multiplying in the wrong order.
Leaving P without the factor 1/27.

app_sections.think_first: AB is a 2x2 times a 2x3, so it is 2x3 and can then be added to C, which is also 2x3.
concepts_required: Determinant and inverse of a 2x2 matrix
app_sections.strategy: Multiply A by B row into column to get a 2x3 matrix, add C entry by entry, then find det A and use the adjugate formula for the inverse; the last part follows from the definition of an inverse.

guided_solution.instruction: Multiply the first row of A into each column of B.
Multiply the second row of A into each column of B.
Add C to AB entry by entry.
Find the determinant of A and then its inverse.
State the product A times A inverse.
guided_solution.note: By definition a matrix multiplied by its inverse gives the identity, and you can verify it: (3)(2) + (2)(-2.5) = 1 and (3)(-1) + (2)(1.5) = 0.

app_sections.final_answer: (ix) AB + C = (22  -3  22 / 39  -1  33)  (x) A inverse = (1/2)(4  -2 / -5  3) = (2  -1 / -2.5  1.5)  (xi) A times A inverse = (1  0 / 0  1), the 2x2 identity matrix.
app_sections.why_it_works: Multiplication is only defined when the inner dimensions agree, and the product keeps the outer ones, so a 2x2 times a 2x3 is 2x3 and can legitimately be added to the 2x3 matrix C, since addition requires matching orders. The inverse of a 2x2 matrix is built from the adjugate over the determinant precisely so that multiplying it by the original returns the identity, the matrix that leaves every other matrix unchanged.
common_mistakes: Trying to add C to A before multiplying, which is impossible because their orders differ.
Stopping AB after two columns and producing a 2x2 matrix.
Negating the leading diagonal rather than the other diagonal when forming the inverse.
Working out A times A inverse by long multiplication and making an arithmetic slip instead of quoting the identity.
app_sections.exam_tip: For 'write down' parts, no working is expected; recognising that A times A inverse is always the identity earns the mark instantly.

quick_check.prompt: Find the inverse of (3  2 / 5  4) and state its determinant.

question.source_text: 12. Given the linear equations 2𝑥+ 5𝑦= 6 3𝑥+ 4𝑦= 8 (i) Write the equations in the form 𝐴𝑋= 𝐵where 𝐴, 𝑋and 𝐵are matrices. (ii) a) Calculate the determinant of the matrix 𝐴. b) Show that 𝐴−1 = ( −4 7 5 7 3 7 −2 7 ) .
question.display_policy: Render verified structured mathematics when available; always retain the linked source visual for fidelity.
question.question_restated: Given the linear equations 2x + 5y = 6 and 3x + 4y = 8: (i) write them in the form AX = B where A, X and B are matrices; (ii) a) calculate the determinant of A, b) show that A inverse = (-4/7  5/7 / 3/7  -2/7), c) use A inverse to solve for x and y.

app_sections.think_first: The coefficients form A, the unknowns form X and the constants form B, in that order, so the matrix form writes itself.
concepts_required: Solving AX = B by X = A inverse times B
app_sections.strategy: Build A, X and B from the equations, compute the determinant, form the adjugate and divide to verify the given inverse, then multiply that inverse by B to obtain x and y.

guided_solution.instruction: Read the coefficients into a 2x2 matrix, the unknowns into a column and the constants into a column.
guided_solution.note: Keep the equations in the order given so the rows match.

guided_solution.instruction: Calculate the determinant of A.
Form the adjugate and divide by the determinant to verify the given inverse.
Multiply the inverse by B to find X.
State and check the solution.

app_sections.why_it_works: Multiplying out AX reproduces the left-hand sides of the two equations, which is why the matrix form is equivalent to the original pair. Multiplying both sides of AX = B on the left by A inverse gives (A inverse A)X = A inverse B, and since A inverse A is the identity this isolates X. The negative determinant is not a problem: it simply flips the sign of every entry of the adjugate, which is exactly the pattern of signs in the given inverse.
common_mistakes: Placing the constants inside A or writing X as a row matrix.
Losing the minus sign of the determinant and getting the inverse with all signs reversed.
Multiplying B by A inverse in the wrong order.
Converting 16/7 to a rounded decimal when an exact fraction is expected.
app_sections.exam_tip: When a 'show that' gives you the inverse, still derive it yourself; you can then use the printed version with confidence in the next part even if your own arithmetic wobbled.

quick_check.prompt: Write 4x - y = 3 and x + 2y = 5 in the form AX = B.
